questions.explanation: Power rule: integral of x^n dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1). Always evaluate upper minus lower bound.
questions.question: Evaluate the definite integral from 0 to 3 of 2x dx.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Integral Calculus section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\int_0^3 2x\,dx\). The power rule gives the antiderivative:

$$\int 2x\,dx = x^2 + C$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to evaluate the definite integral:

$$\begin{aligned}
F(x) &= x^2 \\
a &= 0 \\
b &= 3
\end{aligned}$$

$$\left(\int_0^3 2x\,dx\right) = F(3) - F(0) \rightarrow (3)^2 - (0)^2 = 9 - 0$$

$$\int_0^3 2x\,dx = 9$$
questions.videoTitle: FE Civil Exam Mathematics: Integrals Problem 3 a,3 b &3 c (Easy, Medium & Hard)

questions.explanation: The classic 3-4-5 triangle appears constantly in statics. Recognizing Pythagorean triples saves time.
questions.question: Two perpendicular forces of 3 N and 4 N act at a point. What is the magnitude of their resultant?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Resultant (Two Dimensions) section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(R\). For perpendicular concurrent forces, the resultant follows the Pythagorean relationship:

$$R = \sqrt{F_1^2 + F_2^2}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(R\):

$$\begin{aligned}
F_1 &= 3\ \text{N} \\
F_2 &= 4\ \text{N} \\
R &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(R) = \sqrt{(3)^2 + (4)^2} \rightarrow (R) = \sqrt{9 + 16}$$

$$(R) = \sqrt{25} = 5\ \text{N}$$
questions.videoTitle: How to Find the Resultant of Three Force Vectors – Statics Components and Resultants Problem 18

questions.explanation: Hydrostatic pressure depends only on depth and fluid unit weight: p = gamma*h. Roughly 10 m of water ≈ 1 atm.
questions.question: What is the gage pressure at a depth of 10 m in water? (unit weight of water = 9.81 kN/m^3)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Pressure Field in a Static Liquid section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(p\). Gage pressure varies hydrostatically with depth according to:

$$p = \gamma h$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(p\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\gamma &= 9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3 \\
h &= 10\ \text{m} \\
p &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(p) = (\gamma)(h) \rightarrow (p) = (9.81)(10)$$

$$(p) = 98.1\ \text{kPa (gage)}$$
questions.videoTitle: Estimate the pressure needed to raise a column of water to the same height as a 35-m-tall oak tree.

questions.explanation: Single-payment compound amount factor: (F/P, i%, n) = (1+i)^n. Don't confuse with simple interest ($1,100).
questions.question: $1,000 is invested at 5% annual interest, compounded annually. What is the future worth after 2 years?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(F\). We can determine \(F\) from the single-payment compound amount factor:

$$F = P(1+i)^n$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(F\):

$$\begin{aligned}
P &= \$1{,}000 \\
i &= 5\% = 0.05 \\
n &= 2\ \text{years} \\
F &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(F) = (P)(1+i)^n \rightarrow (F) = (1{,}000)(1.05)^2$$

$$(F) = (1{,}000)(1.1025) = \$1{,}102.50$$
questions.videoTitle: Simple and Compound Interest Explained

questions.explanation: 1 N/mm^2 = 1 MPa. Unit consistency is the most common error — convert kN to N before dividing by mm^2.
questions.question: An axial tensile load of 10 kN acts on a bar with cross-sectional area 100 mm^2. What is the axial stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Uniaxial Loading and Deformation section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\sigma\), the axial stress:

$$\sigma = \frac{P}{A}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\sigma\):

$$\begin{aligned}
P &= 10\ \text{kN} = 10000\ \text{N} \\
A &= 100\ \text{mm}^2 \\
\sigma &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\sigma) = \frac{P}{A} \rightarrow (\sigma) = \frac{10000}{100}$$

$$(\sigma) = 100\ \text{N/mm}^2 = 100\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.videoTitle: [PSAD] Strength of Materials: Axial Stress & Strain

choices: Protect the public health, safety, and welfare
Maintain client confidentiality above all else
questions.explanation: Ethics questions on the FE almost always test this hierarchy: public safety first, then client, then profession.
questions.question: According to standard engineering codes of ethics, an engineer's foremost obligation is to:
questions.solution:
The NSPE Code of Ethics states that engineers shall hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public.

This duty outranks every other obligation: responsibilities to clients, employers, and the profession itself all come second. Maximizing client profit, minimizing project cost, and guarding confidentiality are real duties, but none of them may override public safety.

Therefore the engineer's foremost obligation is to protect the public health, safety, and welfare.

questions.question: A 2 kg mass accelerates at 3 m/s². What is the net force acting on it?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Particle Kinetics section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(F\). Newton's second law relates net force to mass and acceleration:

$$F = ma$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(F\):

$$\begin{aligned}
m &= 2\ \text{kg} \\
a &= 3\ \text{m/s}^2 \\
F &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(F) = (2)(3)$$

$$(F) = 6\ \text{N}$$
questions.explanation: F = ma is the single most-used equation in dynamics. Keep mass in kg and acceleration in m/s² to get newtons directly.
questions.videoTitle: F=ma Rectangular Coordinates

questions.question: Which material property measures a material's stiffness — its resistance to elastic deformation?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Properties of Materials section in the Materials Science/Structure of Matter chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Stiffness is resistance to elastic deformation, governed by Hooke's law in the elastic region, \(\sigma = E\epsilon\). The constant of proportionality \(E\) — the modulus of elasticity (Young's modulus), the slope of the stress–strain curve in the elastic region — is therefore the property that measures stiffness: a higher \(E\) means a stiffer material.

Yield strength marks the onset of permanent deformation, ductility measures the capacity for plastic deformation, and hardness measures resistance to surface indentation — none of them measures elastic stiffness.

The modulus of elasticity is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: Don't confuse stiffness (E, elastic) with strength (stress at yield or fracture). Steel's E ≈ 200 GPa regardless of its grade.

questions.question: A level is set up between a benchmark (elevation 100.00 m) and a turning point. The backsight reads 1.25 m and the foresight reads 0.85 m. What is the turning point's elevation?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the turning point elevation. First find the height of instrument:

$$HI = Elev_{BM} + BS$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
Elev_{BM} &= 100.00\ \text{m} \\
BS &= 1.25\ \text{m} \\
FS &= 0.85\ \text{m} \\
Elev_{TP} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(HI) = 100.00 + 1.25 = 101.25\ \text{m}$$

The turning point elevation is the height of instrument minus the foresight:

$$Elev_{TP} = HI - FS$$

$$(Elev_{TP}) = 101.25 - 0.85$$

$$(Elev_{TP}) = 100.40\ \text{m}$$
questions.explanation: HI = BM + backsight; new elevation = HI − foresight. Backsights go up, foresights come down — the classic leveling mantra.
questions.videoTitle: Survey Leveling Calculations and Adjustment

questions.question: A simply supported beam 6 m long carries a uniform load of 2 kN/m over its full length. What is the maximum bending moment?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Structural Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(M_{\max}\). For a simply supported beam carrying a uniform load over its full length:

$$M_{\max} = \frac{wL^2}{8}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(M_{\max}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
w &= 2\ \text{kN/m} \\
L &= 6\ \text{m} \\
M_{\max} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(M_{\max}) = \frac{wL^2}{8} \rightarrow (M_{\max}) = \frac{(2)(6)^2}{8}$$

$$(M_{\max}) = \frac{72}{8} = 9\ \text{kN}\cdot\text{m}$$

The maximum occurs at midspan.
questions.explanation: wL²/8 (uniform load) and PL/4 (center point load) on a simply supported beam are the two moment formulas to memorize cold.
questions.videoTitle: How to Draw Shear Force and Moment Diagrams

questions.question: At a point in saturated soil, the total vertical stress is 200 kPa and the pore water pressure is 80 kPa. What is the vertical effective stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Effective Stress section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\sigma'\). Terzaghi's effective stress principle:

$$\sigma' = \sigma - u$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\sigma'\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\sigma &= 200\ \text{kPa} \\
u &= 80\ \text{kPa} \\
\sigma' &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\sigma') = (200) - (80)$$

$$(\sigma') = 120\ \text{kPa}$$
questions.explanation: Terzaghi's effective stress principle: soil strength and settlement depend on effective stress, not total stress. Pore pressure carries none of the grain-to-grain load.
questions.videoTitle: Effective Stress Principle

questions.question: Which of the following does NOT affect the stopping sight distance required on a highway?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Stopping Sight Distance section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

The governing relationship is the AASHTO stopping sight distance equation:

$$SSD = 1.47Vt + \frac{V^2}{30(f \pm G)}$$

Design speed \(V\), perception–reaction time \(t\), the friction coefficient \(f\), and grade \(G\) all appear in it. Pavement color appears nowhere in the physics of stopping — it affects neither the distance traveled during perception–reaction time nor the braking distance.

Pavement color is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: SSD = reaction distance + braking distance. Uphill grades shorten it, downhill grades lengthen it — grade matters, color doesn't.

questions.question: Water flows at 2 m/s through a circular pipe with a diameter of 0.5 m. What is the discharge?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Continuity Equation section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(Q\), the discharge:

$$Q = AV \quad\text{with}\quad A = \frac{\pi D^2}{4}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(Q\):

$$\begin{aligned}
D &= 0.5\ \text{m} \\
V &= 2\ \text{m/s} \\
A &= ? \\
Q &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(A) = \frac{\pi (0.5)^2}{4} = 0.1963\ \text{m}^2$$

$$(Q) = (A)(V) \rightarrow (Q) = (0.1963)(2)$$

$$(Q) = 0.393\ \text{m}^3\text{/s}$$
questions.explanation: Q = AV is the continuity equation — the starting point of nearly every water resources problem. Watch the diameter-vs-radius trap.

questions.question: In a CPM (critical path method) schedule, what is the total float of any activity on the critical path?
questions.solution:
The critical path is the longest-duration path through the project network, and it defines the minimum possible project duration.

Total float is the amount an activity can be delayed without delaying the project. By definition, no activity on the longest path has any scheduling slack — any delay to a critical-path activity delays project completion by the same amount.

Therefore the total float of any activity on the critical path is zero.
questions.explanation: The critical path is the longest path through the network and defines the minimum project duration. Zero float is its defining feature.

questions.question: Events A and B are independent. If P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.5, what is P(A and B)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Laws of Probability section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(P(A \text{ and } B)\). For independent events:

$$P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(P(A \cap B)\):

$$\begin{aligned}
P(A) &= 0.4 \\
P(B) &= 0.5 \\
P(A \cap B) &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(P) = (0.4)(0.5)$$

$$(P) = 0.2$$
questions.explanation: 'And' means multiply (for independent events); 'or' means add (minus the overlap). Confirming independence is the step most people skip.
questions.videoTitle: Introduction to Probability, Basic Overview - Sample Space, & Tree Diagrams

questions.question: What is the derivative of f(x) = 3x² with respect to x?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Differential Calculus section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(f'(x)\). The governing rule is the power rule:

$$\frac{d}{dx}(x^n) = nx^{n-1}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
f(x) &= 3x^2 \\
n &= 2 \\
f'(x) &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(f'(x)) = (3)(2)x^{2-1} = 6x^{1}$$

$$(f'(x)) = 6x$$
questions.explanation: Power rule: bring the exponent down, subtract one. It's the inverse of the power rule for integration — know both directions.
questions.videoTitle: Civil FEexam review: Mathematics - derivatives and double derivatives

questions.question: What is the present worth of $1,102.50 to be received 2 years from now, at 5% annual interest compounded annually?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(P\), the present worth of $1,102.50 received 2 years from now at 5% annual interest:

$$P = \frac{F}{(1+i)^n}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(P\):

$$\begin{aligned}
F &= 1102.50\ \text{(future amount)} \\
i &= 0.05\ \text{/yr} \\
n &= 2\ \text{yr} \\
P &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(P) = \frac{1102.50}{(1+0.05)^2} \rightarrow (P) = \frac{1102.50}{1.1025}$$

$$(P) = \$1000.00$$
questions.explanation: Present worth discounts the future back to today — the mirror image of the compound amount factor (F/P, i%, n).
questions.videoTitle: Simple and Compound Interest Explained

questions.question: A 2 m steel bar (E = 200 GPa) with cross-sectional area 100 mm² carries a 10 kN axial tensile load. How much does it elongate?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Uniaxial Loading and Deformation section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\delta\). Axial elongation under a tensile load is:

$$\delta = \frac{PL}{AE}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\delta\):

$$\begin{aligned}
P &= 10\ \text{kN} = 10{,}000\ \text{N} \\
L &= 2\ \text{m} = 2{,}000\ \text{mm} \\
A &= 100\ \text{mm}^2 \\
E &= 200\ \text{GPa} = 200{,}000\ \text{N/mm}^2 \\
\delta &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\delta) = \frac{PL}{AE} \rightarrow (\delta) = \frac{(10{,}000)(2{,}000)}{(100)(200{,}000)}$$

$$(\delta) = \frac{20{,}000{,}000}{20{,}000{,}000} = 1.0\ \text{mm}$$
questions.explanation: δ = PL/AE: keep P in N, L and A in consistent mm units, and E in N/mm² (= MPa × 1000). Unit consistency is where these problems are won or lost.
questions.videoTitle: [PSAD] Strength of Materials: Axial Stress & Strain

questions.explanation: Systems of two equations appear across statics, fluids, and circuits. The common pitfall is solving for only one variable and forgetting to back-substitute for the other.
questions.question: Solve the system of equations: 2x + y = 7 and x - y = -1. What is the solution?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(x\) and \(y\):

$$\begin{aligned}
2x + y &= 7 \\
x - y &= -1
\end{aligned}$$

Adding the equations eliminates \(y\):

$$(2x + y) + (x - y) = 7 + (-1) \rightarrow 3x = 6 \rightarrow x = 2$$

Back-substitute \(x = 2\) into \(2x + y = 7\):

$$(y) = 7 - 2(2) = 3$$

Check in the second equation: \(x - y = 2 - 3 = -1\). Correct.

$$x = 2, \quad y = 3$$
questions.videoTitle: Cramer's Rule

questions.explanation: Recognizing special matrix forms saves time on the FE. The determinant of any triangular matrix is just the product of its diagonal - a full cofactor expansion is wasted work here.
questions.question: What is the determinant of the matrix [[2, 1, 3], [0, 4, 1], [0, 0, 5]]?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Determinants section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\det(A)\). The matrix is upper triangular — every entry below the main diagonal is zero — so its determinant is the product of the diagonal entries:

$$\det(A) = a_{11}a_{22}a_{33}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
a_{11} &= 2 \\
a_{22} &= 4 \\
a_{33} &= 5 \\
\det(A) &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\det A) = (2)(4)(5)$$

$$(\det A) = 40$$

questions.explanation: Partial derivatives underpin multivariable optimization and sensitivity analysis. The typical slip is accidentally differentiating with respect to the wrong variable or forgetting to treat the other variable as a constant.
questions.question: For the function \(f(x, y) = x^2y + 3xy^2\), what is the partial derivative of \(f\) with respect to \(x\), evaluated at the point \((2, 1)\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the The Partial Derivative section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\) at the point \((2, 1)\). Differentiate term by term, treating \(y\) as a constant:

$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 2xy + 3y^2$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
x &= 2 \\
y &= 1 \\
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right) = 2(2)(1) + 3(1)^2 \rightarrow \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right) = 4 + 3$$

$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 7$$
questions.videoTitle: Civil FEexam review: Mathematics - derivatives and double derivatives

questions.explanation: Separable ODEs model simple rate processes (e.g., a velocity that grows linearly with time). The common mistake is dropping the constant of integration or failing to use the initial condition to find it.
questions.question: Solve the differential equation \(\frac{dy}{dx} = 2x\) with the initial condition \(y(0) = 1\). What is \(y(2)\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Differential Equations section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(y(2)\). This is a separable first-order equation:

$$\frac{dy}{dx} = 2x \quad\Rightarrow\quad dy = 2x\,dx$$

Integrating both sides:

$$y = \int 2x\,dx = x^2 + C$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(y(2)\):

$$\begin{aligned}
y(0) &= 1 \\
C &= ? \\
y(2) &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Apply the initial condition: \(y(0) = 0^2 + C = 1\), so \(C = 1\) and \(y = x^2 + 1\).

$$(y(2)) = (2)^2 + 1 = 5$$
questions.videoTitle: Separable Differential Equations - Fundamentals of Engineering FE EIT Exam Review

questions.explanation: Dot products test orthogonality and compute work (force dot displacement) in statics and dynamics. Watch the signs - a single missed negative flips the answer, which is why -2 and 10 are tempting traps.
questions.question: What is the dot product of vectors a = (3, -1, 2) and b = (2, 4, 1)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vectors section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}\). The dot product sums the products of corresponding components:

$$\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = a_x b_x + a_y b_y + a_z b_z$$

List the known components:

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{a} &= (3, -1, 2) \\
\mathbf{b} &= (2, 4, 1)
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}) = (3)(2) + (-1)(4) + (2)(1) \rightarrow 6 - 4 + 2$$

$$(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}) = 4$$
questions.videoTitle: Dot Product of Two Vectors

questions.explanation: Eigenvalues show up in vibration analysis, stability, and principal stresses. A frequent error is forgetting to subtract the off-diagonal product (ad - bc term), which changes the characteristic equation entirely.
questions.question: What is the largest eigenvalue of the matrix [[5, 2], [2, 2]]?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Matrices section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the eigenvalues \(\lambda\) of \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\). They are the roots of the characteristic equation:

$$\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\lambda &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$((5-\lambda)(2-\lambda) - (2)(2)) = 0 \rightarrow (\lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 6) = 0$$

Factoring gives \((\lambda - 6)(\lambda - 1) = 0\), so \(\lambda = 6\) or \(\lambda = 1\):

$$(\lambda_{\max}) = 6$$

questions.explanation: Concrete strength acceptance is judged on statistics, not single tests. Students often grab the mean (8.8) or the mode (7) instead of the median - for even-n datasets, the median is the average of the two middle values.
questions.question: The measured strengths (in MPa) of six concrete test cylinders are: 4, 7, 7, 9, 12, 14. What is the median of this dataset?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Dispersion, Mean, Median, and Mode Values section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the median. With an even number of observations, the median is the average of the two middle values:

$$\text{median} = \frac{x_{(n/2)} + x_{(n/2+1)}}{2}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
n &= 6 \\
x_{(3)} &= 7\ \text{MPa} \\
x_{(4)} &= 9\ \text{MPa} \\
\text{median} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\text{median}) = \frac{7 + 9}{2}$$

$$(\text{median}) = 8\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.videoTitle: Statistics Basics: Mean, Median, Mode, Range & Standard Deviation Explained!

questions.explanation: Binomial models count successes in fixed trials - bids won, welds passing inspection, etc. The most common error is forgetting the combinatorial coefficient C(n,k); without it you get 0.002, which badly underestimates the probability.
questions.question: A construction firm estimates each bid it submits has a 30% chance of being accepted, independently of other bids. If it submits 10 bids, what is the probability that exactly 3 are accepted?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Binomial Distribution section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(P(X = 3)\). Each bid is an independent trial with the same success probability, so the count of acceptances is binomial:

$$P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(P(X = 3)\):

$$\begin{aligned}
n &= 10 \\
p &= 0.30 \\
k &= 3 \\
P(X = 3) &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(P) = \binom{10}{3}(0.3)^3(0.7)^7 \rightarrow (P) = (120)(0.027)(0.0823543)$$

$$(P) = 0.2668 \approx 0.267$$
questions.videoTitle: Finding The Probability of a Binomial Distribution Plus Mean & Standard Deviation

questions.explanation: The normal distribution is the workhorse for quality control and reliability. Mixing up the tail area (15.9%) with the area between the mean and z = 1 (34.1%) is the classic mistake.
questions.question: Compressive test results for a concrete mix are normally distributed with a mean of 100 MPa and a standard deviation of 15 MPa. Approximately what percentage of samples exceed 115 MPa?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Normal Distribution (Gaussian Distribution) section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must find the percentage of samples exceeding 115 MPa. Standardize with the z-score:

$$z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(z\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\mu &= 100\ \text{MPa} \\
\sigma &= 15\ \text{MPa} \\
x &= 115\ \text{MPa} \\
z &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(z) = \frac{115 - 100}{15} = 1$$

The area beyond \(z = 1\) (one standard deviation above the mean) is \(1 - \Phi(1) = 1 - 0.8413 = 0.1587\):

$$P(x > 115) \approx 15.9\%$$
questions.videoTitle: Statistics 6.3 – Finding Probability Using a Normal Distribution

questions.explanation: This is the base-rate fallacy in action: even an excellent test yields mostly false positives when the condition is rare. Engineers making inspection decisions must account for the prior - a positive result here still means only about 1 in 6 members is truly cracked.
questions.question: A bridge inspection test detects cracks with 99% sensitivity (P(positive | crack) = 0.99) and 95% specificity (P(negative | no crack) = 0.95). If 1% of inspected members actually have cracks, what is the probability a member has a crack given a positive test result?
questions.solution:
Refer to Bayes' Theorem in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(P(\text{crack} \mid \text{positive})\):

$$P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A)P(A)}{P(B)}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
P(\text{positive} \mid \text{crack}) &= 0.99 \\
P(\text{positive} \mid \text{no crack}) &= 1 - 0.95 = 0.05 \\
P(\text{crack}) &= 0.01 \\
P(\text{crack} \mid \text{positive}) &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Expand the denominator by the law of total probability:

$$(P(\text{positive})) = (0.99)(0.01) + (0.05)(0.99) \rightarrow (P(\text{positive})) = 0.0099 + 0.0495 = 0.0594$$

$$(P(\text{crack} \mid \text{positive})) = \frac{0.0099}{0.0594} = 0.1667 \approx 16.7\%$$
questions.videoTitle: 3 Word Problems to Master the Bayes' Theorem

questions.explanation: Know whether a problem wants population (divide by n) or sample (divide by n - 1) statistics - here 2.14 is the sample standard deviation, a designed distractor. Also, 4 is the variance, not the standard deviation.
questions.question: The daily rainfall totals (in cm) recorded over 8 days are: 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9. What is the population standard deviation of this dataset?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Dispersion, Mean, Median, and Mode Values section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the population standard deviation (divide by \(n\), not \(n - 1\)):

$$\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \mu)^2}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
n &= 8 \\
\mu &= \frac{40}{8} = 5\ \text{cm} \\
\sigma &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\sigma) = \sqrt{\frac{9 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 4 + 16}{8}} = \sqrt{\frac{32}{8}} = \sqrt{4}$$

$$(\sigma) = 2\ \text{cm}$$
questions.videoTitle: Statistics Basics: Mean, Median, Mode, Range & Standard Deviation Explained!

questions.explanation: Confidence intervals quantify uncertainty in field measurements like compaction. The two classic slips are using n instead of sqrt(n) in the standard error, or rounding z to 2 and then mismatching the stated precision.
questions.question: A sample of 25 soil compaction tests has a mean dry density of 50 pcf and a standard deviation of 10 pcf. What is the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval for the true mean dry density? (Use z = 1.96.)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Confidence Intervals section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval for the true mean:

$$\bar{x} \pm z\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for the lower bound:

$$\begin{aligned}
\bar{x} &= 50\ \text{pcf} \\
s &= 10\ \text{pcf} \\
n &= 25 \\
z &= 1.96\ \text{(95\% confidence)} \\
\text{lower bound} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Standard error: \(s/\sqrt{n} = 10/5 = 2\). Margin: \(1.96 \times 2 = 3.92\).

$$(\text{lower bound}) = 50 - 3.92 = 46.08 \approx 46.1\ \text{pcf}$$
questions.videoTitle: Statistics 101: Confidence Interval Estimation, Sigma Known

questions.explanation: Sampling without replacement (grab samples, inspection lots) changes the denominator on each draw. The distractor 0.391 comes from treating the draws as independent, i.e., (5/8)^2 - with replacement, which is the wrong model here.
questions.question: A grab bag contains 5 red and 3 blue soil sample tags. Two tags are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Laws of Probability section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(P(\text{both red})\). Sampling is without replacement, so the denominator changes on the second draw:

$$P = P(\text{1st red}) \cdot P(\text{2nd red} \mid \text{1st red})$$

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Red tags} &= 5 \\
\text{Blue tags} &= 3 \\
\text{Total tags} &= 8
\end{aligned}$$

After drawing one red tag, 4 red and 3 blue remain out of 7 total:

$$(P) = \left(\frac{5}{8}\right)\left(\frac{4}{7}\right) = \frac{20}{56}$$

$$(P) = 0.357$$
questions.videoTitle: Introduction to Probability, Basic Overview - Sample Space, & Tree Diagrams

questions.explanation: Nominal rates understate the true cost whenever compounding is more frequent than annual. On the FE, always convert a nominal rate to the effective rate for the payment period before using any interest factor - forgetting this step is a guaranteed point lost.
questions.question: A credit card charges a nominal annual interest rate of 12%, compounded monthly. What is the effective annual interest rate?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the effective annual rate \(i_{\text{eff}}\). A nominal rate compounded \(m\) times per year converts by:

$$i_{\text{eff}} = \left(1 + \frac{r}{m}\right)^m - 1$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
r &= 12\% = 0.12 \\
m &= 12\ \text{(monthly)} \\
i_{\text{eff}} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(i_{\text{eff}}) = \left(1 + \frac{0.12}{12}\right)^{12} - 1 \rightarrow (i_{\text{eff}}) = (1.01)^{12} - 1$$

$$(i_{\text{eff}}) = 1.126825 - 1 = 0.126825 = 12.68\%$$
questions.videoTitle: Interest Rate Explained — Nominal, Period, Effective

questions.explanation: The P/A factor converts recurring annual costs (maintenance, operations) to a single present value for comparison. Common errors: using the future worth factor instead, or confusing this with a gradient series.
questions.question: What is the present worth of a uniform series of $100 per year for 10 years at an interest rate of 8% per year?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Uniform Series section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(P\), the present worth, using the uniform series present worth factor:

$$P = A(P/A, i, n) = A\frac{(1+i)^n - 1}{i(1+i)^n}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
A &= 100\ \text{/yr} \\
i &= 0.08\ \text{/yr} \\
n &= 10\ \text{yr} \\
P &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(P/A, 8\%, 10) = \frac{(1.08)^{10} - 1}{0.08(1.08)^{10}} = \frac{1.158925}{0.172714} = 6.7101$$

$$(P) = (100)(6.7101) = \$671.01 \approx \$671$$

questions.explanation: Depreciation affects after-tax cash flows and equipment replacement decisions. The trap answer $27,778 comes from depreciating the full $50,000 without subtracting salvage value - salvage is never depreciated.
questions.question: A piece of construction equipment costs $50,000, has a salvage value of $5,000, and a useful life of 9 years. Using straight-line depreciation, what is the book value of the equipment at the end of year 4?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Depreciation section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the book value at the end of year 4. Straight-line depreciation charges the same amount each year:

$$D = \frac{\text{Cost} - \text{Salvage}}{\text{Life}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for the book value:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Cost} &= \$50{,}000 \\
\text{Salvage} &= \$5{,}000 \\
\text{Life} &= 9\ \text{years} \\
BV_4 &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Annual depreciation: \((D) = (50{,}000 - 5{,}000)/9 = \$5{,}000\text{/year}\).

Accumulated depreciation after 4 years: \(4 \times 5{,}000 = \$20{,}000\).

$$(BV_4) = 50{,}000 - 20{,}000 = \$30{,}000$$
questions.videoTitle: Depreciation

questions.explanation: Public works projects are ranked by benefit-cost ratio, and the hurdle is exactly 1.0. Flipping the ratio (costs over benefits, giving 0.67) is the standard mistake - always put benefits in the numerator.
questions.question: A proposed flood-control project has a present worth of benefits of $450,000 and a present worth of costs of $300,000. What is the benefit-cost ratio, and is the project economically justified?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Benefit-Cost Analysis section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the benefit-cost ratio of the flood-control project:

$$B/C = \frac{\text{PW of benefits}}{\text{PW of costs}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(B/C\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{PW of benefits} &= \text{\$450,000} \\
\text{PW of costs} &= \text{\$300,000} \\
B/C &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(B/C) = \frac{450{,}000}{300{,}000} = 1.50$$

Since \(B/C = 1.50\) exceeds 1.0, benefits outweigh costs and the project is economically justified.
questions.videoTitle: Engineering Economics VI: Benefit–Cost Analysis

questions.explanation: Break-even analysis sets minimum production for profitability. The distractor 1,111 comes from dividing fixed cost by price alone, ignoring variable costs - the contribution margin (price minus variable cost) is what actually pays down fixed costs.
questions.question: A precast concrete plant has fixed costs of $10,000 per month, variable costs of $4 per unit, and sells each unit for $9. What is the monthly break-even production quantity?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the break-even quantity \(Q\), where total revenue equals total cost:

$$PQ = FC + (VC)Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = \frac{FC}{P - VC}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
FC &= \$10{,}000\ \text{per month} \\
VC &= \$4\ \text{per unit} \\
P &= \$9\ \text{per unit} \\
Q &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(Q) = \frac{10{,}000}{9 - 4} \rightarrow (Q) = \frac{10{,}000}{5}$$

$$(Q) = 2{,}000\ \text{units per month}$$

questions.explanation: IRR is the discount rate that zeroes the net present worth - the project's own earned rate. On the FE, bracket the unknown factor between two tabulated interest rates and interpolate; guessing from the cash flows alone without setting PW = 0 leads to the wrong neighborhood entirely.
questions.question: A project requires an initial investment of $5,000 and returns $2,000 per year for 3 years. Approximately what is the internal rate of return (IRR) of this project?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Rate-of-Return section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the IRR, the rate \(i\) at which the present worth equals zero:

$$0 = -5000 + 2000(P/A, i, 3) \quad\Rightarrow\quad (P/A, i, 3) = 2.5$$

Bracket the unknown factor between tabulated values:

$$\begin{aligned}
(P/A, 9\%, 3) &= 2.5313 \\
(P/A, 10\%, 3) &= 2.4869
\end{aligned}$$

Since 2.5 falls between them, interpolate:

$$(i) = 9\% + \frac{2.5313 - 2.5}{2.5313 - 2.4869}(1\%) = 9\% + 0.705\%$$

$$(i) \approx 9.7\%$$

questions.question: An engineer is asked to take on a second client whose project competes directly with a current client's project. The engineer possesses confidential design information from the first client that could benefit the second. Under standard engineering codes of ethics (e.g., NSPE), what should the engineer do?
choices: Accept both clients and use the first client's information to give the second client an advantage
Accept the second client but keep the first client's information confidential without telling either client
Decline or disclose the conflict to both clients and proceed only with their informed consent
Accept the second client and resign from the first client immediately without explanation
questions.solution:
Under the NSPE Code of Ethics, engineers must disclose all known or potential conflicts of interest to their clients and employers, and must never use one client's confidential information for another party's benefit.

Here the engineer faces a textbook conflict: a second, directly competing client plus confidential design information that could advantage them. Silent dual service violates the disclosure duty, and exploiting the first client's information violates confidentiality.

Therefore the engineer must decline the second engagement, or disclose the conflict to both clients and proceed only with their informed consent.
questions.explanation: Conflict of interest is a high-yield FE ethics topic. The correct move is always prompt disclosure, never silent dual service or misuse of confidential information.

questions.question: An engineer reports to her supervisor that a pressure vessel design is undersized and could rupture, but the supervisor overrules her and orders the design released. The engineer reasonably believes the public could be endangered. According to standard engineering codes of ethics, what is the engineer's next obligation?
choices: Notify her employer or client and, if needed, such other authority as may be appropriate
Wait until an incident occurs and then testify about her original concerns
Accept the supervisor's decision since responsibility now rests with the supervisor
Resign quietly and seek employment elsewhere to avoid personal liability
questions.solution:
Under the NSPE Code of Ethics, public safety is paramount: engineers shall hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public. When an engineer's judgment is overruled under circumstances where the public could be endangered, the code requires the engineer to notify the employer or client and, if needed, such other authority as may be appropriate.

Applied here, the engineer already reported the undersized pressure vessel internally and was overruled while reasonably believing a rupture could endanger the public. Waiting for an incident, deferring to the supervisor, or resigning quietly all abandon the paramount duty to public safety.

The engineer must notify her employer or client and, if needed, such other authority as may be appropriate.
questions.explanation: Whistleblowing questions test the escalation ladder: internal report first, then notify employer/client and appropriate authorities. Doing nothing or waiting for harm to occur violates the paramount duty to public safety.

questions.question: A licensed professional engineer is asked by a former employer to stamp and seal drawings for a project. The engineer did not prepare the drawings and did not supervise their preparation. Under typical state licensing laws and codes of ethics, the engineer should:
choices: Seal the drawings as a courtesy, since the former employer vouches for their accuracy
Seal the drawings only after a quick visual review of the title block
Refuse to seal the drawings, because they were not prepared under the engineer's responsible charge
Seal the drawings and add a note stating the engineer is not liable for errors
questions.solution:
The governing rule is responsible charge: a licensed engineer may seal only documents the engineer prepared or that were prepared under the engineer's direct supervisory control. Sealing work prepared by others without that supervision — plan stamping — violates state licensing laws and the NSPE Code of Ethics, and adding a liability disclaimer does not cure the violation.

Here the engineer neither prepared the drawings nor supervised their preparation, and the former employer's vouching for their accuracy changes nothing. A quick visual review of the title block is not responsible charge.

The engineer must refuse to seal the drawings.
questions.explanation: Responsible charge is a classic FE licensure question: your seal means you prepared or directly supervised the work. Plan stamping is one of the most common licensure violations.

questions.question: Which of the following business practices by a group of engineering firms competing for public work is a violation of professional ethics and the law?
choices: Submitting individual competitive bids based on each firm's own cost estimate
Agreeing among the firms in advance which firm will submit the lowest bid
Advertising professional services to the public in a factual, non-deceptive manner
Charging a higher fee for a complex project than for a simple one
questions.solution:
Bid rigging \u2014 agreeing in advance which firm will submit the lowest bid \u2014 is collusion: a per se violation of antitrust law and of professional ethics.

The governing principle is honest competition. Submitting individual competitive bids based on each firm's own cost estimate is lawful price competition (the old NSPE ban on competitive bidding was struck down in 1972), truthful advertising is permitted, and fees may vary with project complexity.

Therefore, the practice that violates both ethics and the law is agreeing among the firms in advance which firm will submit the lowest bid.
questions.explanation: FE exams love the twist that competitive bidding itself is NOT unethical; what is prohibited is collusion among bidders. Distinguish lawful price competition from bid rigging.

questions.question: A contractor bidding on a project an engineer is overseeing offers the engineer two expensive tickets to a professional sporting event. Under standard engineering codes of ethics, the engineer should:
choices: Accept the tickets, since gifts from contractors are a normal business courtesy
Accept the tickets but disclose them to the client afterward
Decline the tickets, because accepting valuable gifts from parties with a financial interest in the engineer's decisions compromises professional judgment
Accept the tickets only if every engineer on the project also receives tickets
questions.solution:
The NSPE Code of Ethics prohibits engineers from accepting valuable consideration from outside parties in connection with work for which they are responsible, where it could compromise their professional judgment.

Two expensive event tickets from a bidding contractor are a substantial gift from a party with a direct financial interest in the engineer's decisions — accepting them creates both the appearance and the risk of impaired objectivity. Disclosing them after the fact does not cure the conflict.

Therefore the engineer should decline the tickets.
questions.explanation: Gifts from anyone with a financial stake in your engineering decisions are a textbook conflict-of-interest trap. When in doubt on the FE: decline.

questions.subtopic: Professional liability and standard of care
questions.question: In a professional negligence claim against an engineer, the 'standard of care' is generally defined as:
choices: The highest degree of care theoretically achievable with current technology
The ordinary skill and care exercised by similarly situated practitioners in the same locality and time
A guarantee that the engineered work will perform without defect for its design life
Compliance with the minimum requirements of the applicable building code
questions.solution:
The professional standard of care is the ordinary skill and care that a reasonably prudent practitioner — similarly situated in field, locality, and time — would exercise under the same circumstances. It is a comparative measure, not perfection: it does not demand the highest theoretically achievable care, guarantee defect-free performance, or reduce to mere code compliance (codes are minimums; the standard of care can exceed them).

Therefore the standard of care is the ordinary skill and care exercised by similarly situated practitioners in the same locality and time.
questions.explanation: Standard of care is a favorite liability question: it is comparative (what peers would do), not absolute. Remember: codes are minimums, not the full measure of the standard of care.

questions.question: An engineer discovers that a client's confidential manufacturing process is emitting a toxic substance at levels that pose a serious health risk to the surrounding community. The client refuses to act. Which statement best describes the engineer's ethical obligations?
choices: The duty of confidentiality is absolute, so the engineer must remain silent about the client's process
The engineer may warn the public only after obtaining the client's written permission
The engineer's paramount duty to protect public health and safety overrides the duty of confidentiality, and the engineer must disclose the hazard to appropriate authorities
The engineer should disclose the information to the news media first to maximize public awareness
questions.solution:
The NSPE Code of Ethics establishes a hierarchy of duties, headed by the paramount obligation to safeguard the life, health, property, and welfare of the public. Confidentiality to a client is a genuine duty, but it is subordinate to public safety.

Here a toxic emission poses a serious health risk to the surrounding community and the client refuses to act. The duty to protect the public therefore overrides confidentiality, and the obligation is to disclose the hazard to appropriate authorities — not to remain silent, not to wait for the client's written permission, and not to go to the news media first.

The engineer must disclose the hazard to appropriate authorities.
questions.explanation: This tests the hierarchy of duties: public safety > confidentiality. On the FE, when two duties collide, the answer is almost always the one that protects public health and safety.

questions.question: A 200 N vertical force acts downward at a point located 1.5 m horizontally from point O on a rigid beam. What is the moment of the force about point O?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Systems of Forces section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(M_O\), the moment about point O, where \(d\) is the perpendicular distance from O to the line of action:

$$M_O = F \cdot d$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
F &= 200\ \text{N (downward)} \\
d &= 1.5\ \text{m} \\
M_O &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(M_O) = (200)(1.5) = 300\ \text{N-m}$$

A downward force to the right of O rotates the beam clockwise, so:

$$(M_O) = 300\ \text{N-m clockwise}$$
questions.explanation: Moment problems are gimmes if you use the perpendicular distance and check the rotation direction. Common slips: dividing instead of multiplying, or flipping clockwise/counterclockwise.
questions.videoTitle: Moment of a Force

questions.question: A simple symmetric roof truss has a pin support at A (0, 0), a roller support at B (4 m, 0), and a peak joint C at (2 m, 3 m). A vertical downward load of 10 kN acts at joint C. Using the method of joints, determine the force in top-chord member AC.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Plane Truss: Method of Joints section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(F_{AC}\). By symmetry, the vertical reactions are:

$$A_y = B_y = \frac{10}{2} = 5\ \text{kN (up)}$$

At joint A, member AC rises at an angle of:

$$\theta = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{3}{2}\right) = 56.31^\circ$$

List the known and unknown parameters for joint A equilibrium:

$$\begin{aligned}
A_y &= 5\ \text{kN (up)} \\
\theta &= 56.31^\circ \\
F_{AC} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\sum F_y = 0: \quad 5 + F_{AC}\sin 56.31^\circ = 0$$

$$(F_{AC}) = \frac{-5}{\sin 56.31^\circ} = \frac{-5}{0.8321} = -6.01\ \text{kN}$$

A negative member force means compression, so the force in AC is \(6.01\ \text{kN (C)}\).
questions.explanation: Method of joints always starts at a joint with at most two unknowns. The sign convention trap: a negative member force means compression, not tension.
questions.videoTitle: Trusses Method of Joints

questions.question: A composite cross-section consists of a 4 m wide by 3 m tall rectangle with a triangle (base 4 m, height 2 m) sitting on top of it, the triangle's base coinciding with the top of the rectangle. Measured from the bottom of the rectangle, what is the y-coordinate of the centroid of the composite area?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Centroids of Masses, Areas, Lengths, and Volumes section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\bar{y}\), the area-weighted average of the component centroids:

$$\bar{y} = \frac{A_1 y_1 + A_2 y_2}{A_1 + A_2}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\bar{y}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
A_1 &= (4)(3) = 12\ \text{m}^2, \quad y_1 = 1.5\ \text{m} \\
A_2 &= \frac{1}{2}(4)(2) = 4\ \text{m}^2, \quad y_2 = 3 + \frac{2}{3} = 3.667\ \text{m} \\
\bar{y} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

The triangle's centroid sits one-third of its height above its base, which coincides with the top of the rectangle.

$$(\bar{y}) = \frac{(12)(1.5) + (4)(3.667)}{12 + 4} \rightarrow (\bar{y}) = \frac{18 + 14.667}{16}$$

$$(\bar{y}) = 2.04\ \text{m above the bottom}$$
questions.explanation: Composite centroids use area-weighted averages. The classic triangle trap: its centroid is 1/3 of the height from the base, not 1/2.
questions.videoTitle: Centroid & Centre of Gravity

questions.question: A 500 N block rests on a plane inclined at 30 degrees to the horizontal. The coefficient of static friction between the block and the plane is 0.25. What minimum force P, applied parallel to the plane and directed up the plane, is required to keep the block from sliding down?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Friction section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(P\). Impending motion is down the plane, so friction acts up the plane, assisting \(P\). Equilibrium along the plane gives:

$$\sum F_{\parallel} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; P + F = W\sin\theta$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
W &= 500\ \text{N} \\
\theta &= 30^\circ \\
\mu_s &= 0.25 \\
N &= W\cos\theta = (500)(0.8660) = 433.0\ \text{N} \\
F &= \mu_s N = (0.25)(433.0) = 108.3\ \text{N} \\
P &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(P) = W\sin\theta - F \rightarrow (P) = (500)(0.5) - 108.3 = 250 - 108.3$$

$$(P) = 141.7\ \text{N} \approx 142\ \text{N up the plane}$$
questions.explanation: Friction always opposes impending motion: with impending slip downward, friction acts upward and assists the holding force P. The 358 N trap is the force needed to push the block UP the plane (impending motion upward).
questions.videoTitle: Determine the magnitude and direction of the friction force. Chapter 6: Friction

questions.question: A triangular distributed load varies from zero intensity at the left end of a 4 m beam to a maximum intensity of 6 kN/m at the right end. The equivalent concentrated resultant force acts at what distance from the left end of the beam?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the location of the equivalent concentrated resultant. Its magnitude is the area of the load diagram:

$$R = \frac{1}{2}wL$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
w &= 6\ \text{kN/m (max intensity)} \\
L &= 4\ \text{m} \\
R &= ? \\
\bar{x} &= ?\ \text{(from left end)}
\end{aligned}$$

$$(R) = \frac{1}{2}(6)(4) = 12\ \text{kN}$$

For a triangular distribution the resultant acts through the centroid, one-third of the length from the maximum-intensity end:

$$(\bar{x}) = L - \frac{L}{3} = 4 - \frac{4}{3} = 4 - 1.33$$

$$(\bar{x}) = 2.67\ \text{m from the left end}$$
questions.explanation: The resultant of a triangular load acts 1/3 of the length from the max-intensity side. The common mistake is measuring 1/3 from the wrong end.
questions.videoTitle: Beam Reactions Under a Triangular Distributed Load

questions.question: A 3 m cantilever beam is fixed at its left end. It carries a uniformly distributed load of 2 kN/m over its entire length plus a concentrated load of 5 kN downward at the free (right) end. What is the magnitude of the fixed-end moment?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Equilibrium Requirements section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the fixed-end moment \(M_{\text{wall}}\), the moment of all loads about the fixed support.

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(M_{\text{wall}}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
L &= 3\ \text{m} \\
w &= 2\ \text{kN/m} \\
P &= 5\ \text{kN (at the free end)} \\
M_{\text{wall}} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

The uniform load acts as a resultant \(wL = 6\ \text{kN}\) at midspan, 1.5 m from the wall:

$$(M_{\text{UDL}}) = (6)(1.5) = 9\ \text{kN}\cdot\text{m}$$

The point load acts 3 m from the wall:

$$(M_P) = (5)(3) = 15\ \text{kN}\cdot\text{m}$$

$$(M_{\text{wall}}) = 9 + 15 = 24\ \text{kN}\cdot\text{m}$$
questions.explanation: Break the loading into the uniform resultant (acts at midspan) and the point load, then sum moments about the fixed end. The 33 kN-m trap comes from placing the uniform resultant at the free end.
questions.videoTitle: How to Find the Reactions at the Supports – Static Equilibrium of Rigid Bodies– Reaction Problem 4

questions.question: A beam has a pin support at A (left) and a roller support at B, 6 m to the right of A. The beam overhangs 2 m past B, and a concentrated downward load of 8 kN acts at the free end of the overhang. There are no other loads. What is the vertical reaction at B?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Equilibrium Requirements section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(B_y\). Summing moments about A eliminates \(A_y\):

$$\sum M_A = 0: \quad B_y(6) - (8)(8) = 0$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(B_y\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Load} &= 8\ \text{kN downward at } 8\ \text{m from A} \\
\text{Span AB} &= 6\ \text{m} \\
B_y &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(B_y) = \frac{(8)(8)}{6} = \frac{64}{6}$$

$$(B_y) = 10.67\ \text{kN upward}$$

Check with \(\sum F_y = 0\): \(A_y = 8 - 10.67 = -2.67\ \text{kN}\), i.e., 2.67 kN downward — the overhang load levers the far support up and pulls the near support down.
questions.explanation: Overhang loads create uplift at the near support - a negative reaction is physically meaningful (it must be held down). Always verify with both equilibrium equations.
questions.videoTitle: How to Find the Reactions at the Supports – Static Equilibrium of Rigid Bodies– Reaction Problem 4

questions.question: A projectile is launched from ground level with an initial speed of 20 m/s at an angle of 30 degrees above the horizontal. Neglect air resistance and use g = 9.81 m/s^2. What is the horizontal range of the projectile?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Particle Kinematics section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the horizontal range \(R\):

$$R = \frac{v_0^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
v_0 &= 20\ \text{m/s} \\
\theta &= 30^\circ \\
g &= 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2 \\
R &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(R) = \frac{(20)^2 \sin 60^\circ}{9.81} \rightarrow (R) = \frac{(400)(0.8660)}{9.81}$$

$$(R) = \frac{346.4}{9.81} = 35.3\ \text{m}$$
questions.explanation: The range formula uses sin(2*theta), not sin(theta) - using sin(30 deg) gives the 20.4 m trap answer. Maximum range occurs at 45 degrees.
questions.videoTitle: How To Solve Projectile Motion Problems In Physics

questions.question: A 10 kg block starts from rest and slides down a frictionless plane inclined at 30 degrees. The length of the incline is 5 m. What is the speed of the block when it reaches the bottom? (g = 9.81 m/s^2)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Principle of Work and Energy section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(v\). With only speeds and distances involved, work–energy is the fastest route:

$$T_1 + \sum U_{1-2} = T_2$$

The block starts from rest and drops a vertical height \(h = 5\sin 30^\circ = 2.5\ \text{m}\), so:

$$\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = mgh \quad\Rightarrow\quad v = \sqrt{2gh}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(v\):

$$\begin{aligned}
g &= 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2 \\
h &= 2.5\ \text{m} \\
v &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(v) = \sqrt{2gh} \rightarrow (v) = \sqrt{2(9.81)(2.5)}$$

$$(v) = \sqrt{49.05} = 7.00\ \text{m/s}$$

Mass cancels out of the solution.
questions.explanation: Work-energy is the fastest route when only speeds and distances matter. The 9.90 m/s trap uses the 5 m incline length as if it were the vertical drop.
questions.videoTitle: Principle of Work and Energy (Learn to solve any problem)

questions.question: A 0.5 kg ball strikes a wall at 12 m/s and rebounds in the opposite direction at 8 m/s. If the contact time with the wall is 0.02 s, what is the magnitude of the average force exerted by the wall on the ball?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Impulse and Momentum section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(F_{avg}\), the average impact force:

$$mv_1 + F_{avg}\Delta t = mv_2$$

Take the incoming direction as positive, so the rebound velocity is negative.

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
m &= 0.5\ \text{kg} \\
v_1 &= 12\ \text{m/s} \\
v_2 &= -8\ \text{m/s} \\
\Delta t &= 0.02\ \text{s} \\
F_{avg} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(0.5)(12) + (F_{avg})(0.02) = (0.5)(-8) \rightarrow 6 + 0.02F_{avg} = -4$$

$$(F_{avg}) = \frac{-10}{0.02} = -500\ \text{N}$$

The magnitude of the average force is:

$$|F_{avg}| = 500\ \text{N}$$
questions.explanation: Rebound problems require a sign change on the final velocity. Forgetting the reversal (using 12 - 8 instead of 12 + 8) is the classic error.
questions.videoTitle: Impulse Momentum Theorem Physics Problems - Average Force & Contact Time

questions.question: A car travels at a constant speed of 25 m/s around a horizontal circular curve of radius 150 m. What is the magnitude of the car's normal (centripetal) acceleration?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Particle Curvilinear Motion section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the normal acceleration \(a_n\). For motion along a curved path:

$$a_n = \frac{v^2}{\rho}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(a_n\):

$$\begin{aligned}
v &= 25\ \text{m/s} \\
\rho &= 150\ \text{m} \\
a_n &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(a_n) = \frac{v^2}{\rho} \rightarrow (a_n) = \frac{(25)^2}{150} = \frac{625}{150}$$

$$(a_n) = 4.17\ \text{m/s}^2$$

Speed is constant, so the tangential acceleration is zero; the full acceleration is the normal component, directed toward the center of curvature.
questions.explanation: a_n = v^2/rho, directed toward the center. The v/rho trap (0.167) forgets to square the velocity.

questions.question: A constant torque of 20 N-m is applied to a disk with a mass moment of inertia of 4 kg-m^2 about its fixed axis of rotation. Neglecting friction, what is the angular acceleration of the disk?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Rigid Body Rotation About a Fixed Axis section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\alpha\). Rotational motion mirrors \(F = ma\):

$$\sum M = I\alpha$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\alpha\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\sum M &= 20\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m} \\
I &= 4\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2 \\
\alpha &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\alpha) = \frac{20}{4}$$

$$(\alpha) = 5.00\ \text{rad/s}^2$$
questions.explanation: Rotational dynamics mirrors F = ma as M = I*alpha. The 80 rad/s^2 trap comes from multiplying torque by inertia instead of dividing.

questions.question: A 4 kg mass is attached to a spring with stiffness k = 100 N/m and released from rest at a displaced position. Neglecting damping, what is the undamped natural frequency of the system in Hz (cycles per second)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Free and Forced Vibration section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the cyclic natural frequency \(f_n\). The undamped circular natural frequency is:

$$\omega_n = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \qquad f_n = \frac{\omega_n}{2\pi}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
m &= 4\ \text{kg} \\
k &= 100\ \text{N/m} \\
\omega_n &= ? \\
f_n &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\omega_n) = \sqrt{\frac{100}{4}} = \sqrt{25} = 5.00\ \text{rad/s}$$

$$(f_n) = \frac{5.00}{2\pi} = 0.796\ \text{Hz}$$
questions.explanation: omega_n is in rad/s; the FE frequently asks for Hz, requiring division by 2*pi. The 5.00 Hz trap skips that conversion.
questions.videoTitle: Solution for Free Vibration of an Undamped SDOF System

questions.question: Car A travels east at 20 m/s and car B travels west at 30 m/s on the same straight road. What is the velocity of car B relative to car A?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Relative Motion section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\mathbf{v}_{B/A}\), the velocity of B relative to A:

$$\mathbf{v}_{B/A} = \mathbf{v}_B - \mathbf{v}_A$$

Take east as positive.

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
v_A &= +20\ \text{m/s} \\
v_B &= -30\ \text{m/s} \\
v_{B/A} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(v_{B/A}) = (-30) - (20) = -50\ \text{m/s}$$

The negative sign means west, so:

$$(v_{B/A}) = 50\ \text{m/s west}$$
questions.explanation: Relative velocity is vector subtraction: v_B/A = v_B - v_A. When two objects approach head-on, their relative speed is the sum of the speeds.

Bending stress uses the section modulus S = I/c. A common pitfall is computing I (mm^4) but forgetting to divide by c (half the depth) to get S (mm^3), which doubles the answer. Always convert kN-m to N-mm before dividing by mm^3.
questions.question: A rectangular beam cross-section is 100 mm wide and 200 mm deep. If the beam is subjected to a bending moment of 20 kN-m, what is the maximum bending stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Stresses in Beams section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\sigma_{\max}\). Bending stress is maximum at the outer fiber:

$$\sigma_{\max} = \frac{M}{S}, \qquad S = \frac{bh^2}{6}\ \text{(rectangle)}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\sigma_{\max}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
b &= 100\ \text{mm} \\
h &= 200\ \text{mm} \\
M &= 20\ \text{kN}\cdot\text{m} = 20 \times 10^6\ \text{N}\cdot\text{mm} \\
\sigma_{\max} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Section modulus: \((S) = (100)(200)^2/6 = 666{,}667\ \text{mm}^3\).

$$(\sigma_{\max}) = \frac{M}{S} \rightarrow (\sigma_{\max}) = \frac{20 \times 10^6}{666{,}667}$$

$$(\sigma_{\max}) = 30\ \text{N/mm}^2 = 30\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.videoTitle: FLEXURAL/BENDING STRESS

questions.explanation: Shear stress in beams follows tau = VQ/(It); for rectangles this simplifies to a parabolic distribution with max = 1.5 x average at the neutral axis. The classic mistake is reporting the average shear stress V/A and forgetting the 1.5 factor.
questions.question: A rectangular beam 80 mm wide and 150 mm deep carries a transverse shear force of 24 kN. What is the maximum shear stress in the beam?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Stresses in Beams section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\tau_{\max}\). For a rectangular cross-section the maximum shear stress occurs at the neutral axis and equals 1.5 times the average:

$$\tau_{\max} = 1.5\frac{V}{A}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\tau_{\max}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
V &= 24\ \text{kN} = 24{,}000\ \text{N} \\
A &= (80)(150) = 12{,}000\ \text{mm}^2 \\
\tau_{\max} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\tau_{\max}) = 1.5\frac{24{,}000}{12{,}000} \rightarrow (\tau_{\max}) = 1.5(2.0)$$

$$(\tau_{\max}) = 3.0\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.videoTitle: Fundamental Problem 7.2 Determine the shear stress if the beam is subjected to a shear force

questions.explanation: Torsional shear stress varies linearly from zero at the center to maximum at the outer surface. Pitfalls: mixing N-m with mm (must convert to N-mm), or using the radius where the diameter belongs in 16T/(pi*d^3).
questions.question: A solid circular steel shaft with diameter 40 mm is subjected to a torque of 500 N-m. What is the maximum torsional shear stress in the shaft?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Torsion section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\tau_{\max}\). For a solid circular shaft:

$$\tau_{\max} = \frac{Tc}{J} = \frac{16T}{\pi d^3}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
T &= 500\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m} = 500{,}000\ \text{N}\cdot\text{mm} \\
d &= 40\ \text{mm} \\
\tau_{\max} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\tau_{\max}) = \frac{16(500{,}000)}{\pi (40)^3} \rightarrow (\tau_{\max}) = \frac{8{,}000{,}000}{201{,}062}$$

$$(\tau_{\max}) = 39.8\ \text{N/mm}^2 = 39.8\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.videoTitle: Torsion of Stepped Shaft: Find Max Moment M & Total Angle of Twist

questions.explanation: Columns always buckle about the axis with the smallest radius of gyration (weak axis), so use I_min. Using the strong-axis I gives 4x the load here (913 kN) - a dangerous overestimate. Pinned-pinned means effective length factor K = 1.0.
questions.question: A 3 m long steel column (E = 200 GPa) with a 50 mm x 100 mm rectangular cross-section is pinned at both ends. What is the Euler critical buckling load?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Columns section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(P_{cr}\), the Euler critical buckling load. The column buckles about its weak axis, so use \(I_{min}\):

$$P_{cr} = \frac{\pi^2 EI}{(KL)^2}$$

Pinned at both ends gives \(K = 1.0\).

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
E &= 200\ \text{GPa} = 200 \times 10^9\ \text{Pa} \\
L &= 3\ \text{m} \\
I_{min} &= \frac{(0.1)(0.05)^3}{12} = 1.0417 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^4 \\
P_{cr} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(P_{cr}) = \frac{\pi^2 (200 \times 10^9)(1.0417 \times 10^{-6})}{(1.0 \times 3)^2} = \frac{2056167}{9}$$

$$(P_{cr}) = 228463\ \text{N} \approx 228\ \text{kN}$$
questions.videoTitle: Euler's Equation for Steel Compression Members

questions.explanation: Hoop stress is twice the longitudinal stress (p*r/(2t)) in a cylindrical vessel, which is why vessels typically split along their length. Common errors: using diameter instead of radius, or reporting the longitudinal stress (45 MPa) instead of the hoop stress.
questions.question: A thin-walled cylindrical pressure vessel has an internal diameter of 1.2 m and a wall thickness of 10 mm. If the internal pressure is 1.5 MPa, what is the hoop (circumferential) stress in the wall?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Cylindrical Pressure Vessel section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the hoop stress \(\sigma_{\text{hoop}}\). For a thin-walled cylindrical vessel:

$$\sigma_{\text{hoop}} = \frac{pr}{t}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\sigma_{\text{hoop}}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
p &= 1.5\ \text{MPa} \\
d &= 1.2\ \text{m} \;\Rightarrow\; r = 0.6\ \text{m} = 600\ \text{mm} \\
t &= 10\ \text{mm} \\
\sigma_{\text{hoop}} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\sigma_{\text{hoop}}) = \frac{pr}{t} \rightarrow (\sigma_{\text{hoop}}) = \frac{(1.5)(600)}{10}$$

$$(\sigma_{\text{hoop}}) = 90\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.videoTitle: Pipe & Pressure-Vessel Stress — PE Mechanical TFS Week 6 (Lesson 05 of 09)

questions.explanation: Restrained heating produces compressive stress; restrained cooling produces tensile stress. The sign is the classic trap. Note thermal stress is independent of bar length and area - it depends only on E, alpha, and deltaT.
questions.question: A 25-mm-diameter steel rod is snugly fitted between two rigid walls at 20 C with no initial stress. The temperature then rises to 70 C. For steel, E = 200 GPa and \(\alpha = 12 \times 10^{-6}/^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\). What stress develops in the rod?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Thermal Deformations section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\sigma\). Fully restrained thermal expansion produces:

$$\sigma = E\alpha\Delta T$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\sigma\):

$$\begin{aligned}
E &= 200\ \text{GPa} \\
\alpha &= 12 \times 10^{-6}/^\circ\text{C} \\
\Delta T &= 70 - 20 = 50^\circ\text{C} \\
\sigma &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\sigma) = (200 \times 10^9)(12 \times 10^{-6})(50)$$

$$(\sigma) = 120 \times 10^6\ \text{Pa} = 120\ \text{MPa compressive}$$

Because the heated rod is restrained, the stress is compressive. (The 25 mm diameter is not needed for stress.)
questions.videoTitle: Thermal Stresses - Problem No 8

choices: It increases up to a ratio of 0.50, then decreases
questions.explanation: The water-cement ratio is the single most important factor controlling concrete strength (Abrams' law). Extra water improves workability but always costs strength - this trade-off drives admixture use in modern mix design.
questions.question: For a concrete mix with all other factors held constant, what happens to the 28-day compressive strength as the water-cement ratio increases?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Materials Science/Structure of Matter chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Abrams' law governs concrete strength: with all other factors held constant, the 28-day compressive strength is inversely related to the water–cement ratio. Water beyond what hydration requires leaves capillary pores in the hardened cement paste, and those pores weaken the concrete.

Therefore increasing the water–cement ratio decreases the 28-day compressive strength. (Extra water improves workability, but always at the cost of strength.)

choices: The stress at which plastic (permanent) deformation begins
The maximum stress the material can withstand
The stress at which the specimen fractures
The slope of the initial linear portion of the curve
questions.explanation: Students often confuse yield strength with ultimate strength. Yield governs serviceability and the start of permanent set; ultimate is the peak of the curve. Design of steel members is typically based on yield, not ultimate.
questions.question: On a typical engineering stress-strain curve for structural steel, the yield strength is best described as:
questions.solution:
On a typical engineering stress-strain curve for structural steel, the governing definitions are:

- Yield strength: the stress at which plastic (permanent) deformation begins \u2014 beyond this point the steel will not return to its original shape when unloaded.
- Ultimate (tensile) strength: the maximum stress on the curve.
- Fracture stress: the stress at which the specimen breaks.
- Modulus of elasticity: the slope of the initial linear portion.

Therefore, yield strength is best described as the stress at which plastic (permanent) deformation begins. Steel member design is typically based on yield, not ultimate.

choices: Increases ductility and weldability while decreasing strength
Increases strength and hardness but decreases ductility and weldability
Has no significant effect on mechanical properties
questions.explanation: This strength-versus-ductility trade-off is fundamental to material selection. Structural steels (e.g., A36) keep carbon low (~0.25%) precisely to preserve ductility and weldability, while tool steels push carbon high for hardness.
questions.question: Increasing the carbon content of plain carbon steel generally:
questions.solution:
Carbon is the primary strengthening element in plain carbon steel.

Increasing carbon content raises yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and hardness — but it does so at the expense of ductility, toughness, and weldability. High-carbon steels are notably prone to cracking in the heat-affected zone during welding.

Therefore increasing carbon content increases strength and hardness but decreases ductility and weldability.

questions.explanation: Absorption is referenced to the oven-dry mass, not the SSD mass - dividing by 5000 g gives 1.00%, the classic error. Absorption matters because aggregates soak up mix water, changing the effective water-cement ratio if not corrected.
questions.question: A coarse aggregate sample has an oven-dry mass of 4950 g and a saturated-surface-dry (SSD) mass of 5000 g. What is the absorption capacity of the aggregate?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Materials Science/Structure of Matter chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the absorption capacity, referenced to the oven-dry mass:

$$\text{Absorption} = \frac{M_{SSD} - M_{OD}}{M_{OD}} \times 100\%$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for the absorption:

$$\begin{aligned}
M_{OD} &= 4950\ \text{g} \\
M_{SSD} &= 5000\ \text{g} \\
\text{Absorption} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\text{Absorption}) = \frac{5000 - 4950}{4950} \times 100\% = \frac{50}{4950} \times 100\%$$

$$(\text{Absorption}) = 1.01\%$$

choices: Sudden fracture under a single overload
Progressive cracking under repeated cyclic loading
Time-dependent deformation under a sustained constant load
Loss of strength due to chemical attack
questions.explanation: Creep versus fatigue is a favorite exam distractor pair: creep = constant load over time, fatigue = repeated load cycles. Concrete creep causes prestress loss and long-term beam sag, so it appears in both materials and structural questions.
questions.question: Creep in a structural material is best defined as:
questions.solution:
Refer to the Materials Science/Structure of Matter chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Creep is time-dependent deformation under a sustained constant load — the slow straining of a material carrying a load below its yield strength. It drives long-term deflections in concrete and matters in metals at elevated temperature.

The distractors name different phenomena: progressive cracking under repeated cyclic loading is fatigue, sudden fracture under a single overload is brittle fracture, and loss of strength from chemical attack is corrosion or degradation.

Time-dependent deformation under a sustained constant load is the correct definition.

questions.explanation: NDT methods estimate properties indirectly: rebound hammer estimates compressive strength via surface hardness, while ultrasonic pulse velocity detects internal voids and cracking. Neither replaces a direct compression test for acceptance.
questions.question: The rebound hammer (Schmidt hammer) test performed on hardened concrete in the field is used to estimate the concrete's:
questions.solution:
The rebound (Schmidt) hammer measures the surface hardness of hardened concrete as a rebound number.

The governing principle is correlation, not direct measurement: the rebound number is empirically correlated with the in-place compressive strength of the concrete, typically calibrated against core or cylinder tests.

Therefore, the test is used to estimate the concrete's compressive strength. It remains an index test \u2014 like ultrasonic pulse velocity for detecting voids \u2014 and does not replace a direct compression test for acceptance.

choices: Increases the bond strength between the steel and concrete
Increases the yield strength of the reinforcement
Acts as a barrier that keeps chlorides away from the steel surface
Makes the steel cathodic to the surrounding concrete
questions.explanation: Chloride-induced corrosion is the leading cause of bridge deck deterioration. The exam tests whether you know protection is about isolation (barrier), not strengthening - and the honest caveat that damaged coating at holidays can actually concentrate corrosion.
questions.question: Epoxy-coated reinforcing bars are commonly specified for bridge decks exposed to deicing salts primarily because the coating:
questions.solution:
Chlorides from deicing salts penetrate concrete and destroy the passive oxide film that protects embedded steel, initiating corrosion.

The epoxy coating is a physical barrier: it keeps chlorides and moisture away from the steel surface, delaying corrosion initiation. It adds no strength, and it slightly reduces bond rather than improving it.

Therefore epoxy-coated bars are specified because the coating acts as a barrier that keeps chlorides away from the steel surface.

questions.explanation: In a constriction the velocity rises and the pressure drops - the Venturi effect behind flow meters. The sign error (adding the velocity-head difference instead of subtracting) gives 219 kPa, the most common mistake.
questions.question: Water flows through a horizontal pipe that tapers from 200 mm diameter at section 1 to 100 mm diameter at section 2. The flow rate is 0.05 m^3/s and the pressure at section 1 is 200 kPa. Neglecting head loss, what is the pressure at section 2?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Bernoulli Equation section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(p_2\). Between sections 1 and 2 at the same elevation, neglecting head loss:

$$\frac{p_1}{\gamma} + \frac{V_1^2}{2g} = \frac{p_2}{\gamma} + \frac{V_2^2}{2g}$$

Continuity gives the velocities: \(V_1 = Q/A_1 = 0.05/0.03142 = 1.592\ \text{m/s}\) and \(V_2 = Q/A_2 = 0.05/0.007854 = 6.366\ \text{m/s}\).

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(p_2\):

$$\begin{aligned}
p_1 &= 200\ \text{kPa} \\
\frac{V_1^2}{2g} &= \frac{(1.592)^2}{2(9.81)} = 0.129\ \text{m} \\
\frac{V_2^2}{2g} &= \frac{(6.366)^2}{2(9.81)} = 2.066\ \text{m} \\
p_2 &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\frac{(p_2)}{\gamma} = \frac{200}{9.81} + 0.129 - 2.066 \rightarrow \frac{(p_2)}{\gamma} = 18.45\ \text{m}$$

$$(p_2) = (18.45)(9.81) = 181\ \text{kPa}$$
questions.videoTitle: FE Exam Practice - Fluid Mechanics and Water Resources - Culvert Flow

questions.explanation: Reynolds number is dimensionless - verify units cancel. The 50 mm must become 0.050 m; forgetting the conversion gives Re ~ 100 (laminar), a factor-of-1000 trap. For pipe flow: Re < 2300 laminar, Re > 4000 turbulent.
questions.question: Water at 20 C (kinematic viscosity = \(1.004 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}^2/\mathrm{s}\)) flows at 2.0 m/s through a pipe with 50 mm inside diameter. The Reynolds number is approximately ______, and the flow is ______.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the Reynolds number \(Re\) and classify the flow:

$$Re = \frac{VD}{\nu}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
V &= 2.0\ \text{m/s} \\
D &= 50\ \text{mm} = 0.050\ \text{m} \\
\nu &= 1.004 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2/\text{s} \\
Re &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(Re) = \frac{(2.0)(0.050)}{1.004 \times 10^{-6}} \rightarrow (Re) = \frac{0.10}{1.004 \times 10^{-6}}$$

$$(Re) = 99{,}600 \approx 1.0 \times 10^5$$

Since \(Re > 4{,}000\) for pipe flow, the flow is turbulent.
