questions.videoTitle: Laminar Flow, Turbulent Flow and Reynolds Number (Lesson 3, Part 2)

questions.explanation: Head loss scales with V^2, so doubling velocity quadruples loss. Watch the 2g denominator: using V^2/g instead doubles the answer (6.12 m). Also confirm D is in meters so L/D is dimensionless.
questions.question: Water flows at 1.5 m/s through a 150-mm-diameter pipe that is 200 m long. If the Darcy friction factor is f = 0.020, what is the friction head loss in the pipe?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Pressure Drop for a Fluid of Constant Density section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(h_f\). We can determine \(h_f\) from the following equation:

$$h_f = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{V^2}{2g}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(h_f\):

$$\begin{aligned}
L &= 200\ \text{m} \\
D &= 0.15\ \text{m} \\
V &= 1.5\ \text{m/s} \\
g &= 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2 \\
f &= 0.020\ (\text{given})
\end{aligned}$$

$$(h_f) = (f)\frac{L}{D}\frac{V^2}{2g} \rightarrow (h_f) = (0.020)\frac{200}{0.15}\frac{(1.5)^2}{2(9.81)}$$

$$(h_f) = (0.020)(1333.3)(0.1147) = 3.06\ \text{m}$$
questions.videoTitle: Head Loss Example

questions.explanation: Buoyancy depends only on displaced volume, not on the block's own weight or material. A frequent error is multiplying by the full 1 m^3 unit weight (9.81 kN) instead of the actual 0.5 m^3 displaced.
questions.question: A 0.5 m^3 solid block is fully submerged in water (unit weight 9.81 kN/m^3). What is the buoyant force acting on the block?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Archimedes Principle and Buoyancy section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(F_b\), the buoyant force. By Archimedes' principle it equals the weight of the displaced fluid:

$$F_b = \gamma V_{displaced}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\gamma &= 9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3 \\
V_{displaced} &= 0.5\ \text{m}^3 \\
F_b &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(F_b) = (9.81)(0.5)$$

$$(F_b) = 4.905\ \text{kN} \approx 4.91\ \text{kN}$$
questions.videoTitle: Buoyant Force and Archimedes' Principle

questions.explanation: The water columns above the mercury partially offset it, so subtract SG = 1 for the water side - ignoring this gives 13.3 kPa. Mercury manometers give large readings for small deflections, which is why a 10 cm deflection reads over 12 kPa.
questions.question: A U-tube manometer containing mercury (specific gravity 13.6) is connected to a water pipe. The difference in mercury levels between the two legs is 0.10 m. What is the pressure difference being measured?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Manometers section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\Delta p\). For a U-tube manometer with the same fluid above the manometer fluid on both legs, the water columns partially offset the mercury:

$$\Delta p = (SG_{\text{Hg}} - SG_{\text{water}})\,\gamma_{\text{water}}\,h$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\Delta p\):

$$\begin{aligned}
SG_{\text{Hg}} &= 13.6 \\
SG_{\text{water}} &= 1.0 \\
\gamma_{\text{water}} &= 9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3 \\
h &= 0.10\ \text{m} \\
\Delta p &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\Delta p) = (13.6 - 1.0)(9.81)(0.10) \rightarrow (\Delta p) = (12.6)(0.981)$$

$$(\Delta p) = 12.36 \approx 12.4\ \text{kPa}$$
questions.videoTitle: Open Tube Manometer, Basic Introduction, Pressure, Height & Density of Fluids - Physics Problems

questions.explanation: Force equals the rate of momentum destroyed: rho*Q*V = rho*A*V^2. If the plate were moving, use the relative velocity (V - U). Halving errors come from inserting a spurious 1/2 (98 N) - the momentum equation has no 1/2, unlike kinetic energy.
questions.question: A horizontal water jet with diameter 50 mm and velocity 10 m/s strikes a stationary flat plate perpendicular to the jet. Neglecting friction and splash losses, what is the force exerted on the plate?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Impulse-Momentum Principle section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(F\). The jet is brought to zero x-velocity against the stationary plate:

$$F = \rho A V^2$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(F\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\rho &= 1000\ \text{kg/m}^3 \\
A &= \frac{\pi(0.05)^2}{4} = 0.0019635\ \text{m}^2 \\
V &= 10\ \text{m/s} \\
F &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(F) = (1000)(0.0019635)(10)^2$$

$$(F) = 196.35 = 196\ \text{N}$$

questions.explanation: Specific gravity is dimensionless; multiply by 1000 kg/m^3 for mass density or 9.81 kN/m^3 for unit weight. The 9,810 kg/m^3 distractor confuses unit weight (kN/m^3) with mass density (kg/m^3) - a unit-consistency trap.
questions.question: An oil has a specific gravity of 0.85. What is its mass density?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Definitions section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\rho_{\text{oil}}\). Specific gravity is the ratio of the fluid's density to the density of water at \(4^\circ\text{C}\) \((1{,}000\ \text{kg/m}^3)\):

$$\rho = (SG)\rho_{\text{water}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
SG &= 0.85 \\
\rho_{\text{water}} &= 1{,}000\ \text{kg/m}^3 \\
\rho_{\text{oil}} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\rho_{\text{oil}}) = (0.85)(1{,}000)$$

$$(\rho_{\text{oil}}) = 850\ \text{kg/m}^3$$
questions.videoTitle: Fluid Mechanics Tutorial 3

questions.question: A stadia survey is taken with a stadia interval factor K = 100 and stadia constant C = 0. The rod intercept is 0.845 m and the vertical angle is 4 degrees 30 minutes above horizontal. What is the horizontal distance from the instrument to the rod?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(H\), the horizontal distance. For an inclined stadia sight:

$$H = Ks\cos^2\theta + C\cos\theta$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
K &= 100 \\
s &= 0.845\ \text{m} \\
\theta &= 4.5^\circ \\
C &= 0 \\
H &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

With \(C = 0\) the additive term drops out:

$$(H) = (100)(0.845)\cos^2(4.5^\circ) = (84.5)(0.99385)$$

$$(H) = 83.98\ \text{m} \approx 84.0\ \text{m}$$
questions.explanation: Stadia tacheometry converts a rod intercept into distance, but on a slope the intercept must be reduced by cos^2 of the vertical angle to get the horizontal component. A common pitfall is using the slope distance K*s (84.5 m) directly as the horizontal distance.
questions.videoTitle: Elementary Surveying

questions.question: The azimuth of line AB is 235 degrees 30 minutes (measured clockwise from north). What is the bearing of line AB?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the bearing of line AB. An azimuth of \(235^\circ 30'\) falls in the third quadrant (between \(180^\circ\) and \(270^\circ\)), so the bearing is referenced to south and west:

$$\text{third quadrant: bearing angle} = \text{azimuth} - 180^\circ$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for the bearing:

$$\begin{aligned}
Az_{AB} &= 235^\circ 30' \\
\text{quadrant} &= \text{III} \\
\text{bearing angle} &= 235^\circ 30' - 180^\circ = 55^\circ 30' \\
\text{bearing} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

The bearing of line AB is \(\text{S } 55^\circ 30'\text{ W}\).
questions.explanation: Azimuth-to-bearing conversion depends on which quadrant the azimuth falls in. The classic mistake is subtracting from 360 or using the wrong cardinal directions; always sketch the quadrant first.
questions.videoTitle: Azimuths and Bearings Traverse Surveying: A Complete Solved Land Problem in Civil & Construction

questions.question: A closed traverse has an algebraic sum of latitudes of +0.42 m and an algebraic sum of departures of -0.31 m. The total length of the traverse is 856 m. What is the relative precision (ratio of closure) of the traverse?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Latitudes and Departures section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the relative precision. The linear misclosure combines the latitude and departure misclosures as a vector:

$$e = \sqrt{(\sum \text{lat})^2 + (\sum \text{dep})^2}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(e\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\sum \text{lat} &= +0.42\ \text{m} \\
\sum \text{dep} &= -0.31\ \text{m} \\
\text{Traverse length} &= 856\ \text{m} \\
e &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(e) = \sqrt{(0.42)^2 + (0.31)^2} = \sqrt{0.2725} = 0.522\ \text{m}$$

$$\text{Relative precision} = \frac{0.522}{856} = \frac{1}{1640} = 1{:}1{,}640$$
questions.explanation: Closure error combines latitude and departure misclosures as a vector (root-sum-square), not a simple sum. Precision is expressed as 1 part in N; a frequent error is adding the two misclosures directly (0.73 m), which understates the precision.
questions.videoTitle: Balance the traverse by using Bowditch rule

questions.question: A parcel has the following corner coordinates in meters, listed in order around the boundary: A(0, 0), B(200, 0), C(200, 120), D(60, 80). Using the coordinate method, what is the area of the parcel?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Area formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the parcel area \(A\) with the coordinate (shoelace) method, listing vertices in order around the boundary and closing back to the start:

$$A = \frac{|\sum x_i y_{i+1} - \sum y_i x_{i+1}|}{2}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
A(0, 0),\; B(200, 0),\; C(200, 120),\; D(60, 80) \\
\sum x_i y_{i+1} &= (0)(0) + (200)(120) + (200)(80) + (60)(0) = 40{,}000 \\
\sum y_i x_{i+1} &= (0)(200) + (0)(200) + (120)(60) + (80)(0) = 7{,}200 \\
A &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(A) = \frac{|40{,}000 - 7{,}200|}{2} \rightarrow (A) = \frac{32{,}800}{2}$$

$$(A) = 16{,}400\ \text{m}^2$$
questions.explanation: The coordinate (shoelace) method requires listing vertices consistently around the polygon and closing back to the start. The most common errors are forgetting to divide by 2 and mixing up the cross-multiplication order, which flips the sign.

questions.question: Two consecutive cross sections on a roadway project are 25 m apart. The cut area at the first section is 42.5 m^2 and at the second section is 61.5 m^2. Using the average end area method, what is the volume of cut between the sections?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earthwork formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(V\), the volume of cut, by the average end area method:

$$V = L\frac{A_1 + A_2}{2}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
L &= 25\ \text{m} \\
A_1 &= 42.5\ \text{m}^2 \\
A_2 &= 61.5\ \text{m}^2 \\
V &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(V) = 25\frac{42.5 + 61.5}{2} = 25\frac{104.0}{2} = 25(52.0)$$

$$(V) = 1300\ \text{m}^3$$
questions.explanation: The average end area method is the workhorse of earthwork quantity takeoffs. The typical slip is forgetting the division by 2 (giving 2,600 m^3) or using the difference of the areas instead of the sum.
questions.videoTitle: FS Exam - Average End Area Problem

questions.question: A simple horizontal curve has a radius of 300 m and an intersection (deflection) angle of 24 degrees. What is the tangent length (distance from the PI to the PC or PT)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Horizontal Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the tangent length \(T\), the distance from the PI to the PC (or PT):

$$T = R\tan\!\left(\frac{\Delta}{2}\right)$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(T\):

$$\begin{aligned}
R &= 300\ \text{m} \\
\Delta &= 24^\circ \\
T &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Note the half-angle: \((T) = 300\tan(24^\circ/2) = 300\tan 12^\circ\).

$$(T) = (300)(0.21256) = 63.77 \approx 63.8\ \text{m}$$
questions.explanation: Curve geometry formulas use half the intersection angle for the tangent (and the full angle in radians for arc length, 125.7 m here). Plugging the full 24 degrees into tan gives 133.6 m, the most common distractor.
questions.videoTitle: Horizontal Curves Elements Part 1 of 2

questions.question: A crest vertical curve connects a +3.0% grade to a -2.5% grade. The curve length is 240 m, and the PVC is at station 10+00 with elevation 150.00 m. What is the elevation of the high point of the curve?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vertical Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the elevation of the high point, which occurs where the grade is zero:

$$x = \frac{L g_1}{g_1 - g_2}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(x\):

$$\begin{aligned}
g_1 &= +3.0\% = 0.030 \\
g_2 &= -2.5\% = -0.025 \\
L &= 240\ \text{m} \\
\text{PVC elevation} &= 150.00\ \text{m} \\
x &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(x) = \frac{(240)(0.030)}{0.030 - (-0.025)} = \frac{7.2}{0.055} = 130.91\ \text{m}$$

Elevation on the curve, with \(r = (g_2 - g_1)/L = -0.00022917\ \text{per m}\):

$$y = y_{PVC} + g_1 x + \frac{r}{2}x^2$$

$$(y) = 150.00 + (0.030)(130.91) + \frac{(-0.00022917)}{2}(130.91)^2$$

$$(y) = 150.00 + 3.927 - 1.964 = 151.96\ \text{m}$$
questions.explanation: On a vertical curve the high/low point is found by setting the tangent grade to zero, not by averaging grades. A frequent mistake is reporting the PVI elevation (153.60 m) instead of locating the true turning point along the curve.
questions.videoTitle: VERTICAL CURVES - Solving for SUMMIT, and ELEVATION and GRADE of CURVE! (SURVEYING)

questions.question: A cantilever beam 3 m long carries a single concentrated load of 4 kN at its free end. What is the maximum bending moment in the beam, and where does it occur?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Structural Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(M_{\max}\). For a cantilever carrying a concentrated load \(P\) at its free end, the shear is constant (\(V = P\)) and the moment varies linearly from zero at the free end to its maximum at the fixed support:

$$M_{\max} = PL$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
P &= 4\ \text{kN} \\
L &= 3\ \text{m} \\
M_{\max} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(M_{\max}) = (4)(3)$$

$$(M_{\max}) = 12\ \text{kN}\cdot\text{m}$$

The maximum moment occurs at the fixed support.
questions.explanation: In a cantilever the fixed support resists both the shear and the full overturning moment. Students often place the maximum moment at the load point; for a cantilever it is always at the wall.
questions.videoTitle: How to Draw Shear Force and Moment Diagrams

questions.question: A planar truss has 8 joints, 13 members, and 3 reaction components. Based on the determinacy check m + r versus 2j, how is this truss classified?
choices: Internally indeterminate to the first degree
Externally indeterminate to the first degree
questions.solution:
The determinacy check for a planar truss compares \(m + r\) against \(2j\):

- \(m + r < 2j\): mechanism (unstable)
- \(m + r = 2j\): externally and internally determinate
- \(m + r > 2j\): indeterminate

Here \(m + r = 13 + 3 = 16\) and \(2j = 2(8) = 16\). Since \(m + r = 2j\), with \(r = 3\) reactions for a planar structure, the truss is externally determinate and internally determinate. (The count is necessary but not sufficient for stability.)
questions.explanation: The m + r vs 2j test is the first screen for truss analysis: less than 2j suggests a mechanism, equal suggests determinate, greater suggests indeterminate. Remember it is necessary but not sufficient for stability.
questions.videoTitle: SA04: Truss Analysis: Method of Joints

questions.question: A cantilever beam 2.5 m long carries a 6 kN concentrated load at its free end. E = 200 GPa and \(I = 8.0 \times 10^6\ \mathrm{mm}^4\). What is the deflection at the free end?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Deflection of Beams section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the free-end deflection \(\delta\). For a cantilever with a concentrated load at the free end:

$$\delta = \frac{PL^3}{3EI}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\delta\):

$$\begin{aligned}
P &= 6\ \text{kN} = 6{,}000\ \text{N} \\
L &= 2.5\ \text{m} \\
E &= 200\ \text{GPa} = 200 \times 10^9\ \text{Pa} \\
I &= 8.0 \times 10^6\ \text{mm}^4 = 8.0 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^4 \\
\delta &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Flexural rigidity: \((EI) = (200 \times 10^9)(8.0 \times 10^{-6}) = 1.60 \times 10^6\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2\).

$$(\delta) = \frac{PL^3}{3EI} \rightarrow (\delta) = \frac{(6{,}000)(2.5)^3}{3(1.60 \times 10^6)}$$

$$(\delta) = \frac{93{,}750}{4.80 \times 10^6} = 0.01953\ \text{m} = 19.5\ \text{mm (downward)}$$
questions.explanation: Deflection formulas punish unit mistakes: mm^4 must become m^4 (x10^-12). The classic errors are dropping the factor of 3 or mixing kN with N while E is in Pa.
questions.videoTitle: Deflection of Beam

questions.question: A 4.0 m long column is fixed at its base and free at its top (like a flagpole). Using theoretical effective length factors, what is the effective length KL of the column?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Columns section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(KL\). The theoretical effective length factor for a fixed-free (cantilever) column is \(K = 2.0\):

$$KL = K \cdot L$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(KL\):

$$\begin{aligned}
K &= 2.0\ \text{(fixed-free)} \\
L &= 4.0\ \text{m} \\
KL &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(KL) = (2.0)(4.0)$$

$$(KL) = 8.0\ \text{m}$$
questions.explanation: End restraint controls buckling: a flagpole-type column buckles with an effective length twice its real length, making it the worst common case. Memorizing K = 2.0 (fixed-free), 1.0 (pinned-pinned), 0.7 (fixed-pinned), 0.5 (fixed-fixed) covers most FE questions.
questions.videoTitle: Buckling Load Theory Explained

questions.question: A reinforced concrete beam is designed as a tension-controlled section per ACI 318. What is the strength reduction factor phi applied to its nominal flexural strength?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Design of Reinforced Concrete Components (ACI 318-14) section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

ACI 318 ties the strength reduction factor \(\phi\) to ductility: sections that give warning before failure earn a higher \(\phi\). A tension-controlled section — where the steel yields well before the concrete crushes — is the most ductile flexural case and receives \(\phi = 0.90\), the highest flexural factor.

Compression-controlled (tied) sections use 0.65 and shear uses 0.75; 0.85 is not an ACI 318 \(\phi\) value.

\(\phi = 0.90\) is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: Phi rewards ductility: tension-controlled flexure gets the highest factor (0.90) because yielding steel gives visible warning before failure. Confusing flexure phi with shear phi (0.75) is the standard trap.

questions.question: A simply supported beam 8 m long carries a single concentrated load of 10 kN at midspan. What are the maximum shear force and maximum bending moment in the beam?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Beams section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(V_{max}\) and \(M_{max}\). By symmetry each reaction carries half the load:

$$R = \frac{P}{2}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
P &= 10\ \text{kN} \\
L &= 8\ \text{m} \\
R &= ? \\
V_{max} &= ? \\
M_{max} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(R) = \frac{10}{2} = 5\ \text{kN}$$

The shear is constant at \(\pm 5\) kN, so \(V_{max} = 5\) kN. The moment peaks under the load:

$$M_{max} = \frac{PL}{4}$$

$$(M_{max}) = \frac{(10)(8)}{4} = 20\ \text{kN-m}$$
questions.explanation: For midspan point loads, reactions split the load in half and the peak moment is PL/4, not PL/2. Mixing up shear (a force) with the reaction value, or using the cantilever formula PL, are the usual errors.
questions.videoTitle: How to Draw Shear Force and Moment Diagrams

questions.question: A roof beam carries only dead load D = 4 kN/m and roof live load L = 10 kN/m. Using ASCE 7 strength-design (LRFD) load combinations, which combination controls and what is the factored design load?
questions.solution:
Refer to the ASCE 7 Load Combinations in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the controlling factored load. Every applicable combination is checked, and the largest governs.

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
D &= 4\ \text{kN/m} \\
L_r &= 10\ \text{kN/m (roof live)} \\
w_u &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Evaluate each relevant combination:

$$\begin{aligned}
1.4D &= 1.4(4) = 5.6\ \text{kN/m} \\
1.2D + 1.6L_r &= 1.2(4) + 1.6(10) = 4.8 + 16.0 = 20.8\ \text{kN/m} \\
0.9D &= 0.9(4) = 3.6\ \text{kN/m}
\end{aligned}$$

The largest value controls:

$$(w_u) = 1.2D + 1.6L_r = 20.8\ \text{kN/m}$$
questions.explanation: Load combinations must all be checked and the maximum governs; with heavy live load, 1.2D + 1.6L almost always controls over 1.4D. A common mistake is designing to 1.4D alone or forgetting that the 1.6 factor applies to the live load.
questions.videoTitle: Intro to Structural Analysis - Loads and LRFD

questions.question: A soil sample has a total volume of 0.0012 m^3 and the volume of the solid particles is 0.00078 m^3. What is the void ratio of the soil?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Phase Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the void ratio \(e = V_v/V_s\). First find the volume of voids:

$$V_v = V_t - V_s$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
V_t &= 0.0012\ \text{m}^3 \\
V_s &= 0.00078\ \text{m}^3 \\
V_v &= ? \\
e &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(V_v) = 0.0012 - 0.00078 = 0.00042\ \text{m}^3$$

$$(e) = \frac{0.00042}{0.00078} = 0.54$$
questions.explanation: Void ratio uses the volume of solids in the denominator (e = Vv/Vs), while porosity uses total volume (n = Vv/Vt = 0.35 here). Swapping them is the classic phase-relationship error.
questions.videoTitle: Module-1 Part-3

questions.question: Water flows through a soil specimen 0.15 m long with a cross-sectional area of 0.008 m^2. The head loss across the specimen is 0.45 m and the hydraulic conductivity is \(k = 2.5 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m/s}\). What is the volumetric flow rate?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Darcy's Law section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

The handbook prints Darcy's law as \(Q = -KA(dh/dx)\), where the hydraulic gradient is \(i = dh/dx\). Flow is in the direction of decreasing head, so we use the magnitude form (the negative sign is dropped) and discretize the gradient over the specimen length as \(i = \Delta h/L\), giving the working form \(q = kiA\).

Notation note: the handbook uses \(Q\) for the discharge (volumetric flow) rate and \(q\) for the specific discharge; here \(q\) denotes the volumetric flow rate.

Ultimately, we must solve for the volumetric flow rate \(q\):

$$q = kiA \qquad i = \frac{\Delta h}{L}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\Delta h &= 0.45\ \text{m} \\
L &= 0.15\ \text{m} \\
k &= 2.5 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m/s} \\
A &= 0.008\ \text{m}^2 \\
q &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(i) = \frac{\Delta h}{L} = \frac{0.45}{0.15}$$

$$(i) = 3.0$$

$$(q) = (k)(i)(A) = (2.5 \times 10^{-5})(3.0)(0.008)$$

$$(q) = 6.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}$$
questions.explanation: Darcy's law needs the gradient, not just the head loss: forgetting to divide by the specimen length (using i = 0.45) gives 2.0 x 10^-7 m^3/s, the standard trap.
questions.videoTitle: Soil Permeability - Darcy's Law

questions.question: A 5 m tall vertical retaining wall retains a level cohesionless backfill with friction angle phi = 30 degrees and unit weight gamma = 18 kN/m^3. What is the total active earth thrust per meter of wall?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Horizontal Stress Profiles and Forces section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(P_a\). First determine the Rankine active earth pressure coefficient:

$$K_a = \frac{1 - \sin\phi}{1 + \sin\phi}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\phi &= 30^\circ \\
\gamma &= 18\ \text{kN/m}^3 \\
H &= 5\ \text{m} \\
K_a &= ? \\
P_a &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(K_a) = \frac{1 - \sin 30^\circ}{1 + \sin 30^\circ} = \frac{0.5}{1.5} = \frac{1}{3} = 0.333$$

Total active thrust per meter of wall:

$$P_a = \frac{1}{2}K_a\gamma H^2$$

$$(P_a) = \frac{1}{2}(0.333)(18)(5)^2 = 75\ \text{kN/m}$$

The thrust acts at \(H/3\) above the base.
questions.explanation: Active pressure grows with the square of wall height, so the 1/2 factor in the triangular distribution is essential (dropping it gives 150 kN/m). Using Ka = 1 or the passive coefficient are the other common slips.
questions.videoTitle: Rankine Theory of Earth Pressure

questions.question: A fine-grained soil has a liquid limit LL = 55 and a plastic limit PL = 28. How is this soil classified under the Unified Soil Classification System (USCS)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Soil Classification section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must classify the soil. Compute the plasticity index:

$$PI = LL - PL$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
LL &= 55 \\
PL &= 28 \\
PI &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(PI) = 55 - 28 = 27$$

Since \(LL = 55 > 50\), the soil is high plasticity (H). Check the A-line:

$$PI_A = 0.73(LL - 20) = 0.73(35) = 25.55$$

\(PI = 27\) plots above the A-line, so the fines are clay (C) rather than silt (M).

Therefore the classification is CH (fat clay).
questions.explanation: USCS fine-grained classification is a two-step test: LL above/below 50 gives H/L, and position relative to the A-line gives C/M. Skipping the A-line check is how CH gets mislabeled MH.

questions.question: A soil has a water content w = 18%, specific gravity of solids Gs = 2.70, and void ratio e = 0.55. What is the degree of saturation?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Phase Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the degree of saturation \(S\). The four phase quantities are tied together by:

$$Se = wG_s$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(S\):

$$\begin{aligned}
w &= 18\% = 0.18 \\
G_s &= 2.70 \\
e &= 0.55 \\
S &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(S) = \frac{wG_s}{e} \rightarrow (S) = \frac{(0.18)(2.70)}{0.55} = \frac{0.486}{0.55}$$

$$(S) = 0.884 \approx 88\%$$
questions.explanation: The identity S*e = w*Gs ties all four phase quantities together. Inverting it (e/(w*Gs) = 113%) is the typical algebra slip, and any saturation above 100% should immediately raise a flag.
questions.videoTitle: Module-1 Part-3

questions.question: A direct shear test on a clean sand (c = 0) gives a friction angle phi = 32 degrees. At failure, the normal stress on the failure plane is 150 kPa. What is the shear strength of the sand at that stress level?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\tau\). The Mohr-Coulomb failure criterion:

$$\tau = c + \sigma \tan\phi$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\tau\):

$$\begin{aligned}
c &= 0\ \text{(clean sand)} \\
\sigma &= 150\ \text{kPa} \\
\phi &= 32^\circ \\
\tau &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\tau) = 0 + (150)\tan 32^\circ = (150)(0.6249)$$

$$(\tau) = 93.7 = 94\ \text{kPa}$$
questions.explanation: For cohesionless soil the strength envelope passes through the origin, so strength is purely frictional: sigma*tan(phi). Using phi in radians mode or confusing tan with sin are the calculator errors to watch for.
questions.videoTitle: Why Landslides happen?

questions.question: In a Proctor compaction test, the dry unit weight of a soil increases with water content up to a peak and then decreases as more water is added. What is the water content at that peak dry unit weight called?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Compaction section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

The compaction curve plots dry unit weight against water content: dry unit weight rises with water content to a peak — the maximum dry unit weight — then falls as added water displaces soil solids. The water content at that peak is the optimum moisture content (OMC) for the given compactive effort.

Compacting dry of optimum leaves excess air voids; wet of optimum, water takes the place of solids. The plastic limit, shrinkage limit, and liquid limit are Atterberg consistency limits describing plasticity, not compaction.

The optimum moisture content is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: OMC is the target for field compaction control. The distractors are all Atterberg consistency limits, which describe plasticity behavior, not compaction — a frequent vocabulary mix-up.

Stopping sight distance has two parts: the distance traveled during perception-reaction time and the braking distance. The most common pitfall is omitting the perception-reaction term (which gives 288 ft), or using a reaction time other than the AASHTO standard 2.5 s.
questions.question: A rural highway segment has a design speed of 55 mph on level grade. Using a perception-reaction time of 2.5 s and a coefficient of friction of 0.35, what is the required stopping sight distance (SSD)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Stopping Sight Distance section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the SSD, the sum of perception-reaction distance and braking distance:

$$SSD = 1.47Vt + \frac{V^2}{30(f \pm G)}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
V &= 55\ \text{mph} \\
t &= 2.5\ \text{s} \\
f &= 0.35 \\
G &= 0\ \text{(level grade)} \\
SSD &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(d_{PR}) = 1.47(55)(2.5) = 202.1\ \text{ft}$$

$$(d_{braking}) = \frac{55^2}{30(0.35)} = \frac{3025}{10.5} = 288.1\ \text{ft}$$

$$(SSD) = 202.1 + 288.1 = 490.2\ \text{ft} \approx 490\ \text{ft}$$
questions.videoTitle: Stopping Sight Distance (SSD) – Explained with Real-Life Examples

questions.explanation: The minimum radius balances centrifugal force with the combined effect of superelevation (e) and side friction (f_s). A common mistake is using only e or only f_s in the denominator, which overestimates the allowable radius and would be unsafe.
questions.question: A horizontal curve is designed for 60 mph with a maximum superelevation rate of 8%. If the side friction factor is 0.12, what is the minimum radius of curvature (AASHTO)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Horizontal Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the minimum radius of curvature \(R_{\min}\). The point-mass equation balances centrifugal force against superelevation plus side friction:

$$R_{\min} = \frac{V^2}{15(e + f_s)}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(R_{\min}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
V &= 60\ \text{mph} \\
e &= 8\% = 0.08 \\
f_s &= 0.12 \\
R_{\min} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(R_{\min}) = \frac{V^2}{15(e + f_s)} \rightarrow (R_{\min}) = \frac{(60)^2}{15(0.08 + 0.12)}$$

$$(R_{\min}) = \frac{3{,}600}{15(0.20)} = \frac{3{,}600}{3} = 1{,}200\ \text{ft}$$
questions.videoTitle: Critical SUPERELEVATION Calculations

questions.explanation: Density = flow / speed is the fundamental identity of traffic flow theory. Density is the key service measure for freeway level of service, so this relationship appears constantly on the FE exam.
questions.question: A traffic stream has a measured flow rate of 1,800 vehicles per hour and an average space mean speed of 30 mph. What is the traffic density?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Traffic Flow Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the traffic density \(k\). The fundamental relationship:

$$q = kv$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(k\):

$$\begin{aligned}
q &= 1800\ \text{veh/hr} \\
v &= 30\ \text{mph} \\
k &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(k) = \frac{1800}{30}$$

$$(k) = 60\ \text{veh/mi}$$

choices: Density in passenger cars per mile per lane
questions.explanation: Each facility type has its own LOS measure: density for freeways, control delay for signalized intersections, and percent time spent following for two-lane highways. Mixing these up is a classic conceptual trap.
questions.question: According to the Highway Capacity Manual, which measure of effectiveness defines the level of service (LOS) for a basic freeway segment?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Level of Service (LOS) section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

The Highway Capacity Manual assigns each facility type its own measure of effectiveness for level of service. For a basic freeway segment that measure is density in passenger cars per mile per lane (pc/mi/ln) — LOS A at densities of 11 pc/mi/ln or less, LOS F above 45 pc/mi/ln.

Average travel speed, volume-to-capacity ratio, and percent time spent following govern other facility types (percent time spent following, for example, defines LOS on two-lane highways), not basic freeway segments.

Density in passenger cars per mile per lane is the correct choice.

questions.explanation: Crest and sag curves use different sight-distance constants (2158 for crest SSD, 1320 for sag SSD). Using the sag constant by mistake gives 1,136 ft. Always verify the S < L or S > L assumption after computing.
questions.question: A crest vertical curve connects a +3% grade to a -3% grade on a highway with a required stopping sight distance of 500 ft. What is the minimum curve length L? (Assume S < L.)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vertical Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(L\), the minimum crest curve length. For \(S < L\):

$$L = \frac{AS^2}{2158}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
g_1 &= +3\% \\
g_2 &= -3\% \\
A &= |3 - (-3)| = 6\% \\
S &= 500\ \text{ft} \\
L &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(L) = \frac{6(500)^2}{2158} = \frac{1500000}{2158}$$

$$(L) = 695.1\ \text{ft} \approx 695\ \text{ft}$$

Check: \(S = 500\) ft \(< L = 695\) ft, so the assumption holds.
questions.videoTitle: Vertical Curves: The Secret to Smooth Road Design

choices: No, the required (e + f_s) of 0.24 exceeds the available 0.18
Yes, because the 6% superelevation is less than the friction factor
Yes, a 1,000-ft radius always satisfies 60 mph
It cannot be determined without knowing the grade
questions.explanation: Adequacy is checked by comparing the required sum (e + f_s) from the point-mass equation against what the design provides. The common error is checking e alone against f_s, which has no physical meaning.
questions.question: A horizontal curve with radius 1,000 ft is designed for 60 mph with a superelevation rate of 6%. If the available side friction factor is 0.12, is the superelevation design adequate?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Horizontal Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must determine whether the design is adequate by comparing the required \((e + f_s)\) from the point-mass equation against what the design provides:

$$e + f_s = \frac{V^2}{15R}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
V &= 60\ \text{mph} \\
R &= 1{,}000\ \text{ft} \\
e_{\text{provided}} &= 6\% = 0.06 \\
f_{s,\text{available}} &= 0.12
\end{aligned}$$

Required: \((e + f_s)_{\text{req}} = (60)^2/[15(1{,}000)] = 3{,}600/15{,}000 = 0.24\).

Provided: \((e + f_s)_{\text{prov}} = 0.06 + 0.12 = 0.18\).

Since \(0.24 > 0.18\), the required superelevation-plus-friction exceeds what is available — the design is not adequate for 60 mph.

choices: A linear relationship between axle weight and pavement damage
Tire inflation pressure only, independent of axle weight
Equal damage per axle regardless of load magnitude
The fourth-power law relating axle load to pavement damage
questions.explanation: The fourth-power law is why overloaded trucks dominate pavement damage and why ESAL counts, not vehicle counts, drive pavement thickness design. Assuming damage is linear with weight drastically underestimates heavy-axle effects.
questions.question: In flexible pavement design, the mixed traffic stream is converted to 18-kip equivalent single axle loads (ESALs) using load equivalency factors. These factors are based on which relationship between axle load and pavement damage?
questions.solution:
The AASHTO load equivalency factors convert mixed traffic to 18-kip equivalent single axle loads (ESALs) using the fourth-power law: the pavement damage caused by an axle is proportional to the fourth power of the ratio of its load to the 18-kip reference load, \((\text{axle load}/18\ \text{kips})^4\).

Consequences: doubling an axle load causes roughly \(2^4 = 16\) times the damage — which is why overloaded trucks dominate pavement deterioration and why ESAL counts, not vehicle counts, drive pavement thickness design. A linear damage assumption would drastically underestimate heavy-axle effects.

The factors are based on the fourth-power law relating axle load to pavement damage.

questions.explanation: In a constant-diameter pipe the velocity heads cancel, so the pressure head rises by exactly the elevation drop (6 m). The classic sign error is subtracting the elevation difference instead of adding it, giving 91 kPa.
questions.question: Water flows through a constant-diameter pipe. At point A the pressure is 150 kPa and the elevation is 20 m; at point B the elevation is 14 m. Neglecting head loss, what is the pressure at point B? (gamma = 9.81 kN/m^3)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Bernoulli Equation section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(p_B\). With head loss neglected:

$$\frac{p_A}{\gamma} + \frac{V_A^2}{2g} + z_A = \frac{p_B}{\gamma} + \frac{V_B^2}{2g} + z_B$$

The constant diameter makes \(V_A = V_B\), so the velocity heads cancel. List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
p_A &= 150\ \text{kPa} \\
\gamma &= 9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3 \\
z_A &= 20\ \text{m} \\
z_B &= 14\ \text{m} \\
p_B &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\left(\frac{p_B}{\gamma}\right) = \frac{150}{9.81} + 20 - 14 \rightarrow \left(\frac{p_B}{\gamma}\right) = 15.29 + 6 = 21.29\ \text{m}$$

$$(p_B) = (21.29)(9.81) = 208.9\ \text{kPa} \approx 209\ \text{kPa}$$
questions.videoTitle: Bernoulli's Equation Example Problem - Fluid Mechanics

questions.explanation: The wetted perimeter of a rectangular channel includes both side walls (P = b + 2y), not just one. Omitting a side wall inflates R and gives 2.69 m/s, and misreading n or the slope is another common slip.
questions.question: A rectangular concrete channel is 3 m wide and carries water 1.2 m deep. The channel slope is 0.002 and Manning's n is 0.015. What is the flow velocity?
questions.solution:
Refer to Manning's Equation in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(V\), the flow velocity:

$$V = \frac{1}{n}R^{2/3}S^{1/2} \quad\text{with}\quad R = \frac{A}{P}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
b &= 3\ \text{m} \\
y &= 1.2\ \text{m} \\
A &= (3)(1.2) = 3.6\ \text{m}^2 \\
P &= 3 + 2(1.2) = 5.4\ \text{m} \\
R &= \frac{3.6}{5.4} = 0.6667\ \text{m} \\
n &= 0.015 \\
S &= 0.002 \\
V &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(V) = \frac{1}{0.015}(0.6667)^{2/3}(0.002)^{1/2} = (66.667)(0.7631)(0.04472)$$

$$(V) = 2.275\ \text{m/s} \approx 2.28\ \text{m/s}$$
questions.videoTitle: How to Calculate Discharge (Q) in a Trapezoidal Channel

questions.explanation: The rational method is trivial in formula but treacherous in units: intensity must be converted to m/s and area to m^2. Plugging in 75 and 2.5 directly gives the absurd 112.5 m^3/s.
questions.question: A 2.5-hectare parking lot has a runoff coefficient of 0.6. If the design rainfall intensity is 75 mm/hr, what is the peak runoff rate by the rational method?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Rational Formula section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the peak runoff rate \(Q\):

$$Q = CiA$$

List the known and unknown parameters, converting to consistent SI units:

$$\begin{aligned}
C &= 0.6 \\
i &= 75\ \text{mm/hr} = \frac{0.075}{3{,}600}\ \text{m/s} \\
A &= 2.5\ \text{ha} = 25{,}000\ \text{m}^2 \\
Q &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(Q) = CiA \rightarrow (Q) = (0.6)\left(\frac{0.075}{3{,}600}\right)(25{,}000)$$

$$(Q) = \frac{1{,}125}{3{,}600} = 0.3125 \approx 0.313\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}$$
questions.videoTitle: 7.5 Rainwater Harvesting & Stormwater

questions.explanation: Efficiency divides the water power because the motor must supply more than the water receives. Multiplying by efficiency instead (11.0 kW) or omitting it entirely (14.7 kW) are the standard traps.
questions.question: A pump delivers 0.05 m^3/s of water against a total dynamic head of 30 m. If the pump efficiency is 75%, what input power is required? (gamma = 9.81 kN/m^3)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Pump Power Equation section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the input (brake) power. First compute the water power:

$$P_{water} = \gamma Q H$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\gamma &= 9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3 \\
Q &= 0.05\ \text{m}^3\text{/s} \\
H &= 30\ \text{m} \\
\eta &= 0.75 \\
P_{input} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(P_{water}) = (9.81)(0.05)(30) = 14.715\ \text{kW}$$

The motor must supply more than the water receives, so efficiency divides:

$$(P_{input}) = \frac{14.715}{0.75}$$

$$(P_{input}) = 19.62 = 19.6\ \text{kW}$$
questions.videoTitle: Mechanical HVAC PE Exam - Question 104 - Sizing Pump and Motor Horsepower

questions.explanation: Memorize the head exponents: rectangular weir 3/2, triangular weir 5/2, orifice 1/2. The exam loves swapping these among the answer choices.
questions.question: For a sharp-crested rectangular weir, how does the discharge Q vary with the head H measured above the weir crest?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Weir Formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

The sharp-crested rectangular weir equation is \(Q = CLH^{3/2}\): discharge scales with head to the 3/2 power. The other exponents belong to other devices — a triangular (V-notch) weir gives \(H^{5/2}\) and an orifice gives \(H^{1/2}\) — which is exactly how the exam builds its distractors.

\(Q\) is proportional to \(H^{3/2}\) is the correct choice.

questions.explanation: The velocity head term is V^2/(2g); forgetting the 2 in the denominator doubles the answer to 9.94 ft, and forgetting the friction factor entirely gives the absurd 248 ft.
questions.question: Water flows at 4 ft/s through a 1,000-ft-long pipe with a diameter of 1 ft. If the Darcy friction factor is 0.02, what is the head loss due to friction? (g = 32.2 ft/s^2)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Pressure Drop for a Fluid of Constant Density section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(h_f\). We can determine \(h_f\) from the Darcy\u2013Weisbach equation:

$$h_f = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{V^2}{2g}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(h_f\):

$$\begin{aligned}
L &= 1000\ \text{ft} \\
D &= 1\ \text{ft} \\
V &= 4\ \text{ft/s} \\
g &= 32.2\ \text{ft/s}^2 \\
f &= 0.02 \\
h_f &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(h_f) = (f)\frac{L}{D}\frac{V^2}{2g} \rightarrow (h_f) = (0.02)\frac{1000}{1}\frac{(4)^2}{2(32.2)}$$

$$(h_f) = (20)(0.24845) = 4.97\ \text{ft}$$

questions.explanation: Linearity (proportionality) is the core assumption of the unit hydrograph. It only applies when the storm duration equals the unit hydrograph duration; otherwise an S-hydrograph conversion is needed first.
questions.question: The 1-hour unit hydrograph for a watershed has a peak discharge of 50 m^3/s for 1 cm of excess rainfall. Assuming linear watershed response, what is the peak discharge of the direct runoff hydrograph produced by 2 cm of excess rainfall in 1 hour?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the peak of the direct runoff hydrograph. Unit hydrograph theory assumes a linear watershed response: scaling the excess rainfall depth scales every hydrograph ordinate by the same factor.

$$\frac{Q_{\text{peak, new}}}{Q_{\text{peak, unit}}} = \frac{P_{\text{new}}}{P_{\text{unit}}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
Q_{\text{peak, unit}} &= 50\ \text{m}^3/\text{s (1 cm excess)} \\
P_{\text{new}} &= 2\ \text{cm (same 1-hour duration)} \\
Q_{\text{peak, new}} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(Q_{\text{peak, new}}) = 2 \times 50 = 100\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}$$
questions.videoTitle: 6-Hour Unit Hydrograph Derivation

questions.explanation: The forward pass takes the maximum of predecessor early finishes, which identifies the critical path. Taking the shorter path (day 9) is the classic error; the critical path is always the longest-duration path.
questions.question: A small project has these activities: A (3 days) precedes B (4 days) and C (5 days); both B and C precede D (2 days). What is the early finish time of activity D?
questions.solution:
Refer to the CPM Precedence Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the early finish of activity D. Run the forward pass along each path:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Path A-B-D} &= 3 + 4 + 2 = 9\ \text{days} \\
\text{Path A-C-D} &= 3 + 5 + 2 = 10\ \text{days}
\end{aligned}$$

The early finish is governed by the longest (critical) path:

$$EF_D = \max(9, 10) = \text{Day } 10$$
questions.videoTitle: Master Project Deadlines With CPM A Full Guide

questions.explanation: Swell applies to bank-to-loose (trucking) conversions; shrinkage applies to bank-to-compacted (fill) conversions. Applying the swell factor to a fill question gives 1,125 CCY, a very common mistake.
questions.question: An excavation measures 1,000 bank cubic yards (BCY). The soil has a swell factor of 25% and a shrinkage factor of 10%. How many compacted cubic yards (CCY) of fill will this excavation produce?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earthwork formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the compacted volume. A bank-to-compacted conversion uses only the shrinkage factor — swell governs the loose (trucking) volume, not the fill:

$$CCY = BCY \times (1 - \text{shrinkage})$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
BCY &= 1{,}000 \\
\text{shrinkage} &= 10\% = 0.10 \\
CCY &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(CCY) = (1{,}000)(1 - 0.10) \rightarrow (CCY) = (1{,}000)(0.90)$$

$$(CCY) = 900\ \text{CCY}$$

(The 25% swell gives \(1{,}000 \times 1.25 = 1{,}250\) LCY — the loose volume that governs hauling, not the compacted fill.)

questions.explanation: Production problems chain three adjustments: cycle rate, efficiency factor (50-min hour), and swell. Omitting swell gives 200 BCY/hr; omitting the efficiency factor gives 240 BCY/hr.
questions.question: An excavator has a 2-CY bucket, a 30-second cycle time, and works a 50-minute hour. The soil swells 20%. What is the hourly production rate in bank cubic yards per hour?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the hourly production in bank cubic yards. Chain the three adjustments \u2014 cycle rate, efficiency, swell:

$$\text{Production} = \frac{3600}{\text{cycle time}} \times \text{bucket} \times \text{efficiency} \div (1 + \text{swell})$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{bucket} &= 2\ \text{CY} \\
\text{cycle time} &= 30\ \text{s} \\
\text{efficiency} &= \frac{50}{60} \\
\text{swell} &= 20\% = 0.20 \\
\text{production} &= ?\ \text{BCY/hr}
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\text{cycles/hr}) = \frac{3600}{30} = 120$$

$$(\text{loose}) = (120)(2)\left(\frac{50}{60}\right) = 200\ \text{LCY/hr}$$

$$(\text{bank}) = \frac{200}{1.20} = 166.7\ \text{BCY/hr} \approx 167\ \text{BCY/hr}$$
questions.videoTitle: FECivil 98 Production analysis of the Best Excavator

questions.explanation: Two conversion steps trip people up: inches to feet for thickness, and cubic feet to cubic yards (divide by 27). Forgetting the waste factor gives 18.5 CY; forgetting the ft^3-to-CY conversion gives 500.
questions.question: How many cubic yards of concrete should be ordered for a 40 ft by 25 ft slab that is 6 in. thick, allowing 5% for waste?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the cubic yards of concrete to order, including the waste allowance.

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{length} &= 40\ \text{ft} \\
\text{width} &= 25\ \text{ft} \\
\text{thickness} &= 6\ \text{in} = 0.5\ \text{ft} \\
\text{waste} &= 5\% \\
V_{\text{order}} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Theoretical volume: \((V) = (40)(25)(0.5) = 500\ \text{ft}^3\). Convert to cubic yards (\(27\ \text{ft}^3 = 1\ \text{CY}\)):

$$(V) = \frac{500}{27} = 18.52\ \text{CY}$$

Add the 5% waste allowance:

$$(V_{\text{order}}) = (18.52)(1.05) = 19.44 \approx 19.4\ \text{CY}$$

questions.explanation: Estimate classes form a sequence of increasing accuracy: order-of-magnitude, budget, definitive, and bid/control. The exam tests whether you know that the earliest estimate is the least accurate.
questions.question: Which type of construction cost estimate is prepared earliest in a project, uses the least project definition, and has the lowest expected accuracy?
questions.solution:
The order-of-magnitude (conceptual) estimate is prepared earliest in a project, when project definition is minimal — typically at inception or feasibility. With the least definition comes the lowest expected accuracy, roughly ±30 to 50\%.

Accuracy improves through the later estimate classes in sequence: budget, definitive, and finally bid (control) estimates. Because the question asks for the earliest estimate with the least definition and lowest accuracy, the answer is the order-of-magnitude (conceptual) estimate.

questions.explanation: Weaker soil needs a flatter slope: the H:V ratio increases as soil quality decreases (A < B < C). Reversing this ordering is the standard trap.
questions.question: For an excavation less than 20 ft deep in Type C soil, what is the maximum allowable slope under OSHA standards?
questions.solution:
OSHA's maximum allowable excavation slopes get flatter as soil weakens: Type A soil 3/4H:1V, Type B soil 1H:1V, and Type C soil — the weakest — 1-1/2H:1V for excavations less than 20 ft deep.

Reversing the A < B < C ordering is the standard trap.

1-1/2H:1V is the correct choice.

questions.explanation: Risk allocation is the heart of contract-type questions: lump sum shifts quantity and price risk to the contractor, while unit price keeps quantity risk with the owner. Design-build is a delivery method, not a payment-risk distinction.
questions.question: Under which contract type does the owner bear the risk of quantity overruns, because the contractor is paid for each measured unit of work actually performed?
questions.solution:
The governing principle is risk allocation: in a unit price contract, the owner pays the contractor for each measured unit of work actually performed.

Applied to the facts: if quantities overrun the estimate, the owner pays for the extra units \u2014 so the risk of quantity overruns stays with the owner.

By contrast, a lump sum contract shifts quantity and price risk to the contractor, and design-build is a delivery method, not a payment-risk distinction.

Therefore, the owner bears quantity-overrun risk under a unit price contract.

questions.question: What is the slope of the tangent line to the curve y = x³ − 4x at x = 2?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Differential Calculus section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(m\), the slope of the tangent line, which equals the derivative evaluated at \(x = 2\):

$$\frac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2 - 4$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
y &= x^3 - 4x \\
x &= 2 \\
m &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(m) = 3(2)^2 - 4 \rightarrow (m) = 12 - 4$$

$$(m) = 8$$
questions.explanation: The slope is the derivative evaluated at the point — 12 comes from differentiating only the x³ term and forgetting the −4x term.
questions.videoTitle: Civil FEexam review: Mathematics - derivatives and double derivatives

questions.question: Evaluate the definite integral \(\displaystyle\int_0^1 3x^2 e^{x^3}\,dx\).
questions.solution:
Refer to the Integral Calculus section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(I\). Substitute \(u = x^3\) so that \(du = 3x^2 \, dx\):

$$I = \int_{0}^{1} e^{u} \, du = e^{u}\Big|_{0}^{1}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
u &= x^3 \\
u(0) &= 0 \\
u(1) &= 1 \\
I &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(I) = e^{1} - e^{0} \rightarrow (I) = e - 1$$

$$(I) = e - 1$$
questions.explanation: With u-substitution the bounds map 0→0 and 1→1 — e comes from forgetting to evaluate the lower bound, and 1 − e from swapping the bounds.
questions.videoTitle: FE Civil Exam Mathematics: Integrals Problem 3 a,3 b &3 c (Easy, Medium & Hard)

questions.question: What is the cross product a × b for vectors a = (2, 1, −1) and b = (1, 2, 3)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vectors section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}\):

$$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ a_x & a_y & a_z \\ b_x & b_y & b_z \end{vmatrix}$$

List the known components:

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{a} &= (2, 1, -1) \\
\mathbf{b} &= (1, 2, 3)
\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})_x &= (1)(3) - (-1)(2) = 5 \\
(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})_y &= -[(2)(3) - (-1)(1)] = -7 \\
(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})_z &= (2)(2) - (1)(1) = 3
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) = (5, -7, 3)$$
questions.explanation: Cross products are anti-commutative — (−5, 7, −3) is b × a, the most common trap, and the j-component carries a minus sign that is easy to drop.

questions.question: Solve the differential equation \(y'' + 9y = 0\) with initial conditions \(y(0) = 0\) and \(y'(0) = 3\). What is \(y(\pi/6)\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Differential Equations section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(y\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\). The characteristic equation \(r^2 + 9 = 0\) gives \(r = \pm 3i\), so:

$$y = C_1 \cos(3x) + C_2 \sin(3x)$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
y(0) &= 0 \\
y'(0) &= 3 \\
x &= \frac{\pi}{6} \\
y &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Apply the initial conditions: \(y(0) = C_1 = 0\) and \(y'(0) = 3C_2 = 3 \rightarrow C_2 = 1\), so \(y = \sin(3x)\):

$$(y) = \sin\left(3 \cdot \frac{\pi}{6}\right) \rightarrow (y) = \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$$

$$(y) = 1$$
questions.explanation: The argument is 3x, not x — evaluating sin(π/6) = 1/2 instead of sin(3·π/6) is the designed trap.
questions.videoTitle: Separable Differential Equations - Fundamentals of Engineering FE EIT Exam Review

questions.question: What is the area of the region enclosed by the curves y = x² and y = 4x?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Integral Calculus section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the enclosed area \(A\). The curves intersect where \(x^2 = 4x\), i.e. at \(x = 0\) and \(x = 4\), and \(4x \geq x^2\) between them:

$$A = \int_{0}^{4} (4x - x^2) \, dx = \left[2x^2 - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{4}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{lower bound} &= 0 \\
\text{upper bound} &= 4 \\
A &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(A) = \left(2(4)^2 - \frac{(4)^3}{3}\right) - 0 \rightarrow (A) = 32 - \frac{64}{3}$$

$$(A) = \frac{32}{3}$$
questions.explanation: Always integrate upper curve minus lower curve — integrating x² − 4x and dropping the sign, or doubling the region, produces the 64/3 and 32 traps.
questions.videoTitle: FE Civil Exam Mathematics: Integrals Problem 3 a,3 b &3 c (Easy, Medium & Hard)

questions.question: What is the product (3 + 4i)(1 − 2i)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Algebra of Complex Numbers section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the product \(z\). Expand and use \(i^2 = -1\):

$$z = (3 + 4i)(1 - 2i) = 3 - 6i + 4i - 8i^2$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
i^2 &= -1 \\
z &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(z) = 3 - 2i - 8(-1) \rightarrow (z) = 3 - 2i + 8$$

$$(z) = 11 - 2i$$
questions.explanation: The entire problem turns on i² = −1 — forgetting it gives −5 − 2i, the most common wrong answer on complex-number questions.
questions.videoTitle: FE Problem of the Day #16

questions.question: A raffle ticket costs $2. The ticket pays $10 with probability 0.3 and nothing otherwise. What is the expected net gain per ticket?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Expected Values section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the expected net gain \(E\). Subtract the ticket cost from the expected payout:

$$E = \sum p_i x_i - \text{cost}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
p &= 0.3 \\
\text{payout} &= \$10 \\
\text{cost} &= \$2 \\
E &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(E) = (0.3)(10) - 2 \rightarrow (E) = 3 - 2$$

$$(E) = \$1.00$$
questions.explanation: Expected value of a gamble must subtract what you paid to play — $3.00 is the expected payout, not the net gain.
questions.videoTitle: Expected Value & Variance (Discrete Random Variables)

questions.question: Each concrete cylinder in a batch has a 10% chance of testing below the specified strength, independently. If 5 cylinders are tested, what is the probability that exactly 2 test below specification?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Binomial Distribution section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(P(X = 2)\):

$$P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^{k}(1 - p)^{n-k}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
n &= 5 \\
k &= 2 \\
p &= 0.10 \\
P(X = 2) &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(P) = \binom{5}{2}(0.10)^{2}(0.90)^{3} \rightarrow (P) = (10)(0.01)(0.729)$$

$$(P) = 0.0729$$
questions.explanation: Binomial problems require the C(n,k) coefficient — 0.0073 is p²(1−p)³ without it, and 0.5905 is the probability that none fail.
questions.videoTitle: Finding The Probability of a Binomial Distribution Plus Mean & Standard Deviation

questions.question: Steel rod diameters are normally distributed with mean 50 mm and standard deviation 0.5 mm. What is the probability a randomly selected rod has a diameter greater than 51 mm?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Normal Distribution (Gaussian Distribution) section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(P(X > 51)\). Standardize to \(z\):

$$z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\mu &= 50\ \text{mm} \\
\sigma &= 0.5\ \text{mm} \\
x &= 51\ \text{mm} \\
z &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(z) = \frac{51 - 50}{0.5} \rightarrow (z) = 2.0$$

From the standard normal table, the upper tail beyond \(z = 2.0\) is:

$$(P) = 0.0228 = 2.28\%$$
questions.explanation: A one-sided 'greater than' question wants a single tail — 4.56% doubles it and 97.72% is the complement below 51 mm.
questions.videoTitle: Statistics 6.3 – Finding Probability Using a Normal Distribution

questions.question: For the data points (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 5), what is the slope of the least-squares regression line?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Linear Regression and Goodness of Fit section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the least-squares slope \(b\):

$$b = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\bar{x} &= 3 \\
\bar{y} &= 4 \\
\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y}) &= 4 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 2 = 6 \\
\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 &= 4 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 4 = 10 \\
b &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(b) = \frac{6}{10}$$

$$(b) = 0.6$$
questions.explanation: Eyeballing the trend suggests a slope near 1, but least squares weights every deviation — always compute the ratio rather than guessing from the scatterplot.
questions.videoTitle: Statistics 12.2 – Linear Regression

questions.question: Vehicles arrive at a toll booth at an average rate of 3 per minute. What is the probability that exactly 4 vehicles arrive in a given minute?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Probability and Density Functions: Means and Variances section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(P(X = 4)\):

$$P(X = k) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{k}}{k!}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\lambda &= 3 \\
k &= 4 \\
P(X = 4) &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(P) = \frac{e^{-3}(3)^{4}}{4!} \rightarrow (P) = \frac{(0.0498)(81)}{24}$$

$$(P) = 0.168$$
questions.explanation: Match k to the question exactly — 0.224 is P(X = 3) at the mean, and 0.815 is P(X ≤ 4), the cumulative trap.
questions.videoTitle: Poisson Distribution

questions.question: How much must be deposited today to accumulate $5,000 in 5 years at 6% annual interest, compounded annually?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the present worth \(P\):

$$P = F(P/F, i, n) = \frac{F}{(1 + i)^n}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
F &= \$5{,}000 \\
i &= 6\% = 0.06 \\
n &= 5\ \text{years} \\
P &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(P) = \frac{5000}{(1.06)^{5}} \rightarrow (P) = \frac{5000}{1.3382}$$

$$(P) = \$3{,}736$$
questions.explanation: Discounting uses compound interest — $3,846 comes from simple interest and $6,691 compounds in the wrong direction.
questions.videoTitle: Simple and Compound Interest Explained

questions.question: A machine costs $20,000, has a salvage value of $2,000, and a useful life of 9 years. Using straight-line depreciation, what is the book value after 4 years?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Depreciation section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the book value \(BV_4\). Straight-line annual depreciation is:

$$D = \frac{\text{cost} - \text{salvage}}{n}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{cost} &= \$20{,}000 \\
\text{salvage} &= \$2{,}000 \\
n &= 9\ \text{years} \\
D &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(D) = \frac{20000 - 2000}{9} \rightarrow (D) = \$2{,}000\text{/yr}$$

$$(BV_4) = 20000 - 4(2000) = \$12{,}000$$
questions.explanation: Book value is cost minus accumulated depreciation — $8,000 is the depreciation taken so far, not what remains.
questions.videoTitle: Depreciation

questions.question: Annual maintenance costs are $1,000 in year 1, increasing by $200 each year through year 5. At 8% annual interest, what is the present worth of these costs?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the present worth \(P\) of a base series plus an arithmetic gradient:

$$P = A(P/A, i, n) + G(P/G, i, n)$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
A &= \$1{,}000 \\
G &= \$200 \\
i &= 8\% \\
n &= 5\ \text{years} \\
P &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(P) = 1000(3.9927) + 200(7.3724) \rightarrow (P) = 3992.71 + 1474.49$$

$$(P) = \$5{,}467$$
questions.explanation: A gradient series is base amount plus gradient — $3,993 prices only the $1,000 base and $5,000 ignores the time value of money entirely.
questions.videoTitle: Engineering Economic Analysis - Gradient Series

questions.question: A bridge requires a $100,000 initial investment plus $10,000 of major rehabilitation every 5 years, forever. At 6% annual interest, what is the capitalized cost?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Capitalized Costs section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the capitalized cost \(CC\). Convert the recurring cost to an equivalent annual amount, then capitalize it:

$$CC = \text{initial cost} + \frac{A}{i}, \quad A = 10000(A/F, i, 5)$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{initial cost} &= \$100{,}000 \\
\text{rehab} &= \$10{,}000\ \text{every 5 years} \\
i &= 6\% \\
(A/F, 6\%, 5) &= 0.1774 \\
CC &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(A) = 10000(0.1774) \rightarrow (A) = \$1{,}774\text{/yr}$$

$$(CC) = 100000 + \frac{1774}{0.06} = \$129{,}566$$
questions.explanation: A cost every 5 years is not an annual cost — $266,667 capitalizes $10,000 as if it were spent every year.
questions.videoTitle: Capitalized Value - Engineering Economics Lightboard

questions.question: What is the equivalent uniform annual cost of a $50,000 present investment over 20 years at 7% annual interest?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the equivalent uniform annual cost \(A\):

$$A = P(A/P, i, n) = P\left[\frac{i(1+i)^n}{(1+i)^n - 1}\right]$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
P &= \$50{,}000 \\
i &= 7\% = 0.07 \\
n &= 20\ \text{years} \\
(A/P, 7\%, 20) &= 0.09439 \\
A &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(A) = 50000(0.09439)$$

$$(A) = \$4{,}720$$
questions.explanation: Capital recovery includes interest on the unrecovered balance — $2,500 simply divides by 20 and ignores the time value of money.

questions.question: An engineer's supervisor overrules her professional judgment and orders a design change that the engineer believes endangers public safety. Under the NSPE Code of Ethics, the engineer must:
choices: Notify the employer of the consequences and, if the issue is not resolved, advise the proper authority
Follow the supervisor's instructions without question
Resign quietly and say nothing to anyone
Immediately report the supervisor to law enforcement
questions.solution:
The governing principle is NSPE Canon 1: engineers shall hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public.

When professional judgment on a public-safety matter is overruled, the Code requires the engineer to advise the employer or client of the consequences and, if the concern is not satisfactorily resolved, to notify the proper authority. Blind obedience violates the engineer's independent professional duty; quiet resignation abandons the public the Code exists to protect; and law enforcement is not the first step — the employer and the proper technical authority are.

Therefore, the engineer must notify the employer of the consequences and, if unresolved, advise the proper authority.
questions.explanation: The Code never permits silent obedience on safety matters — the trap answers all skip the required step of notifying the employer first, then the proper authority.

questions.question: A licensed professional engineer is asked to review, sign, and seal structural plans prepared by an unlicensed drafter working under her direct supervision. Under the NSPE Code of Ethics, she may do so only if:
choices: She thoroughly reviews the plans and exercised responsible charge over their preparation
The drafter has more than 10 years of drafting experience
She adds a note disclaiming responsibility for any errors
The client agrees in writing to accept the risk
questions.solution:
The governing principle is responsible charge: a PE may seal only work prepared under her direct supervisory control with detailed professional review.

Years of drafter experience do not substitute for the engineer's own review; disclaimers cannot transfer away professional responsibility; and a client's written acceptance does not waive the Code's requirements.

Therefore, sealing is proper only if she thoroughly reviewed the plans and exercised responsible charge over their preparation.
questions.explanation: Plan-stamping turns on responsible charge, not the drafter's résumé — experience, disclaimers, and client waivers are all classic distractors.

questions.question: An engineer serving as a paid consultant to a city also holds an ownership interest in a firm bidding on the city's construction project. Under the NSPE Code of Ethics, the engineer must:
choices: Disclose the financial interest to the city before any decisions are made
Keep the ownership confidential because it is a personal matter
Recuse herself from voting but say nothing about the interest
Sell the ownership interest after the contract is awarded
questions.solution:
The governing principle is NSPE Canon 4: engineers shall act for each employer or client as faithful agents, which requires disclosing any interest that could influence — or appear to influence — professional judgment.

A hidden ownership stake in a bidder is a textbook conflict of interest; confidentiality, silent recusal, and after-the-fact divestiture all leave the city deciding without material facts.

Therefore, the engineer must disclose the financial interest to the city before any decisions are made.
questions.explanation: Conflicts of interest are cured by up-front disclosure, not secrecy — every wrong answer tries to hide the interest instead of revealing it.

questions.question: Which of the following best reflects an engineer's ethical obligation regarding professional competence under the NSPE Code of Ethics?
choices: Pursuing continuing education to stay current in her areas of practice
Relying solely on the knowledge gained during her engineering degree
Delegating all technical decisions to less experienced staff
Avoiding unfamiliar technologies to minimize personal risk
questions.solution:
The governing principle is NSPE Canon 2: engineers shall perform services only in areas of their competence, supported by the Code's expectation of continued professional development.

A degree is a starting point, not a permanent credential; delegating technical judgment downward and avoiding new technology both erode competence rather than maintain it.

Therefore, pursuing continuing education to stay current best reflects the obligation.
questions.explanation: Competence is a continuing duty, not a one-time degree — the distractors all describe letting competence decay.

questions.question: An engineer proposes to a developer client that her design fee for a new subdivision be contingent on the local planning board approving the project — if the board rejects it, she collects no fee. Under the NSPE Code of Ethics, this arrangement is:
choices: Unethical, because a contingent fee compromises the engineer's independent professional judgment
Ethical, as long as the contingency is disclosed to the planning board
Ethical, because it aligns the engineer's incentives with the client's goals
Unethical only if the subdivision is publicly funded
questions.solution:
The NSPE Code of Ethics provides that engineers shall not request, propose, or accept compensation on a contingent basis when their professional judgment may be compromised.

Here, tying the fee to project approval gives the engineer a personal financial stake in the outcome, which can bias both the design itself and the advice given to the client. Disclosure to the board does not remove that bias, and the client's enthusiasm for the deal does not cure it either.

Therefore the arrangement is unethical: a contingent fee compromises the engineer's independent professional judgment.
questions.explanation: The trap is thinking disclosure or client consent fixes it — contingent fees are barred precisely because the financial stake distorts independent judgment, and consent doesn't remove that distortion.

questions.question: A Pratt truss spans 12 m with a pin support at A (left end) and a roller support at E (right end). Bottom-chord joints are A(0, 0), B(4 m, 0), C(8 m, 0), E(12 m, 0); top-chord joints are D(4 m, 3 m) and F(8 m, 3 m). A single vertical load of 20 kN acts downward at top joint F. Using the method of sections, what is the force in diagonal member BF?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Statically Determinate Truss section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(F_{BF}\). Cut through members \(DF\), \(BF\), and \(BC\), and apply vertical equilibrium to the left section:

$$\sum F_y = 0$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(F_{BF}\):

$$\begin{aligned} A_y &= 6.67\ \text{kN (up)} \\ \theta_{BF} &= \tan^{-1}(3/4) = 36.9^\circ \\ F_{BF} &= ? \end{aligned}$$

The left reaction is \(A_y = 20(4)/12 = 6.67\ \text{kN}\). On the left section, only \(A_y\) and the vertical component of \(F_{BF}\) act vertically:

$$(A_y) + (F_{BF})\sin(36.9^\circ) = 0 \rightarrow 6.67 + 0.600\,F_{BF} = 0$$

$$(F_{BF}) = -11.1\ \text{kN} = 11.1\ \text{kN (C)}$$
questions.explanation: The trap is the sign: a negative tensile force means compression. Students who solve the equilibrium correctly but report 11.1 kN (T) misread the sign convention.
questions.videoTitle: Trusses Method of Joints

questions.question: A 200 N traffic sign hangs from two cables attached to a horizontal support. The left cable makes 60° with the horizontal and the right cable makes 45° with the horizontal. What is the tension in the left cable?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Equilibrium Requirements section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(T_L\). We can determine \(T_L\) from the two equilibrium equations:

$$\sum F_x = 0, \quad \sum F_y = 0$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(T_L\):

$$\begin{aligned} W &= 200\ \text{N} \\ \theta_L &= 60^\circ \\ \theta_R &= 45^\circ \\ T_L &= ? \\ T_R &= ? \end{aligned}$$

From \(\sum F_x = 0\): \(T_L \cos 60^\circ = T_R \cos 45^\circ\). Substituting \(T_R\) into \(\sum F_y = 0\) gives \(T_L(\sin 60^\circ + \cos 60^\circ \tan 45^\circ) = 200\):

$$(T_L) = \frac{200}{\sin 60^\circ + \cos 60^\circ \tan 45^\circ} \rightarrow (T_L) = \frac{200}{0.866 + 0.500}$$

$$(T_L) = 146\ \text{N}$$
questions.explanation: The trap is 104 N — that's the right cable's tension. Always label which cable you solved for before picking a choice.
questions.videoTitle: static equilibrium 2 cables different angles

questions.question: Two equal and opposite parallel forces of 50 N are separated by a perpendicular distance of 0.8 m, forming a couple. What is the magnitude of the couple moment?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Moments (Couples) section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(M\). We can determine \(M\) from the couple-moment equation:

$$M = Fd$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(M\):

$$\begin{aligned} F &= 50\ \text{N} \\ d &= 0.8\ \text{m} \\ M &= ? \end{aligned}$$

$$(M) = (50)(0.8) \rightarrow (M) = 40\ \text{N-m}$$
questions.explanation: The trap is doubling the force — a couple moment is one force times the separation, not the sum of both forces times the distance.
questions.videoTitle: Couple Moments

questions.subtopic: Centroid of composite area with hole
questions.question: A 300 mm wide by 200 mm tall rectangular steel plate has a circular hole of 100 mm diameter punched through it. The hole's center is 100 mm from the left edge and 60 mm from the bottom edge. Measured from the left edge, where is the centroidal x-coordinate of the remaining plate?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Centroids of Masses, Areas, Lengths, and Volumes section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\bar{x}\). We can determine \(\bar{x}\) by treating the hole as a negative area:

$$\bar{x} = \frac{\sum A_i x_i}{\sum A_i}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\bar{x}\):

$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= (300)(200) = 60000\ \text{mm}^2,\ x_1 = 150\ \text{mm} \\ A_2 &= -\pi(50)^2 = -7854\ \text{mm}^2,\ x_2 = 100\ \text{mm} \\ \bar{x} &= ? \end{aligned}$$

$$(\bar{x}) = \frac{(60000)(150) - (7854)(100)}{60000 - 7854} \rightarrow (\bar{x}) = \frac{8.21 \times 10^6}{52146}$$

$$(\bar{x}) = 158\ \text{mm}$$
questions.explanation: The trap is subtracting the hole's area in the numerator but forgetting to subtract it in the denominator (137 mm) — the hole removes area from the total too.
questions.videoTitle: Centroid & Centre of Gravity

questions.question: A rope is wrapped 1.5 turns around a rough capstan. The coefficient of static friction between the rope and the capstan is 0.30. What is the maximum ratio of the tight-side tension to the loose-side tension just before slipping impends?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Belt Friction section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(T_2/T_1\). We can determine it from the capstan equation:

$$\frac{T_2}{T_1} = e^{\mu \beta}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(T_2/T_1\):

$$\begin{aligned} \mu &= 0.30 \\ \beta &= 1.5(2\pi) = 9.42\ \text{rad} \\ T_2/T_1 &= ? \end{aligned}$$

$$\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right) = e^{(0.30)(9.42)} \rightarrow e^{2.83}$$

$$\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right) = 16.9$$
questions.explanation: The trap is plugging 1.5 straight in for β — the capstan equation needs the contact angle in radians, so 1.5 turns must become 3π radians first.

questions.question: At one joint of a simple truss, three members meet: two are collinear and the third is perpendicular to them. No external load or support reaction acts at the joint. Which member(s) must be zero-force members?
questions.solution:
The governing principle is joint equilibrium: \(\sum F_x = 0\) and \(\sum F_y = 0\) must both hold at every truss joint.

Summing forces perpendicular to the collinear pair, the only force component in that direction comes from the perpendicular member \u2014 and with no external load at the joint, that component must be zero. Hence the perpendicular member is a zero-force member.

The two collinear members, by contrast, can still carry equal and opposite forces that balance each other, so they are not necessarily zero-force. Therefore only the perpendicular member must be a zero-force member.
questions.explanation: The trap is 'all three' — the two collinear members can carry equal and opposite forces that cancel; only the perpendicular member has nothing to balance it.

questions.question: A 5 kg block slides on a frictionless horizontal surface at 4 m/s and strikes a spring of stiffness 800 N/m, compressing it until the block momentarily stops. What is the maximum compression of the spring?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Principle of Work and Energy section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).
