Ultimately, we must solve for \(x_{max}\). At maximum compression the block's kinetic energy has been fully converted to elastic potential energy:

$$T_1 + V_{e1} = T_2 + V_{e2} \rightarrow \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}kx_{max}^2$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(x_{max}\):

$$\begin{aligned} m &= 5\ \text{kg} \\ v &= 4\ \text{m/s} \\ k &= 800\ \text{N/m} \\ x_{max} &= ? \end{aligned}$$

$$(x_{max}) = v\sqrt{m/k} \rightarrow (4)\sqrt{5/800}$$

$$(x_{max}) = 0.316\ \text{m} = 316\ \text{mm}$$
questions.explanation: The trap is dropping the 1/2 on only one side of the energy equation (224 mm) — kinetic and elastic potential energy both carry the one-half factor.
questions.videoTitle: Principle of Work and Energy (Learn to solve any problem)

questions.question: A flywheel rotating at 600 rpm is brought to rest with constant angular deceleration in 20 s. How many revolutions does it make while stopping?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Rigid Body Rotation About a Fixed Axis section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(\\theta\\). The handbook gives, for constant angular acceleration \\(\\alpha\\):

$$\\omega = \\omega_0 + \\alpha\\,t$$

$$\\theta = \\theta_0 + \\omega_0\\,t + \\tfrac{1}{2}\\alpha\\,t^2$$

Eliminate \\(\\alpha\\) using \\(\\alpha = (\\omega - \\omega_0)/t\\) (taking \\(\\theta_0 = 0\\)):

$$\\theta = \\omega_0\\,t + \\tfrac{1}{2}(\\omega - \\omega_0)\\,t = \\frac{\\omega_0 + \\omega}{2}\\,t$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \\(\\theta\\):

$$\\begin{aligned} \\omega_0 &= 600\\ \\text{rpm} = 10\\ \\text{rev/s} \\\\ \\omega &= 0 \\\\ t &= 20\\ \\text{s} \\\\ \\theta &= ? \\end{aligned}$$

$$(\\theta) = \\frac{10 + 0}{2}(20) \\rightarrow (\\theta) = 100\\ \\text{rev}$$
questions.explanation: The trap is 6000 — multiplying 600 rpm by 20 s without converting revolutions per minute to revolutions per second first.

questions.question: A 1500 kg car traveling at 20 m/s rear-ends a stationary 1000 kg car, and the two lock together on impact. Neglect external impulses during the short impact. What is their common speed just after impact?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Impulse and Momentum section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(v'\). Linear momentum is conserved through the impact:

$$m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2 = (m_1 + m_2)v'$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(v'\):

$$\begin{aligned} m_1 &= 1500\ \text{kg},\ v_1 = 20\ \text{m/s} \\ m_2 &= 1000\ \text{kg},\ v_2 = 0 \\ v' &= ? \end{aligned}$$

$$(v') = \frac{(1500)(20) + (1000)(0)}{1500 + 1000} \rightarrow \frac{30000}{2500}$$

$$(v') = 12.0\ \text{m/s}$$
questions.explanation: The trap is 8.00 m/s — using the struck car's mass in the numerator instead of the moving car's mass.
questions.videoTitle: Impulse Momentum Theorem Physics Problems - Average Force & Contact Time

questions.question: A point on a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis is 0.5 m from the axis. If the angular acceleration of the body is 6 rad/s², what is the magnitude of the point's tangential acceleration?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Plane Circular Motion section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the tangential acceleration. For plane circular motion, the handbook gives the transverse (tangential) acceleration as the radius times the angular acceleration:

$$a_\theta = r\alpha$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(a_\theta\):

$$\begin{aligned} r &= 0.5\ \text{m} \\ \alpha &= 6\ \text{rad/s}^2 \\ a_\theta &= ? \end{aligned}$$

$$(a_\theta) = (0.5)(6) \rightarrow (a_\theta) = 3.00\ \text{m/s}^2$$
questions.explanation: The trap is 12.0 — dividing α by r instead of multiplying; tangential acceleration grows with radius, a_t = rα.

questions.question: A car enters a horizontal curve of radius 100 m at a speed of 20 m/s while accelerating tangentially at 2.0 m/s². What is the magnitude of the car's total acceleration at that instant?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Particle Curvilinear Motion section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(a\). The normal and tangential components combine as perpendicular vectors:

$$a = \sqrt{a_n^2 + a_t^2}, \quad a_n = \frac{v^2}{\rho}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(a\):

$$\begin{aligned} v &= 20\ \text{m/s} \\ \rho &= 100\ \text{m} \\ a_t &= 2.0\ \text{m/s}^2 \\ a &= ? \end{aligned}$$

First, \((a_n) = (20)^2/100 = 4.00\ \text{m/s}^2\). Then:

$$(a) = \sqrt{(4.00)^2 + (2.00)^2} \rightarrow \sqrt{20.0}$$

$$(a) = 4.47\ \text{m/s}^2$$
questions.explanation: The trap is 6.00 — adding the components directly; normal and tangential accelerations are perpendicular, so they combine by the Pythagorean theorem.

questions.question: A hoist motor lifts a 500 N weight vertically at a constant speed of 2 m/s. What mechanical power does the motor develop?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Power and Efficiency section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(P\). Mechanical power is force times velocity in the direction of the force:

$$P = F \cdot v$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(P\):

$$\begin{aligned} F &= 500\ \text{N} \\ v &= 2\ \text{m/s} \\ P &= ? \end{aligned}$$

$$(P) = (500)(2) \rightarrow (P) = 1000\ \text{W} = 1.00\ \text{kW}$$
questions.explanation: The trap is 0.25 kW — dividing force by velocity; power is force times velocity, and at constant speed the motor force equals the weight.

questions.question: A short 100 mm × 150 mm rectangular column carries a 60 kN compressive load applied with an eccentricity of 40 mm from the centroidal axis (measured along the 150 mm dimension). What is the maximum compressive stress in the column?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\sigma_{max}\). Eccentric loading superimposes uniform axial stress and bending stress:

$$\sigma_{max} = \frac{P}{A} + \frac{Mc}{I}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\sigma_{max}\):

$$\begin{aligned} P &= 60.0\ \text{kN} \\ A &= (0.100)(0.150) = 0.0150\ \text{m}^2 \\ M &= Pe = (60.0)(0.040) = 2.40\ \text{kN-m} \\ c &= 75.0\ \text{mm} \\ I &= 2.81 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m}^4 \\ \sigma_{max} &= ? \end{aligned}$$

$$(\sigma_{max}) = \frac{60000}{0.0150} + \frac{(2400)(0.075)}{2.81 \times 10^{-5}} \rightarrow 4.00\ \text{MPa} + 6.40\ \text{MPa}$$

$$(\sigma_{max}) = 10.4\ \text{MPa (C)}$$
questions.explanation: The trap is 6.40 MPa — computing only the bending stress and forgetting the uniform axial compression adds on top of it.
questions.videoTitle: Strength of Materials - Combined Stresses (Sample Problem)

questions.question: A 4 m simply supported beam carries a uniformly distributed load of 5 kN/m over its entire span. With E = 200 GPa and I = 40 × 10⁶ mm⁴, what is the maximum deflection of the beam?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Deflection of Beams section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\delta_{max}\). For a simply supported beam under uniform load:

$$\delta_{max} = \frac{5wL^4}{384EI}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\delta_{max}\):

$$\begin{aligned} w &= 5.00\ \text{kN/m} = 5000\ \text{N/m} \\ L &= 4.00\ \text{m} \\ E &= 200\ \text{GPa} \\ I &= 40.0 \times 10^6\ \text{mm}^4 = 40.0 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^4 \\ \delta_{max} &= ? \end{aligned}$$

$$(\delta_{max}) = \frac{5(5000)(4.00)^4}{384(200 \times 10^9)(40.0 \times 10^{-6})} \rightarrow \frac{6.40 \times 10^6}{3.07 \times 10^9}$$

$$(\delta_{max}) = 2.08 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m} = 2.08\ \text{mm downward}$$
questions.explanation: The trap is 3.33 mm — using the point-load formula PL³/48EI with P = wL; the uniform-load formula has its own 5/384 coefficient.
questions.videoTitle: Problem 12.39 Determine the maximum deflection of the beam

questions.question: At a point in a machine part, the in-plane stress state is σ_x = 80 MPa (tensile), σ_y = 40 MPa (compressive), and τ_xy = 30 MPa. What are the in-plane principal stresses?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Principal Stresses section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\):

$$\sigma_{1,2} = \frac{\sigma_x + \sigma_y}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{\sigma_x - \sigma_y}{2}\right)^2 + \tau_{xy}^2}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\):

$$\begin{aligned} \sigma_x &= 80.0\ \text{MPa} \\ \sigma_y &= -40.0\ \text{MPa} \\ \tau_{xy} &= 30.0\ \text{MPa} \\ \sigma_1, \sigma_2 &= ? \end{aligned}$$

$$(\sigma_{1,2}) = \frac{80.0 + (-40.0)}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{80.0 - (-40.0)}{2}\right)^2 + (30.0)^2} \rightarrow 20.0 \pm 67.1\ \text{MPa}$$

$$(\sigma_1, \sigma_2) = (87.1\ \text{MPa},\ -47.1\ \text{MPa})$$
questions.explanation: The trap is answering with the given 80/−40 stresses — those act on the x and y faces, not the principal planes; the shear term rotates the principal values away from them.
questions.videoTitle: For each of the plane stress states listed below, draw a Mohr's circle diagram...

questions.question: A 20 mm diameter bolt fastens three plates together so that the bolt is subjected to double shear. If the total shear force transferred through the joint is 60 kN, what is the shear stress in the bolt?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Shear Stress-Strain section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\tau\). With two shear planes the force is spread over twice the cross-sectional area:

$$\tau = \frac{V}{2A}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\tau\):

$$\begin{aligned} V &= 60.0\ \text{kN} \\ d &= 20.0\ \text{mm} \\ A &= \pi(10.0)^2 = 314\ \text{mm}^2 \\ \tau &= ? \end{aligned}$$

$$(\tau) = \frac{60000}{2(3.14 \times 10^{-4})} \rightarrow \frac{60000}{6.28 \times 10^{-4}}$$

$$(\tau) = 95.5\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.explanation: The trap is 191 MPa — treating it as single shear; with three plates there are two shear planes, so the resisting area doubles.
questions.videoTitle: Double Shear Joint – Solved Example Step by Step

questions.question: A 200 mm long aluminum bar with a 20 mm diameter (E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.33) is subjected to a 50 kN axial tensile load. What is the change in the bar's diameter?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Poisson's ratio definition in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6), in the elastic-constants definitions just above the "Bulk (Volume) Modulus of Elasticity" section on printed p. 131. That section defines \(\nu = -(\text{lateral strain})/(\text{longitudinal strain})\), so \(\epsilon_{lat} = -\nu\,\epsilon_{axial}\) is a direct rearrangement of the printed definition.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\Delta d\). Lateral strain is Poisson's ratio times the axial strain, with opposite sign:

$$\epsilon_{lat} = -\nu\,\epsilon_{axial}, \quad \Delta d = d\,\epsilon_{lat}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\Delta d\):

$$\begin{aligned} P &= 50.0\ \text{kN} \\ d &= 20.0\ \text{mm} \\ E &= 70.0\ \text{GPa} \\ \nu &= 0.33 \\ \Delta d &= ? \end{aligned}$$

$$(\sigma) = P/A = 50000/[\pi(0.010)^2]$$

$$(\sigma) = 159\ \text{MPa}$$

$$(\epsilon_{axial}) = \sigma/E = 159 \times 10^6/(70 \times 10^9)$$

$$(\epsilon_{axial}) = 2.27 \times 10^{-3}$$

$$(\Delta d) = (d)(-\nu)(\epsilon_{axial}) = (20.0)(-0.33)(2.27 \times 10^{-3})$$

$$(\Delta d) = -0.0150\ \text{mm (the diameter decreases)}$$
questions.explanation: The trap is 0.0455 mm — using the axial strain directly as the lateral strain and skipping Poisson's ratio entirely.
questions.videoTitle: Fundamental Problem 3.13 Relating Stress, elongation, change in dimensions due to applied forces

questions.question: A solid steel shaft (G = 79 GPa) with a diameter of 50 mm and a length of 2 m transmits a torque of 800 N-m. What is the angle of twist between its ends?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Torsion section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\phi\):

$$\phi = \frac{TL}{GJ}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\phi\):

$$\begin{aligned} T &= 800\ \text{N-m} \\ L &= 2.00\ \text{m} \\ d &= 50.0\ \text{mm} \\ J &= \pi d^4/32 = 6.14 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^4 \\ G &= 79.0\ \text{GPa} \\ \phi &= ? \end{aligned}$$

$$(\phi) = \frac{(800)(2.00)}{(79 \times 10^9)(6.14 \times 10^{-7})} \rightarrow 0.0330\ \text{rad}$$

$$(\phi) = 0.0330\ \text{rad} = 1.89^\circ$$
questions.explanation: The trap is 0.0330° — forgetting to convert radians to degrees; the formula gives radians, and 0.033 rad is nearly two degrees.
questions.videoTitle: Torsion of Stepped Shaft: Find Max Moment M & Total Angle of Twist

questions.question: A sieve analysis of a fine aggregate gives these cumulative percentages retained: 2% on the No. 4 sieve, 15% on No. 8, 35% on No. 16, 60% on No. 30, 82% on No. 50, and 95% on the No. 100 sieve. What is the fineness modulus of this aggregate?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Materials Science/Structure of Matter chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(FM\). The fineness modulus is the sum of the cumulative percentages retained on the standard sieves, divided by 100:

$$FM = \frac{\sum (\text{cumulative \% retained})}{100}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(FM\):

$$\begin{aligned} \text{No. 4, 8, 16, 30, 50, 100 retained} &= 2,\ 15,\ 35,\ 60,\ 82,\ 95\ \% \\ FM &= ? \end{aligned}$$

$$(FM) = \frac{2 + 15 + 35 + 60 + 82 + 95}{100} \rightarrow \frac{289}{100}$$

$$(FM) = 2.89$$
questions.explanation: The trap is 3.11 — summing the percent passing instead of the percent retained; fineness modulus is defined on cumulative retained.
questions.videoTitle: How To Calculate Fineness Modulus Of Aggregate

questions.question: A steel test specimen has a yield strength of 250 MPa and a modulus of elasticity of 200 GPa. What is the modulus of resilience of the steel?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Elastic Strain Energy section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(U_r\). We can determine \(U_r\) from the following equation:

$$U_r = \frac{\sigma_y^2}{2E}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(U_r\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\sigma_y &= 250\ \text{MPa} \\
E &= 200\ \text{GPa} = 200{,}000\ \text{MPa} \\
U_r &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(U_r) = \frac{(\sigma_y)^2}{2E} \rightarrow (U_r) = \frac{(250)^2}{2(200{,}000)}$$

$$(U_r) = 0.156\ \text{MPa} = 156\ \text{kJ/m}^3$$
questions.explanation: The modulus of resilience needs the 2 in the denominator — dropping it doubles the answer to 313 kJ/m^3. Convert GPa to MPa before dividing, and remember 1 MPa equals 1,000 kJ/m^3.

questions.question: A unidirectional fiber-reinforced composite is loaded parallel to the fibers. The composite contains 60% by volume glass fibers (E = 70 GPa) and 40% by volume epoxy matrix (E = 3 GPa). Estimate the elastic modulus of the composite.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Composite Materials section in the Materials Science/Structure of Matter chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(E_c\). We can determine \(E_c\) from the following equation:

$$E_c = E_f V_f + E_m V_m$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(E_c\):

$$\begin{aligned}
E_f &= 70\ \text{GPa} \\
V_f &= 0.60 \\
E_m &= 3\ \text{GPa} \\
V_m &= 0.40 \\
E_c &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(E_c) = E_f V_f + E_m V_m \rightarrow (E_c) = (70)(0.60) + (3)(0.40)$$

$$(E_c) = 42 + 1.2 = 43.2\ \text{GPa}$$
questions.explanation: Loading parallel to the fibers means the isostrain (Voigt) rule of mixtures applies. The inverse harmonic form (7.05 GPa) is for loading transverse to the fibers — the classic mix-up.

questions.question: The specified 28-day compressive strength of a normal-weight concrete is f'_c = 25 MPa. Using the ACI 318 relationship, estimate the modulus of elasticity of the concrete.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(E_c\). We can determine \(E_c\) from the following equation:

$$E_c = 4700\sqrt{f'_c}\ \text{(MPa)}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(E_c\):

$$\begin{aligned}
f'_c &= 25\ \text{MPa} \\
E_c &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(E_c) = 4700\sqrt{f'_c} \rightarrow (E_c) = 4700\sqrt{25}$$

$$(E_c) = 23{,}500\ \text{MPa} = 23.5\ \text{GPa}$$
questions.explanation: The 4,700 multiplier already expects f'_c in MPa under the square root — skipping the root gives 117.5 GPa, and plugging in a doubled strength gives 33.2 GPa.

questions.question: The ductile-to-brittle transition temperature of a structural steel, determined from Charpy V-notch impact tests, is best described as:
choices: The temperature below which the steel fractures with little plastic deformation
The temperature at which creep deformation becomes significant
The highest temperature at which the steel retains its full yield strength
The temperature at which the fatigue endurance limit drops to zero
questions.solution:
Structural steels with a body-centered cubic crystal structure absorb far less impact energy below a critical temperature.

The Charpy V-notch test measures the energy absorbed in fracturing a notched specimen at various temperatures. Above the transition temperature the fracture is ductile (high energy absorbed); below it the fracture is brittle cleavage with little plastic deformation.

Therefore the transition temperature marks the boundary below which the steel fractures with little plastic deformation — a fracture-mode boundary, not a strength limit.
questions.explanation: Do not confuse the transition temperature with a strength limit — it is about fracture mode (energy absorbed), which is why an impact test, not a tensile test, defines it.

questions.question: A pitot tube in a water stream indicates a stagnation pressure head 0.15 m above the static pressure head. What is the flow velocity?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Fluid Flow Measurement section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(V\). We can determine \(V\) from the following equation:

$$V = \sqrt{2g(\Delta h)}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(V\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\Delta h &= 0.15\ \text{m} \\
g &= 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2 \\
V &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(V) = \sqrt{2g(\Delta h)} \rightarrow (V) = \sqrt{2(9.81)(0.15)}$$

$$(V) = 1.72\ \text{m/s}$$
questions.explanation: The pitot equation has 2g under the radical — using just sqrt(g times delta-h) gives 1.21 m/s. Also confirm delta-h is in meters of the flowing fluid, not millimeters.
questions.videoTitle: Solved Problem: Measurement of Air Velocity with a Pitot Tube

questions.question: Water discharges to the atmosphere through a sharp-edged circular orifice 50 mm in diameter at the bottom of a large tank. The water surface is 4.0 m above the orifice centerline, and the discharge coefficient is C_d = 0.62. What is the discharge?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Orifice Discharging Freely into Atmosphere section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(Q\). We can determine \(Q\) from the following equation:

$$Q = C_d A\sqrt{2gh}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(Q\):

$$\begin{aligned}
d &= 0.05\ \text{m} \\
A &= \frac{\pi d^2}{4} = 0.00196\ \text{m}^2 \\
h &= 4.0\ \text{m} \\
g &= 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2 \\
C_d &= 0.62 \\
Q &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(Q) = C_d A\sqrt{2gh} \rightarrow (Q) = (0.62)(0.00196)\sqrt{2(9.81)(4.0)}$$

$$(Q) = 0.0108\ \text{m}^3/\text{s} = 10.8\ \text{L/s}$$
questions.explanation: Two classic traps: omitting C_d (17.4 L/s) and using the diameter as the radius (43.1 L/s). Always compute A = pi-d-squared over 4 first, then multiply by C_d last as a sanity check.
questions.videoTitle: Flow through an Orifice - Explained.

questions.question: Oil with dynamic viscosity 0.10 Pa-s flows at 0.50 m/s through a horizontal pipe 100 m long with 50 mm inside diameter. Assuming fully developed laminar flow, what is the pressure drop in the pipe?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Pressure Drop for a Fluid of Constant Density section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\Delta p\). We can determine \(\Delta p\) from the following equation:

$$\Delta p = \frac{32\mu L V}{D^2}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\Delta p\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\mu &= 0.10\ \text{Pa}\cdot\text{s} \\
L &= 100\ \text{m} \\
V &= 0.50\ \text{m/s} \\
D &= 0.05\ \text{m} \\
\Delta p &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\Delta p) = \frac{32\mu L V}{D^2} \rightarrow (\Delta p) = \frac{32(0.10)(100)(0.50)}{(0.05)^2}$$

$$(\Delta p) = 64{,}000\ \text{Pa} = 64.0\ \text{kPa}$$
questions.explanation: In the velocity form the diameter is squared (D-squared), not raised to the fourth power — D-to-the-fourth belongs to the discharge form. Plugging the radius in as D quadruples the answer to 256 kPa.

questions.question: A 2.0 m cube floats in fresh water with 1.2 m of its depth submerged. What is the mass density of the cube?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Archimedes Principle and Buoyancy section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\rho_{body}\). At equilibrium the weight of the body equals the buoyant force:

$$\rho_{body} V_{total} = \rho_{water} V_{submerged}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\rho_{body}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\rho_{water} &= 1000\ \text{kg/m}^3 \\
h_{sub} &= 1.2\ \text{m} \\
h_{total} &= 2.0\ \text{m} \\
\rho_{body} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\rho_{body}) = \rho_{water}\frac{h_{sub}}{h_{total}} \rightarrow (\rho_{body}) = (1000)\frac{1.2}{2.0}$$

$$(\rho_{body}) = 600\ \text{kg/m}^3$$
questions.explanation: The body density is the water density times the submerged fraction — always submerged over total, which must come out less than water. Inverting the fraction gives the impossible 1,667 kg/m^3 for a floating object.
questions.videoTitle: Buoyant Force and Archimedes' Principle

questions.question: Water flows at 2.0 m/s through a pipe entrance (K = 0.5), a fully open gate valve (K = 2.5), and a pipe exit (K = 1.0). What is the total minor head loss?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Minor Losses in Pipe Fittings, Contractions, and Expansions section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(h_m\). We can determine \(h_m\) from the following equation:

$$h_m = \left(\sum K\right)\frac{V^2}{2g}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(h_m\):

$$\begin{aligned}
K_{entrance} &= 0.5 \\
K_{valve} &= 2.5 \\
K_{exit} &= 1.0 \\
\sum K &= 4.0 \\
V &= 2.0\ \text{m/s} \\
g &= 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2 \\
h_m &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(h_m) = \left(\sum K\right)\frac{V^2}{2g} \rightarrow (h_m) = (4.0)\frac{(2.0)^2}{2(9.81)}$$

$$(h_m) = 0.82\ \text{m}$$
questions.explanation: The velocity head is V-squared over 2g — forgetting the 2 doubles it to 1.63 m, and the pipe exit (K = 1.0) is the minor-loss coefficient most often left out (0.61 m).
questions.videoTitle: Mechanical HVAC PE Exam - Question 112 - Minor System Head Loss

questions.question: A differential leveling run starts at BM-A (elevation 50.00 m). The backsight readings are 1.42 m, 2.15 m, and 0.98 m; the foresight readings are 0.85 m, 1.77 m, and 1.60 m. What is the elevation of the final point?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the final elevation. The arithmetic (page) check gives:

$$\text{Elev}_{final} = \text{Elev}_{initial} + \sum BS - \sum FS$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for the final elevation:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Elev}_{initial} &= 50.00\ \text{m} \\
\sum BS &= 1.42 + 2.15 + 0.98 = 4.55\ \text{m} \\
\sum FS &= 0.85 + 1.77 + 1.60 = 4.22\ \text{m} \\
\text{Elev}_{final} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\text{Elev}_{final}) = 50.00 + \sum BS - \sum FS \rightarrow (\text{Elev}_{final}) = 50.00 + 4.55 - 4.22$$

$$(\text{Elev}_{final}) = 50.33\ \text{m}$$
questions.explanation: The page check is final minus initial equals sum-of-backsights minus sum-of-foresights — backsights add, foresights subtract. Reversing them gives 49.67 m, and adding the foresights instead of subtracting gives 54.55 m.
questions.videoTitle: Survey Leveling Calculations and Adjustment

questions.question: A course has an azimuth of 150 degrees (measured clockwise from north) and a length of 120 m. What is the departure of the course?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Latitudes and Departures section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the departure. We can determine it from the following equation:

$$\text{Departure} = L\sin(\text{azimuth})$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for the departure:

$$\begin{aligned}
L &= 120\ \text{m} \\
\text{Azimuth} &= 150^\circ \\
\text{Departure} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\text{Departure}) = L\sin(150^\circ) \rightarrow (\text{Departure}) = (120)(0.50)$$

$$(\text{Departure}) = +60.0\ \text{m}$$
questions.explanation: Departure uses sine of the azimuth (latitude uses cosine) — swapping them gives the latitude, -103.9 m. In the southeast quadrant (90 to 180 degrees) the departure is eastward, hence positive.
questions.videoTitle: Balance the traverse by using Bowditch rule

questions.question: A simple horizontal curve has a radius of 300 m and an intersection angle of 24 degrees. What is the external distance (from the PI to the curve)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Horizontal Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(E\). We can determine \(E\) from the following equation:

$$E = R\left(\sec\frac{I}{2} - 1\right)$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(E\):

$$\begin{aligned}
R &= 300\ \text{m} \\
I &= 24^\circ \\
E &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(E) = R\left(\sec\frac{I}{2} - 1\right) \rightarrow (E) = (300)\left(\sec 12^\circ - 1\right)$$

$$(E) = (300)(0.02234) = 6.70\ \text{m}$$
questions.explanation: E = R(sec(I/2) - 1) is the distance from the PI to the curve; the middle ordinate M = R(1 - cos(I/2)) = 6.56 m looks nearly identical numerically but measures from the curve to the chord midpoint. And 63.8 m is the tangent length — a different element entirely.
questions.videoTitle: Horizontal Curves Elements Part 1 of 2

questions.question: A sag vertical curve connects a -2.0% grade to a +3.0% grade. The curve is 200 m long, and the PVC is at station 10+00 with elevation 100.00 m. What is the elevation on the curve at the PVI station?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vertical Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the curve elevation at the PVI. The PVI is at \(x = L/2 = 100\) m from the PVC:

$$\text{Elev}_{curve} = \text{Elev}_{tangent} + \frac{Ax^2}{2L}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for the curve elevation:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Elev}_{PVC} &= 100.00\ \text{m} \\
g_1 &= -0.02 \\
x &= 100\ \text{m} \\
\text{Elev}_{tangent} &= 100.00 + (-0.02)(100) = 98.00\ \text{m} \\
A &= g_2 - g_1 = 0.03 - (-0.02) = 0.05 \\
\text{Elev}_{curve} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\text{Elev}_{curve}) = 98.00 + \frac{Ax^2}{2L} \rightarrow (\text{Elev}_{curve}) = 98.00 + \frac{(0.05)(100)^2}{2(200)}$$

$$(\text{Elev}_{curve}) = 98.00 + 1.25 = 99.25\ \text{m}$$
questions.explanation: On a sag curve the parabola sits above the tangent, so the offset adds (+1.25 m) — subtracting it (96.75 m) is the crest-curve habit. Compute the tangent elevation at the PVI first, then apply the offset.
questions.videoTitle: VERTICAL CURVES - Solving for SUMMIT, and ELEVATION and GRADE of CURVE! (SURVEYING)

questions.question: An embankment requires 10,000 m^3 of compacted fill. Laboratory tests indicate the borrow soil will undergo 15% shrinkage when compacted. What volume of borrow (bank cubic meters) must be excavated?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earthwork formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(V_{bank}\). Shrinkage relates bank and compacted volumes by:

$$V_{bank} = \frac{V_{compacted}}{1 - \text{shrinkage}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(V_{bank}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
V_{compacted} &= 10{,}000\ \text{m}^3 \\
\text{shrinkage} &= 0.15 \\
V_{bank} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(V_{bank}) = \frac{V_{compacted}}{1 - 0.15} \rightarrow (V_{bank}) = \frac{10{,}000}{0.85}$$

$$(V_{bank}) = 11{,}765\ \text{m}^3$$
questions.explanation: Shrinkage means you need MORE bank volume, so divide by (1 - shrinkage) — multiplying by 0.85 (8,500 m^3) goes the wrong direction, and multiplying by 1.15 (11,500 m^3) confuses shrinkage with swell.

questions.question: A cantilever beam 4 m long carries a uniformly distributed load of 3 kN/m over its entire length. What is the maximum bending moment, and where does it occur?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Structural Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(M_{max}\). We can determine \(M_{max}\) from the following equation:

$$M_{max} = \frac{wL^2}{2}\ \text{(at the fixed support)}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(M_{max}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
w &= 3\ \text{kN/m} \\
L &= 4\ \text{m} \\
M_{max} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(M_{max}) = \frac{wL^2}{2} \rightarrow (M_{max}) = \frac{(3)(4)^2}{2}$$

$$(M_{max}) = 24\ \text{kN}\cdot\text{m}\ \text{at the fixed support}$$
questions.explanation: The simply supported formula wL-squared over 8 gives 6 kN-m — the classic wrong-formula trap. On a cantilever the moment accumulates toward the wall, peaking at wL-squared over 2.
questions.videoTitle: How to Draw Shear Force and Moment Diagrams

questions.question: A symmetric triangular roof truss spans 6 m with a peak height of 3 m at midspan. It is pin-supported at A (left) and roller-supported at B (right), and carries a single 20 kN vertical load at the peak joint C. Using the method of joints at A, what is the force in the top-chord member AC?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Structural Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(F_{AC}\). By symmetry each vertical reaction is 10 kN, and joint A equilibrium in the vertical direction gives:

$$\sum F_y = 0 = A_y + F_{AC}\sin\theta$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(F_{AC}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
A_y &= 10\ \text{kN (upward)} \\
\theta &= \tan^{-1}\frac{3}{3} = 45^\circ \\
F_{AC} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(F_{AC}) = \frac{-A_y}{\sin\theta} \rightarrow (F_{AC}) = \frac{-10}{\sin 45^\circ}$$

$$(F_{AC}) = -14.1\ \text{kN} = 14.1\ \text{kN (C)}$$
questions.explanation: The negative sign from joint equilibrium means compression — taking the magnitude as tension is the standard sign error. And 10.0 kN comes from forgetting to divide by sin(theta), using the reaction directly as the member force.
questions.videoTitle: SA04: Truss Analysis: Method of Joints

questions.question: A rectangular reinforced concrete beam has b = 300 mm, effective depth d = 550 mm, and is reinforced with 3-25 mm bars (A_s = 1,473 mm^2). Given f'_c = 28 MPa and f_y = 420 MPa, what is the nominal flexural strength M_n? (Assume the section is tension-controlled and the Whitney stress block applies.)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Beams—Flexure section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(M_n\). First find the Whitney stress block depth, then the nominal strength:

$$a = \frac{A_s f_y}{0.85 f'_c b}, \qquad M_n = A_s f_y\left(d - \frac{a}{2}\right)$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(M_n\):

$$\begin{aligned}
A_s &= 1473\ \text{mm}^2 \\
f_y &= 420\ \text{MPa} \\
f'_c &= 28\ \text{MPa} \\
b &= 300\ \text{mm} \\
d &= 550\ \text{mm} \\
a &= \frac{(1473)(420)}{0.85(28)(300)} = 86.6\ \text{mm} \\
M_n &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(M_n) = A_s f_y\left(d - \frac{a}{2}\right) \rightarrow (M_n) = (1473)(420)\left(550 - \frac{86.6}{2}\right)$$

$$(M_n) = 313 \times 10^6\ \text{N}\cdot\text{mm} = 313\ \text{kN}\cdot\text{m}$$
questions.explanation: Nominal strength uses the full Whitney block with the (d - a/2) lever arm — dropping the a/2 gives 340 kN-m, and applying phi = 0.90 gives the design strength (282 kN-m), not the nominal strength the question asks for.
questions.videoTitle: [2/3] Singly Reinforced Rectangular Beam: Design Problem (NSCP 2010/2015)

questions.question: A steel column has an effective slenderness ratio KL/r = 100. Using E = 200 GPa, what is the Euler critical buckling stress?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Columns section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\sigma_{cr}\). We can determine \(\sigma_{cr}\) from the following equation:

$$\sigma_{cr} = \frac{\pi^2 E}{(KL/r)^2}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\sigma_{cr}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
E &= 200\ \text{GPa} = 200{,}000\ \text{MPa} \\
KL/r &= 100 \\
\sigma_{cr} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\sigma_{cr}) = \frac{\pi^2 E}{(KL/r)^2} \rightarrow (\sigma_{cr}) = \frac{\pi^2(200{,}000)}{(100)^2}$$

$$(\sigma_{cr}) = 197\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.explanation: Euler stress falls with the SQUARE of KL/r — forgetting the square blows the answer up to 19.7 GPa, which should immediately look wrong since it exceeds the steel's yield strength by nearly 100 times.
questions.videoTitle: Buckling Load Theory Explained

questions.question: A simply supported beam 6 m long carries a uniform load of 10 kN/m over its full length. E = 200 GPa and \(I = 40 \times 10^6\ \mathrm{mm}^4\). What is the maximum deflection?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Deflection of Beams section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\Delta_{max}\). We can determine \(\Delta_{max}\) from the following equation:

$$\Delta_{max} = \frac{5wL^4}{384EI}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\Delta_{max}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
w &= 10\ \text{kN/m} = 10{,}000\ \text{N/m} \\
L &= 6\ \text{m} \\
E &= 200\ \text{GPa} = 200 \times 10^9\ \text{Pa} \\
I &= 40 \times 10^6\ \text{mm}^4 = 4.0 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m}^4 \\
\Delta_{max} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\Delta_{max}) = \frac{5wL^4}{384EI} \rightarrow (\Delta_{max}) = \frac{5(10{,}000)(6)^4}{384(200 \times 10^9)(4.0 \times 10^{-5})}$$

$$(\Delta_{max}) = 0.0211\ \text{m} = 21.1\ \text{mm downward}$$
questions.explanation: Two traps: the mm^4-to-m^4 conversion (10^-12) — botching it shifts the answer by orders of magnitude — and grabbing the cantilever formula wL^4/(8EI), which gives 202 mm for a beam that is simply supported.
questions.videoTitle: Deflection of Beam

questions.question: A prismatic beam fixed at both ends carries a uniformly distributed load over its entire span. Where are the inflection points (points of zero moment) located?
questions.solution:
For a fixed-fixed beam under uniform load, the fixed-end moments are wL-squared over 12 (hogging) while the midspan moment is only wL-squared over 24 (sagging).

Because the support moment is twice the midspan moment, the moment diagram crosses zero closer to the supports than a symmetric quarter-point assumption would suggest. Solving the moment equation M(x) = 0 along the span gives the zero crossings at 0.211L from each fixed end.

Therefore the inflection points are located 0.211L from each fixed end.
questions.explanation: 0.25L is the trap for anyone who assumes the moment diagram is symmetric about the quarter points — the fixed-end moment (wL^2/12) is twice the midspan moment (wL^2/24), which pushes the zero crossing out to 0.211L.

questions.question: A 3-m-thick normally consolidated clay layer has an initial void ratio e₀ = 0.85 and a compression index Cc = 0.32. The initial vertical effective stress at the midpoint of the layer is 90 kPa, and a proposed building adds an average vertical stress increase of 60 kPa. What is the primary consolidation settlement of the layer?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Ultimate consolidation settlement in soil layer section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(s_c\). We can determine \(s_c\) from the following equation:

$$s_c = \frac{H_0}{1 + e_0} C_c \log\frac{\sigma'_{v0} + \Delta\sigma}{\sigma'_{v0}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(s_c\):

$$\begin{aligned}
H_0 &= 3.0\ \text{m} \\
e_0 &= 0.85 \\
C_c &= 0.32 \\
\sigma'_{v0} &= 90\ \text{kPa} \\
\Delta\sigma &= 60\ \text{kPa} \\
s_c &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(s_c) = \frac{3.0}{1 + 0.85}(0.32)\log\frac{90 + 60}{90} \rightarrow (s_c) = (1.6216)(0.32)(0.2219)$$

$$(s_c) = 0.115\ \text{m} = 11.5\ \text{cm}$$
questions.explanation: The (1 + e₀) term in the denominator is the classic trap — dropping it gives 21.3 cm. Also use base-10 log as the handbook writes it; natural log gives 26.5 cm.

questions.question: A soil profile consists of 3 m of dry sand (γ = 17 kN/m³) over 5 m of saturated clay (γ_sat = 19 kN/m³). The water table is at the sand–clay interface. What is the vertical effective stress at a depth of 8 m?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Effective Stress section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\sigma'\). We can determine \(\sigma'\) from the following equation:

$$\sigma' = \sigma - u$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\sigma'\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\gamma_{sand} &= 17\ \text{kN/m}^3 \\
\gamma_{sat} &= 19\ \text{kN/m}^3 \\
z_{sand} &= 3\ \text{m} \\
z_{clay} &= 5\ \text{m} \\
\sigma' &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\sigma) = 3(17) + 5(19) = 146\ \text{kPa}, \quad (u) = 5(9.81) = 49.1\ \text{kPa}$$

$$(\sigma') = 146 - 49.1 = 96.9 \approx 97\ \text{kPa}$$
questions.explanation: Pore pressure acts only below the water table — compute u from the 5 m of saturated clay, not the full 8 m. The 146 kPa total-stress answer is the most common trap.
questions.videoTitle: Effective Stress Principle

questions.question: A long natural slope inclined at β = 20° has seepage parallel to the ground surface. The soil has cohesion c = 12 kPa, friction angle φ = 25°, and saturated unit weight γ_sat = 20 kN/m³. For a potential failure plane 4 m below the surface, what is the factor of safety against sliding?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Slope Failure Along Planar Surface section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(FS\). We can determine \(FS\) from the following equation:

$$FS = \frac{c + \gamma' z \cos^2\beta \tan\phi}{\gamma_{sat} z \sin\beta \cos\beta}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(FS\):

$$\begin{aligned}
c &= 12\ \text{kPa} \\
\phi &= 25^\circ \\
\beta &= 20^\circ \\
z &= 4\ \text{m} \\
\gamma_{sat} &= 20\ \text{kN/m}^3 \\
\gamma' &= 20 - 9.81 = 10.19\ \text{kN/m}^3 \\
FS &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(FS) = \frac{12 + (10.19)(4)(0.8830)(0.4663)}{(20)(4)(0.3420)(0.9397)} \rightarrow (FS) = \frac{28.78}{25.71}$$

$$(FS) = 1.12$$
questions.explanation: With seepage parallel to the slope, the numerator uses buoyant weight γ′ while the denominator uses saturated weight — using γ_sat in both gives 1.75. Never drop the cohesion term (that gives 0.65).

questions.question: A 2-m-wide strip footing bears 1 m below the ground surface on a saturated clay with undrained shear strength c = 60 kPa (φ = 0) and total unit weight γ = 18 kN/m³. Using Terzaghi's bearing capacity theory, what is the ultimate bearing capacity of the soil?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Ultimate Bearing Capacity section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(q_{ult}\). We can determine \(q_{ult}\) from the following equation:

$$q_{ult} = cN_c + \gamma D_f N_q + \tfrac{1}{2}\gamma B N_{\gamma}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(q_{ult}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
c &= 60\ \text{kPa} \\
\phi &= 0^\circ \; \Rightarrow \; N_c = 5.7,\ N_q = 1.0,\ N_{\gamma} = 0 \; (\text{Terzaghi}) \\
B &= 2\ \text{m} \\
D_f &= 1\ \text{m} \\
\gamma &= 18\ \text{kN/m}^3 \\
q_{ult} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(q_{ult}) = (60)(5.7) + (18)(1)(1.0) + 0 \rightarrow (q_{ult}) = 342 + 18$$

$$(q_{ult}) = 360\ \text{kPa}$$
questions.explanation: For φ = 0, Nγ = 0 so the width term vanishes, but the overburden term γD_fN_q still counts — dropping it gives 342 kPa. Use Terzaghi's N_c = 5.7, not the general 5.14 (which gives 326 kPa).
questions.videoTitle: Bearing Capacity of Soil EXPLAINED: Terzaghi, Meyerhof, Hansen, Vesic, Skempton & IS Code

questions.question: A “quicksand” condition develops in a saturated sand deposit when which of the following occurs?
choices: The upward hydraulic gradient reaches the critical gradient, so the effective stress becomes zero
The downward hydraulic gradient exceeds the critical gradient
The void ratio exceeds the maximum void ratio of the sand
The degree of saturation drops below 100%
questions.solution:
The governing principle is the critical hydraulic gradient from the Seepage section of the Geotechnical Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook: upward seepage reduces effective stress, and quicksand occurs when \(i = i_c = \gamma'/\gamma_w\), at which point \(\sigma' = 0\).

Applying this to the choices: only upward seepage at the critical gradient wipes out intergranular contact stress. Downward seepage increases effective stress, void ratio limits are unrelated, and quicksand requires full saturation.

Therefore the quicksand condition is the upward gradient reaching the critical gradient with zero effective stress.
questions.explanation: Quicksand is a zero-effective-stress condition, not a “soil type” — the trap answers describe downward seepage (which strengthens soil) or unrelated index properties.

questions.question: A highway has a design speed of 60 mph and a 4% downgrade. Using a perception–reaction time of 2.5 s and a wet-pavement friction coefficient f = 0.35, what is the required stopping sight distance?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Stopping Sight Distance section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(SSD\). We can determine \(SSD\) from the following equation:

$$SSD = 1.47Vt + \frac{V^2}{30(f \pm G)}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(SSD\):

$$\begin{aligned}
V &= 60\ \text{mph} \\
t &= 2.5\ \text{s} \\
f &= 0.35 \\
G &= -0.04 \; (\text{downgrade, use } f - G = f + |G|) \\
SSD &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(SSD) = 1.47(60)(2.5) + \frac{(60)^2}{30(0.35 - 0.04)} \rightarrow (SSD) = 220.5 + 387.1$$

$$(SSD) = 607.6 \approx 608\ \text{ft}$$
questions.explanation: On a downgrade the grade term subtracts from friction (f − G with G negative), lengthening SSD — ignoring grade gives 563 ft, and adding it as an upgrade gives 528 ft.
questions.videoTitle: Stopping Sight Distance (SSD) – Explained with Real-Life Examples

questions.question: A traffic count shows a peak-hour volume of 3,800 veh/hr and a peak 15-minute volume of 1,050 veh within that hour. What is the peak hour factor (PHF)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Peak Hour Factor section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(PHF\). We can determine \(PHF\) from the following equation:

$$PHF = \frac{V}{4 \times V_{15}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(PHF\):

$$\begin{aligned}
V &= 3800\ \text{veh/hr} \\
V_{15} &= 1050\ \text{veh} \\
PHF &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(PHF) = \frac{3800}{4(1050)} \rightarrow (PHF) = \frac{3800}{4200}$$

$$(PHF) = 0.905 \approx 0.90$$
questions.explanation: PHF is always ≤ 1.0 — if your answer exceeds 1 (the inverted 1.11), you divided upside down. The 4 converts the 15-minute count to an hourly rate.

questions.question: A horizontal curve has a radius of 800 ft. If the required stopping sight distance along the curve is 500 ft, what is the minimum middle ordinate (lateral clearance) needed for sight distance?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Horizontal Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(M\). We can determine \(M\) from the following equation:

$$M = R\left[1 - \cos\left(\frac{28.65\,S}{R}\right)\right]$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(M\):

$$\begin{aligned}
R &= 800\ \text{ft} \\
S &= 500\ \text{ft} \\
M &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(M) = 800\left[1 - \cos\left(\frac{28.65(500)}{800}\right)\right] \rightarrow (M) = 800[1 - \cos(17.91^\circ)]$$

$$(M) = 800(0.0485) = 38.8\ \text{ft}$$
questions.explanation: The 28.65 factor converts the arc ratio to degrees — make sure the calculator is in degree mode. Halving or doubling the result (19.4 / 77.6 ft) comes from misplacing S in the formula.

questions.question: In flexible pavement design, what is the load equivalency factor (LEF) of a 24-kip single axle relative to the 18-kip standard axle, using the AASHTO fourth-power law?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Highway Pavement Design section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(LEF\). We can determine \(LEF\) from the following equation:

$$LEF = \left(\frac{W}{18}\right)^4$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(LEF\):

$$\begin{aligned}
W &= 24\ \text{kips} \\
LEF &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(LEF) = \left(\frac{24}{18}\right)^4 \rightarrow (LEF) = (1.333)^4$$

$$(LEF) = 3.16$$
questions.explanation: Damage scales with the FOURTH power of the load ratio — each wrong exponent is a trap: linear gives 1.33, squared 1.78, cubed 2.37.

questions.question: Under ideal conditions, what is the approximate capacity of a basic freeway segment per lane according to the Highway Capacity Manual?
choices: 2,400 passenger cars per hour per lane
1,900 passenger cars per hour per lane
3,400 passenger cars per hour per lane
1,000 passenger cars per hour per lane
questions.solution:
The governing reference is the capacity of basic freeway segments in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (per the Highway Capacity Manual): approximately 2,400 passenger cars per hour per lane under ideal conditions.

Applying this to the choices: 1,900 pc/h/ln is closer to a two-lane highway or signalized capacity, and 3,400 exceeds any realistic lane capacity.

Therefore the capacity is 2,400 passenger cars per hour per lane.
questions.explanation: 2,400 pc/h/ln is the HCM ideal freeway lane capacity — the trap answers borrow values from other facility types (two-lane highways, arterials).

questions.question: Water flows at 2 cfs through a 2,000-ft-long, 12-in.-diameter pipe with a Hazen-Williams coefficient C = 120. What is the head loss due to friction?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Hazen-Williams Equation section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(h_f\). We can determine \(h_f\) from the following equation:

$$h_f = \frac{4.73\,L\,Q^{1.852}}{C^{1.852}\,D^{4.87}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(h_f\):

$$\begin{aligned}
L &= 2000\ \text{ft} \\
Q &= 2.0\ \text{cfs} \\
C &= 120 \\
D &= 12\ \text{in.} = 1.0\ \text{ft} \\
h_f &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(h_f) = \frac{4.73(2000)(2.0)^{1.852}}{(120)^{1.852}(1.0)^{4.87}} \rightarrow (h_f) = \frac{34131}{7089.5}$$

$$(h_f) = 4.82\ \text{ft}$$
questions.explanation: Convert the 12-in. diameter to 1.0 ft before using the English-unit formula — with D = 12 the answer explodes. Head loss scales with Q^1.852, so doubling Q does not double h_f.

questions.question: A vertical rectangular gate 3 m wide and 2 m high has its top edge 1 m below the water surface. What is the magnitude of the total hydrostatic force on the gate?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Forces on Submerged Surfaces and the Center of Pressure section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(F\). We can determine \(F\) from the following equation:

$$F = \gamma h_c A$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(F\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\gamma &= 9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3 \\
h_c &= 1 + \tfrac{2}{2} = 2.0\ \text{m} \; (\text{centroid depth}) \\
A &= (3)(2) = 6.0\ \text{m}^2 \\
F &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(F) = (9.81)(2.0)(6.0)$$

$$(F) = 117.7 \approx 118\ \text{kN}$$
questions.explanation: Use the CENTROID depth (2 m), not the top edge (58.9 kN) or the bottom edge (177 kN) — that single choice of depth is the whole question.
questions.videoTitle: Sample problem on hydrostatic pressure on plane surfaces

questions.question: A 24-in.-diameter concrete pipe flows full on a slope of 0.004. If Manning's n = 0.013, what is the discharge?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Open-Channel Flow and/or Pipe Flow of Water section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(Q\). We can determine \(Q\) from the following equation:

$$Q = \frac{1.486}{n}\,A\,R^{2/3}\,S^{1/2}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(Q\):

$$\begin{aligned}
n &= 0.013 \\
D &= 24\ \text{in.} = 2.0\ \text{ft} \\
A &= \tfrac{\pi}{4}(2.0)^2 = 3.1416\ \text{ft}^2 \\
R &= D/4 = 0.50\ \text{ft} \; (\text{full circular pipe}) \\
S &= 0.004 \\
Q &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(Q) = \frac{1.486}{0.013}(3.1416)(0.50)^{2/3}(0.004)^{1/2} \rightarrow (Q) = (114.31)(3.1416)(0.6300)(0.06325)$$

$$(Q) = 14.3\ \text{cfs}$$
questions.explanation: English units need the 1.486 factor — dropping it gives 9.63 cfs. For a full circular pipe R = D/4, not D/2.
questions.videoTitle: How to Calculate Discharge (Q) in a Trapezoidal Channel

questions.question: In open-channel flow, a Froude number equal to 1.0 indicates which flow condition?
questions.solution:
The governing principle is the Froude number from the Open Channel Flow section of the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook: \(Fr = V/\sqrt{gy}\), with \(Fr < 1\) subcritical, \(Fr = 1\) critical, and \(Fr > 1\) supercritical.

Applying this to the choices: subcritical and supercritical correspond to Fr below and above 1.0, while uniform flow describes a constant-depth condition, not a Froude value.

Therefore a Froude number of 1.0 indicates critical flow.
questions.explanation: Fr = 1 is the dividing line by definition — subcritical is below, supercritical above. “Uniform” describes depth constancy, not the Froude regime.

questions.question: A watershed has a curve number CN = 80. For a storm with total rainfall P = 5.0 in., what is the direct runoff depth using the SCS (NRCS) method?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(Q\). We can determine \(Q\) from the following equations:

$$S = \frac{1000}{CN} - 10 \qquad Q = \frac{(P - 0.2S)^2}{P + 0.8S}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(Q\):

$$\begin{aligned}
CN &= 80 \\
P &= 5.0\ \text{in.} \\
S &= \tfrac{1000}{80} - 10 = 2.5\ \text{in.} \\
Q &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(Q) = \frac{(5.0 - 0.2(2.5))^2}{5.0 + 0.8(2.5)} \rightarrow (Q) = \frac{(4.5)^2}{7.0} = \frac{20.25}{7.0}$$

$$(Q) = 2.89\ \text{in.}$$
questions.explanation: Subtract the initial abstraction I_a = 0.2S before squaring — skipping it gives 3.57 in. The storage S itself (2.50 in.) is not the runoff.
questions.videoTitle: Example PE question: NRCS Runoff Depth for a Multi-Land-Use Watershed — PE WRE Exam Prep

questions.question: A loader needs 3 min to fill a truck. Each truck then hauls 4 min, dumps and spots in 2 min, and returns in 6 min. How many trucks are required to keep the loader working continuously?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(N\). We can determine \(N\) from the following equation:

$$N = \frac{\text{truck cycle time}}{\text{loader cycle time}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(N\):

$$\begin{aligned}
t_{load} &= 3\ \text{min} \\
t_{haul} &= 4\ \text{min} \\
t_{dump} &= 2\ \text{min} \\
t_{return} &= 6\ \text{min} \\
N &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(N) = \frac{3 + 4 + 2 + 6}{3} \rightarrow (N) = \frac{15}{3}$$

$$(N) = 5\ \text{trucks}$$
questions.explanation: The truck cycle includes the loading time itself — leaving it out gives 4 trucks and the loader idles. Round fractional results UP in practice.

questions.question: A crew of 6 workers places 120 CY of concrete in an 8-hour workday. What is the crew's labor productivity?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for productivity. We can determine it from the following equation:

$$\text{Productivity} = \frac{(\text{workers})(\text{hours})}{\text{quantity}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Workers} &= 6 \\
\text{Hours} &= 8\ \text{hr} \\
\text{Quantity} &= 120\ \text{CY} \\
\text{Productivity} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\text{Productivity} = \frac{(6)(8)}{120} \rightarrow \frac{48}{120}$$

$$\text{Productivity} = 0.40\ \text{worker-hr/CY}$$
questions.explanation: Productivity here is input per unit of output — inverting it gives 2.50 CY/worker-hr. Include ALL workers: forgetting the crew size gives 0.067 hr/CY.

questions.question: A CPM activity has an early start of day 5, a duration of 4 days, and a late finish of day 12. What is its total float?
questions.solution:
Refer to the CPM Precedence Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(TF\). We can determine \(TF\) from the following equation:

$$TF = LF - EF = LF - (ES + \text{duration})$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(TF\):

$$\begin{aligned}
ES &= 5 \\
\text{Duration} &= 4\ \text{days} \\
EF &= 5 + 4 = 9 \\
LF &= 12 \\
TF &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(TF) = 12 - 9$$

$$(TF) = 3\ \text{days}$$
questions.explanation: Total float is late finish minus EARLY finish — using early start instead (12 − 5) gives 7 days. Only critical-path activities have zero float.
questions.videoTitle: Master Project Deadlines With CPM A Full Guide

questions.question: Under OSHA construction standards, at what elevation above a lower level must fall protection be provided for workers?
questions.solution:
The governing rule is OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart M (Fall Protection), covered in the Safety chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6): each employee on a walking/working surface with an unprotected edge 6 feet or more above a lower level must be protected.

Applying this to the choices: 4 ft is the general-industry trigger, while 10 ft and 15 ft have no basis in the construction standard.

Therefore fall protection is required above 6 ft.
questions.explanation: Construction = 6 ft is the number to memorize — 4 ft is the GENERAL INDUSTRY trigger and the classic cross-contamination trap.

questions.question: A contractor purchases equipment for $180,000 with an estimated salvage value of $20,000 and a useful life of 5 years. What is the annual depreciation using the straight-line method?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Depreciation section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(D\). We can determine \(D\) from the following equation:

$$D = \frac{\text{Cost} - \text{Salvage}}{n}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(D\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Cost} &= \$180{,}000 \\
\text{Salvage} &= \$20{,}000 \\
n &= 5\ \text{years} \\
D &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(D) = \frac{180000 - 20000}{5} \rightarrow (D) = \frac{160000}{5}$$

$$(D) = \$32{,}000\ \text{per year}$$
questions.explanation: Subtract salvage BEFORE dividing by life — skipping it gives $36,000. The $160,000 total is not annualized, and $72,000 is a double-declining-balance rate misapplied.
questions.videoTitle: Depreciation

questions.question: Use the first two nonzero terms of the Maclaurin series for \(\sin x\) to approximate \(\sin(0.2)\). What is the approximate value?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Taylor's Series section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\sin(0.2)\). We can approximate it with the first two nonzero terms of its Maclaurin series:

$$\sin x \approx x - \frac{x^3}{3!}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\sin(0.2)\):

$$\begin{aligned}
x &= 0.2 \\
\sin(0.2) &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\sin(0.2)) \approx x - \frac{x^3}{6} \rightarrow (\sin(0.2)) \approx 0.2 - \frac{(0.2)^3}{6}$$

$$(\sin(0.2)) \approx 0.2 - 0.00133 = 0.19867$$
questions.explanation: The Maclaurin series for sine alternates signs — adding the x³/6 term instead of subtracting it gives the 0.20133 trap.
questions.videoTitle: Taylor and Maclaurin Series - Example 1

questions.question: If \(x^2 + y^2 = 25\), what is \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) at the point \((3, 4)\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Derivatives section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\frac{dy}{dx}\). Differentiate implicitly with respect to \(x\):

$$2x + 2y\frac{dy}{dx} = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x}{y}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\frac{dy}{dx}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
x &= 3 \\
y &= 4 \\
\frac{dy}{dx} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) = -\frac{x}{y} \rightarrow \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) = -\frac{3}{4}$$

$$\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) = -\frac{3}{4}$$
questions.explanation: Implicit differentiation gives dy/dx = −x/y; the 3/4 trap drops the negative sign from moving the 2x term across the equals sign.
questions.videoTitle: Civil FEexam review: Mathematics - derivatives and double derivatives

questions.question: For the scalar field \(f(x, y) = x^2y + xy^2\), what is the gradient \(\nabla f\) evaluated at the point \((1, 2)\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Gradient, Divergence, and Curl section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\nabla f(1, 2)\). The gradient is the vector of partial derivatives:

$$\nabla f = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\mathbf{i} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\mathbf{j}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\nabla f\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= 2xy + y^2 = 2(1)(2) + (2)^2 = 8 \\
\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} &= x^2 + 2xy = (1)^2 + 2(1)(2) = 5 \\
\nabla f(1, 2) &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\nabla f(1, 2)) = 8\mathbf{i} + 5\mathbf{j} \rightarrow (8, 5)$$

$$(\nabla f(1, 2)) = (8, 5)$$
questions.explanation: Each component needs both product-rule terms — the (4, 4) trap differentiates only one term of each product.
questions.videoTitle: Civil FEexam review: Mathematics - derivatives and double derivatives

questions.question: Evaluate the definite integral \(\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin(2x)\,dx\).
questions.solution:
Refer to the Integral Calculus section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the definite integral. Substitute \(u = 2x\) so that \(du = 2\,dx\):

$$\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin(2x)\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin u\,du = \frac{1}{2}\left[-\cos u\right]_{0}^{\pi}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve:

$$\begin{aligned}
u &= 2x \\
I &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(I) = \frac{1}{2}\left[-\cos(\pi) + \cos(0)\right] \rightarrow (I) = \frac{1}{2}(1 + 1)$$

$$(I) = 1$$
questions.explanation: The u-substitution brings a 1/2 factor from du = 2dx — skipping it doubles the answer to the 2 trap.
questions.videoTitle: FE Civil Exam Mathematics: Integrals Problem 3 a,3 b &3 c (Easy, Medium & Hard)

questions.question: For the matrix \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\), what is the \((1, 2)\) entry of \(A^{-1}\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Matrices section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the \((1, 2)\) entry of \(A^{-1}\). For a \(2 \times 2\) matrix:

$$A^{-1} = \frac{1}{\det A}\begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve:

$$\begin{aligned}
\det A &= (2)(4) - (3)(1) = 5 \\
(A^{-1})_{12} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$((A^{-1})_{12}) = \frac{-b}{\det A} \rightarrow ((A^{-1})_{12}) = \frac{-3}{5}$$

$$((A^{-1})_{12}) = -\frac{3}{5}$$
questions.explanation: The adjugate swaps a and d and negates b and c, then everything is divided by the determinant — the −3 trap skips that final division.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct definition of a linearly independent set of vectors?
choices: The vectors are all mutually perpendicular
Every vector in the set can be written as a linear combination of the others
The only scalars \(c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_n\) satisfying \(c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \cdots + c_nv_n = 0\) are \(c_1 = c_2 = \cdots = c_n = 0\)
The number of vectors in the set equals the dimension of the space
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vectors section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

A set of vectors \(\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n\}\) is linearly independent exactly when the only scalars \(c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_n\) satisfying \(c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \cdots + c_nv_n = 0\) are \(c_1 = c_2 = \cdots = c_n = 0\).

In other words, no vector in the set can be written as a linear combination of the others. Mutual perpendicularity (orthogonality) is a stronger, separate condition, and it is not required for independence.
questions.explanation: Linear independence means no vector is a combination of the others; perpendicularity (orthogonality) is stricter and not required.

questions.question: Two concurrent forces act at a point: \(\mathbf{F}_1 = 3\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}\) kN and \(\mathbf{F}_2 = 12\mathbf{k}\) kN. What is the magnitude of their resultant?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Concurrent Forces section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(|R|\). Add the force vectors component-wise, then take the magnitude:

$$R = \sum F, \qquad |R| = \sqrt{R_x^2 + R_y^2 + R_z^2}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(|R|\):

$$\begin{aligned}
R_x &= 3\ \text{kN} \\
R_y &= 4\ \text{kN} \\
R_z &= 12\ \text{kN} \\
|R| &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(|R|) = \sqrt{(3)^2 + (4)^2 + (12)^2} \rightarrow (|R|) = \sqrt{169}$$

$$(|R|) = 13\ \text{kN}$$
questions.explanation: In 3D the Pythagorean theorem just gains a third term — the 19 kN trap adds the components as scalars instead of squaring them first.
questions.videoTitle: How to Find the Resultant of Three Force Vectors – Statics Components and Resultants Problem 18

questions.subtopic: Moment of a force as a vector
questions.question: A force \(\mathbf{F} = (40\mathbf{i} - 30\mathbf{j} + 50\mathbf{k})\) N acts at a point whose position vector from the origin is \(\mathbf{r} = (2\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k})\) m. What is the magnitude of the moment of \(\mathbf{F}\) about the origin?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Systems of Forces section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(|M_O|\). The moment about the origin is the cross product:

$$M_O = r \times F$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(|M_O|\):

$$\begin{aligned}
r &= (2\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k})\ \text{m} \\
F &= (40\mathbf{i} - 30\mathbf{j} + 50\mathbf{k})\ \text{N} \\
M_O &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(M_O) = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2 & 1 & -3 \\ 40 & -30 & 50 \end{vmatrix} \rightarrow (M_O) = (-40\mathbf{i} - 220\mathbf{j} - 100\mathbf{k})\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}$$

$$(|M_O|) = \sqrt{(-40)^2 + (-220)^2 + (-100)^2} = \sqrt{60000} = 245\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}$$
questions.explanation: Watch the signs in each 2×2 minor — the 360 N·m trap adds the raw component magnitudes as if they were scalars.
questions.videoTitle: Moment of a Force

questions.question: A simply supported beam spans 5 m. A uniformly distributed load of 3 kN/m acts only over the middle 3 m of the span (from 1 m to 4 m measured from the left support). What is the vertical reaction at the left support?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(A_y\). Replace the partial uniform load with its equivalent resultant acting at its midpoint, then use moment equilibrium:

$$F_R = wL_{loaded}, \qquad \sum M_A = 0$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(A_y\):

$$\begin{aligned}
w &= 3\ \text{kN/m} \\
L_{loaded} &= 3\ \text{m} \\
F_R &= (3)(3) = 9\ \text{kN at 2.5 m from A} \\
A_y &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(A_y) = F_R\frac{2.5}{5} \rightarrow (A_y) = (9)\frac{2.5}{5}$$

$$(A_y) = 4.50\ \text{kN upward}$$
questions.explanation: Only the loaded 3 m counts toward the resultant — the 7.50 kN trap treats the load as if it covered the whole 5 m span.
questions.videoTitle: Beam Reactions Under a Triangular Distributed Load

questions.question: Joint E of a truss carries a 20 kN downward external load. Two members meet at E: a horizontal member EB and a diagonal member ED that rises at 60° above the horizontal. Using the method of joints at E, determine the force in member ED.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Plane Truss: Method of Joints section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(F_{ED}\). At joint E, vertical equilibrium involves only the diagonal member and the applied load:

$$\sum F_y = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad F_{ED}\sin 60^\circ - 20 = 0$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(F_{ED}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\theta &= 60^\circ \\
P &= 20\ \text{kN downward} \\
F_{ED} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(F_{ED}) = \frac{20}{\sin 60^\circ} \rightarrow (F_{ED}) = \frac{20}{0.866}$$

$$(F_{ED}) = 23.1\ \text{kN}$$

The diagonal must pull up and to the left on the joint to balance the downward load, so it is in tension: \(23.1\ \text{kN (T)}\).
questions.explanation: Vertical equilibrium alone isolates the diagonal — the (C) trap gets the magnitude right but misreads the direction of the member force on the joint.
questions.videoTitle: Trusses Method of Joints

questions.question: A rectangular cross-section is 200 mm wide and 300 mm deep. What is its area moment of inertia about an axis along its bottom edge?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Area Moment of Inertia section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(I_{base}\). For a rectangle about an axis along its base, the parallel-axis result gives:

$$I_{base} = \frac{bh^3}{3}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(I_{base}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
b &= 200\ \text{mm} \\
h &= 300\ \text{mm} \\
I_{base} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(I_{base}) = \frac{(200)(300)^3}{3} \rightarrow (I_{base}) = 1.80 \times 10^9$$

$$(I_{base}) = 1.80 \times 10^9\ \text{mm}^4$$
questions.explanation: About the base the rectangle's own bh³/12 shifts outward by Ad² to give bh³/3 — the 4.50×10⁸ trap answers for the centroidal axis instead.
questions.videoTitle: Statics: Lesson 69 - Moment of Inertia, Composite Shape Method

questions.question: A structural member is connected to the rest of a frame by frictionless pins at exactly two points, and no other loads act on it. Which statement about this two-force member is correct?
choices: The resultant forces at the two pins are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and collinear with the line joining the pins
The member can carry a bending moment at its ends
Each pin reaction must be zero
The pin forces act perpendicular to the member axis
questions.solution:
Refer to the Concurrent Forces section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

With forces acting only at the two pins, moment equilibrium about either pin forces the two resultants to be collinear with the line joining the pins; force equilibrium then forces them equal and opposite.

Hence the resultant forces at the two pins are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and collinear with the line joining the pins — and the member carries axial load only, never bending moment.
questions.explanation: A two-force member carries pure axial load along the line joining its pins — if bending moment appears, it is not a two-force member.

questions.question: A 2 kg mass is attached to a spring of stiffness \(k = 200\) N/m. The damping ratio of the system is \(\zeta = 0.30\). What is the damped natural frequency \(f_d\) in Hz?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Free and Forced Vibration section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(f_d\). Damping lowers the natural frequency by the factor \(\sqrt{1 - \zeta^2}\):

$$f_d = f_n\sqrt{1 - \zeta^2}, \qquad f_n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(f_d\):

$$\begin{aligned}
k &= 200\ \text{N/m} \\
m &= 2\ \text{kg} \\
\zeta &= 0.30 \\
f_n &= \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{200}{2}} = 1.59\ \text{Hz} \\
f_d &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(f_d) = (1.59)\sqrt{1 - (0.30)^2} \rightarrow (f_d) = (1.59)(0.954)$$

$$(f_d) = 1.52\ \text{Hz}$$
questions.explanation: Damping always lowers the frequency by √(1−ζ²) — the 1.59 Hz trap reports the undamped value, and 1.45 Hz skips the square root.
questions.videoTitle: Solution for Free Vibration of an Undamped SDOF System

questions.question: In the pulley system shown, blocks A and B are connected by a single cable that is anchored to the ceiling, passes around a movable pulley attached to block B, then passes over a fixed pulley to block A. Block B moves downward at 1.5 m/s. What is the velocity of block A?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Particle Kinematics section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(v_A\). The total cable length is constant; with one movable pulley at B, two cable segments shorten as B descends:

$$2s_B + s_A = l \quad\Rightarrow\quad 2v_B + v_A = 0$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(v_A\):

$$\begin{aligned}
v_B &= 1.5\ \text{m/s downward} \\
v_A &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(v_A) = -2v_B \rightarrow (v_A) = -2(1.5)$$

$$(v_A) = 3.00\ \text{m/s upward}$$
questions.explanation: Two rope segments feed the movable pulley, so A moves twice as fast as B in the opposite direction — the 1.50 m/s trap treats it as a single fixed pulley.
questions.videoTitle: Pulley Kinematics Problem

questions.subtopic: Mass moment of inertia (rigid body kinetics)
questions.question: A uniform slender rod of mass 5 kg and length 2 m is pinned at one end, held horizontal, and released from rest. What is the initial angular acceleration of the rod? (Use \(g = 9.81\) m/s².)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Mass Moment of Inertia section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\alpha\). At the instant of release the weight acts at the rod's midpoint, and the mass moment of inertia about the pin is \(mL^2/3\):

$$\sum M_{pin} = I_{pin}\alpha, \qquad \tau = mg\frac{L}{2}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\alpha\):

$$\begin{aligned}
m &= 5\ \text{kg} \\
L &= 2\ \text{m} \\
\tau &= (5)(9.81)(1) = 49.05\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m} \\
I_{pin} &= \frac{(5)(2)^2}{3} = 6.67\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2 \\
\alpha &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\alpha) = \frac{49.05}{6.67} \rightarrow (\alpha) = 7.36$$

$$(\alpha) = 7.36\ \text{rad/s}^2$$
questions.explanation: The pin is not the center, so I = mL²/3, not mL²/12 — the 29.4 rad/s² trap uses the centroidal inertia about the wrong axis.
questions.videoTitle: Moment of Inertia For Slender Rod - Formula Derivation Via Integration Physics With Calculus

questions.question: A 20 kg block rests on a horizontal surface with coefficient of kinetic friction \(\mu_k = 0.20\). A 100 N force pulls the block at 30° above the horizontal. What is the block's acceleration? (Use \(g = 9.81\) m/s².)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Particle Kinetics section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(a\). The angled pull reduces the normal force, which reduces the kinetic friction:

$$\sum F_x = ma, \qquad F_k = \mu_k N, \qquad N = mg - P\sin 30^\circ$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(a\):

$$\begin{aligned}
m &= 20\ \text{kg} \\
P &= 100\ \text{N} \\
N &= (20)(9.81) - (100)(0.5) = 146.2\ \text{N} \\
F_k &= (0.20)(146.2) = 29.2\ \text{N} \\
a &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(a) = \frac{P\cos 30^\circ - F_k}{m} \rightarrow (a) = \frac{86.6 - 29.2}{20}$$

$$(a) = 2.87\ \text{m/s}^2$$
questions.explanation: The upward component of the pull lightens the block, so friction drops — the 2.37 m/s² trap computes friction from the full weight.
questions.videoTitle: F=ma Rectangular Coordinates

questions.question: A 2 kg mass is suspended by a 1.0 m cord and swung in a horizontal circle so that the cord makes a constant angle of 30° with the vertical. What is the speed of the mass? (Use \(g = 9.81\) m/s².)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Normal and Tangential Kinetics for Planar Problems section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(v\). Vertical equilibrium gives the tension, and the horizontal component of tension provides the centripetal force:

$$T\cos\theta = mg, \qquad T\sin\theta = \frac{mv^2}{r}, \qquad r = L\sin\theta$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(v\):

$$\begin{aligned}
m &= 2\ \text{kg} \\
L &= 1.0\ \text{m} \\
\theta &= 30^\circ \\
r &= (1.0)\sin 30^\circ = 0.5\ \text{m} \\
v &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(v) = \sqrt{gL\sin\theta\tan\theta} \rightarrow (v) = \sqrt{(9.81)(1.0)(0.5)(0.577)}$$

$$(v) = \sqrt{2.83} = 1.68\ \text{m/s}$$
questions.explanation: Eliminating T leaves v² = gr·tanθ — the 2.21 m/s trap keeps the radius but drops the tanθ, as if the string were horizontal.

questions.question: The work done by a conservative force (such as gravity) on a particle moving between two points ...
choices: depends only on the endpoints of the path, not the path taken
depends on the length of the path traveled
is always zero over any displacement
equals the change in kinetic energy only when the force is constant
questions.solution:
Refer to the Principle of Work and Energy section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

A conservative force can be written as the gradient of a potential energy function, so its work between two points equals the drop in potential energy — a function of the endpoints only. Gravity is the classic example: raising a mass 2 m takes the same work whether the path is straight up or a long ramp.

The work done by a conservative force depends only on the endpoints of the path, not the path taken.
questions.explanation: Conservative work is path-independent — it depends only on where the particle starts and ends, never the route between.

questions.question: A thin-walled closed rectangular tube (centerline dimensions 200 mm × 100 mm) with uniform wall thickness 6 mm is subjected to a torque of 1.5 kN·m. Using Bredt's formula, what is the shear stress in the tube wall?
questions.solution:
Refer to the For Hollow, Thin-Walled Shafts section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\tau\). Bredt's formula relates the torque to the shear flow around the section:

$$\tau = \frac{T}{2A_m t}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\tau\):

$$\begin{aligned}
T &= 1.5\ \text{kN}\cdot\text{m} = 1.5 \times 10^6\ \text{N}\cdot\text{mm} \\
A_m &= (200)(100) = 20000\ \text{mm}^2 \\
t &= 6\ \text{mm} \\
\tau &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\tau) = \frac{1.5 \times 10^6}{2(20000)(6)} \rightarrow (\tau) = \frac{1.5 \times 10^6}{240000}$$

$$(\tau) = 6.25\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.explanation: The factor of 2 in Bredt's formula is easy to drop — doing so doubles the answer to the 12.5 MPa trap.

questions.question: At a point in a thin plate, the in-plane stress state is \(\sigma_x = 60\) MPa (tensile), \(\sigma_y = -20\) MPa (compressive), with \(\tau_{xy} = 0\). What is the normal stress on a plane inclined at \(\theta = 30°\) counterclockwise from the x-face?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Mohr's Circle—Stress, 2D section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\sigma_{x'}\). With \(\tau_{xy} = 0\) the transformation reduces to the average stress plus the deviatoric term at twice the angle:

$$\sigma_{x'} = \frac{\sigma_x + \sigma_y}{2} + \frac{\sigma_x - \sigma_y}{2}\cos 2\theta$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\sigma_{x'}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\sigma_x &= 60\ \text{MPa} \\
\sigma_y &= -20\ \text{MPa} \\
\theta &= 30^\circ \\
\sigma_{x'} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\sigma_{x'}) = \frac{60 + (-20)}{2} + \frac{60 - (-20)}{2}\cos 60^\circ \rightarrow (\sigma_{x'}) = 20 + 40(0.5)$$

$$(\sigma_{x'}) = 40.0\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.explanation: The transformation uses 2θ = 60°, not θ = 30° — plugging the raw angle gives the 54.6 MPa trap.
questions.videoTitle: For each of the plane stress states listed below, draw a Mohr's circle diagram...

questions.question: A thin plate is in a state of plane stress with in-plane principal stresses \(\sigma_1 = 80\) MPa and \(\sigma_2 = 30\) MPa. What is the absolute maximum shear stress at the point?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Principal Stresses section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\tau_{abs\ max}\). In plane stress the out-of-plane principal stress is zero, so check all three pairings:

$$\tau_{abs\ max} = \frac{\sigma_{max} - \sigma_{min}}{2}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\tau_{abs\ max}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\sigma_1 &= 80\ \text{MPa} \\
\sigma_2 &= 30\ \text{MPa} \\
\sigma_3 &= 0\ \text{(out of plane)} \\
\tau_{abs\ max} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\tau_{abs\ max}) = \frac{80 - 0}{2} \rightarrow (\tau_{abs\ max}) = 40$$

$$(\tau_{abs\ max}) = 40.0\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.explanation: The zero out-of-plane principal stress pairs with σ₁ to beat the in-plane value — the 25.0 MPa trap reports only the in-plane maximum shear.
questions.videoTitle: For each of the plane stress states listed below, draw a Mohr's circle diagram...

questions.question: A steel bar of length 2.0 m is fixed at both ends. An axial load of 90 kN acts on the bar at a point 1.2 m from the left end (0.8 m from the right end). What is the reaction at the left wall?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Uniaxial Loading and Deformation section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).
