Ultimately, we must solve for \(R_L\). Equilibrium plus the compatibility condition (the total deformation is zero) distribute the load in proportion to the opposite segment lengths:

$$R_L + R_R = P, \qquad \frac{R_L a}{AE} = \frac{R_R b}{AE}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(R_L\):

$$\begin{aligned}
P &= 90\ \text{kN} \\
a &= 1.2\ \text{m (left segment)} \\
b &= 0.8\ \text{m (right segment)} \\
R_L &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(R_L) = P\frac{b}{a + b} \rightarrow (R_L) = (90)\frac{0.8}{2.0}$$

$$(R_L) = 36\ \text{kN}$$
questions.explanation: Each wall reaction scales with the opposite segment's length — the 54 kN trap assigns the far wall's value to the near wall.
questions.videoTitle: Statically indeterminate problem 1 (English)

questions.question: A solid circular cross-section with diameter 80 mm carries a transverse shear force of 30 kN. What is the maximum shear stress in the cross-section?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Stresses in Beams section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\tau_{max}\). For a solid circular cross-section the maximum shear stress at the neutral axis is 4/3 of the average:

$$\tau_{max} = \frac{4}{3}\frac{V}{A}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\tau_{max}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
V &= 30\ \text{kN} = 30000\ \text{N} \\
d &= 80\ \text{mm} \\
A &= \frac{\pi(80)^2}{4} = 5027\ \text{mm}^2 \\
\tau_{max} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\tau_{max}) = \frac{4}{3}\frac{30000}{5027} \rightarrow (\tau_{max}) = \frac{4}{3}(5.97)$$

$$(\tau_{max}) = 7.96\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.explanation: Shear stress peaks at the neutral axis at 4/3 of the average for a circle (3/2 for a rectangle) — the 5.97 MPa trap reports the average V/A.
questions.videoTitle: Fundamental Problem 7.2 Determine the shear stress if the beam is subjected to a shear force

questions.question: In fatigue testing, what does the endurance limit (fatigue limit) of a material represent?
choices: The stress at which the material fractures in a single tensile test
The maximum stress reached in the first loading cycle
The stress amplitude below which the material can theoretically endure an infinite number of load cycles without failing
The stress amplitude that causes failure in exactly one million cycles
questions.solution:
Refer to the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

On an S–N curve, the endurance limit is the stress amplitude below which the curve flattens — the material can theoretically endure an infinite number of load cycles without fatigue failure. It is a property read off the horizontal asymptote of the S–N diagram, not a single-cycle strength. (Many nonferrous metals show no true endurance limit.)
questions.explanation: The endurance limit is the S–N curve's flat asymptote — cycle below it and fatigue failure theoretically never occurs.

questions.question: A simply supported beam spans 12 m. A single moving concentrated load \(P = 25\) kN can be placed anywhere on the span. What is the maximum bending moment that can develop at a section located 3 m from the left support?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Influence Lines for Beams and Trusses section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(M_{max}\) at the section. The influence-line ordinate for moment at a section distance \(a\) from the left peaks when the unit load sits exactly at the section:

$$M = P\frac{ab}{L}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(M_{max}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
P &= 25\ \text{kN} \\
a &= 3\ \text{m} \\
b &= 12 - 3 = 9\ \text{m} \\
L &= 12\ \text{m} \\
M_{max} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(M_{max}) = (25)\frac{(3)(9)}{12} \rightarrow (M_{max}) = (25)(2.25)$$

$$(M_{max}) = 56.3\ \text{kN}\cdot\text{m}$$
questions.explanation: Maximum moment at a section occurs with the load directly on it — the 75.0 kN·m trap multiplies P by a alone, and 37.5 kN·m halves the influence-line ordinate.
questions.videoTitle: Solved Problems on Influence Lines for Beams, Part 1

questions.question: A continuous beam rests on three supports: the left support is fixed, and the middle and right supports are rollers. The beam is prismatic with no internal hinges. To what degree is the beam statically indeterminate?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Determinacy and Stability section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Count the reaction components: the fixed support supplies 3 (two force components plus a moment) and each roller supplies 1, so \(r = 3 + 1 + 1 = 5\). A planar beam has 3 equilibrium equations and no internal hinges, so the degree of external indeterminacy is \(r - 3 = 5 - 3 = 2\).

The beam is indeterminate to the second degree.
questions.explanation: Fixed = 3 reactions, roller = 1 each, minus 3 equilibrium equations: 5 − 3 = 2nd-degree indeterminate.
questions.videoTitle: Statically Indeterminate Beam Solved using Superposition - Find Reaction Forces

questions.question: A reinforced concrete beam has \(b = 300\) mm and effective depth \(d = 540\) mm. Given \(f'_c = 28\) MPa and normal-weight concrete (\(\lambda = 1.0\)), what is the nominal one-way shear strength \(V_c\) provided by the concrete per ACI 318?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Shear and torsion section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(V_c\). The nominal one-way shear strength provided by the concrete is:

$$V_c = 0.17\lambda\sqrt{f'_c}\,b_w d$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(V_c\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\lambda &= 1.0 \\
f'_c &= 28\ \text{MPa} \\
b_w &= 300\ \text{mm} \\
d &= 540\ \text{mm} \\
V_c &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(V_c) = 0.17(1.0)\sqrt{28}(300)(540) \rightarrow (V_c) = (0.900)(162000)$$

$$(V_c) = 145700\ \text{N} = 146\ \text{kN}$$
questions.explanation: This is the nominal strength — the 109 kN trap multiplies by φ = 0.75, which gives the design strength, not the nominal strength asked for.

questions.question: A pin-ended steel column must resist a concentric axial load of 500 kN without buckling. The column is 6 m long and \(E = 200\) GPa. Using the Euler formula, what is the minimum required area moment of inertia \(I\) of the cross-section?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Columns section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the minimum \(I\). Rearrange the Euler buckling formula to solve for the required moment of inertia:

$$P_{cr} = \frac{\pi^2 EI}{(KL)^2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad I = \frac{P(KL)^2}{\pi^2 E}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(I\):

$$\begin{aligned}
P &= 500\ \text{kN} = 500000\ \text{N} \\
KL &= (1.0)(6)\ \text{m} = 6\ \text{m} \\
E &= 200\ \text{GPa} = 200 \times 10^9\ \text{Pa} \\
I &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(I) = \frac{(500000)(6)^2}{\pi^2(200 \times 10^9)} \rightarrow (I) = 9.12 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^4$$

$$(I) = 9.12 \times 10^6\ \text{mm}^4$$
questions.explanation: Pin-ended means K = 1.0, and π² stays in the denominator — the 2.28×10⁶ trap uses K = 0.5 and 90.0×10⁶ drops π² entirely.
questions.videoTitle: Buckling Load Theory Explained

questions.question: A propped cantilever beam (fixed at the left end, roller-supported at the right end) spans 4 m and carries a uniformly distributed load of 5 kN/m over its full length. Using the force method with the roller reaction as the redundant, what is the roller reaction?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Elementary Statically Indeterminate Structures by Force Method of Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(R_B\). Release the roller as the redundant: the downward tip deflection of a cantilever under uniform load must be cancelled by the upward tip deflection from \(R_B\):

$$\Delta_{cantilever} = \frac{wL^4}{8EI}, \qquad \Delta_{redundant} = \frac{R_B L^3}{3EI}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(R_B\):

$$\begin{aligned}
w &= 5\ \text{kN/m} \\
L &= 4\ \text{m} \\
R_B &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(R_B) = \frac{3wL}{8} \rightarrow (R_B) = \frac{3(5)(4)}{8}$$

$$(R_B) = 7.50\ \text{kN upward}$$
questions.explanation: Compatibility of deflection gives the classic 3wL/8 — the 10.0 kN trap answers as if the beam were simply supported (wL/2).
questions.videoTitle: Statically Indeterminate Beam Solved using Superposition - Find Reaction Forces

questions.question: What is the primary structural purpose of stirrups in a reinforced concrete beam?
choices: To increase the flexural (bending) strength of the beam
To reduce concrete creep and shrinkage
To resist shear forces and confine the longitudinal reinforcement
To replace the longitudinal tension steel
questions.solution:
Refer to the Beams—Shear section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Stirrups are the transverse (vertical or U-shaped) reinforcement in a beam. Their primary job is to resist diagonal-tension shear forces that the concrete alone cannot carry, and they simultaneously confine the longitudinal bars and hold them in position. They do not meaningfully add flexural strength — that is the longitudinal steel's job.
questions.explanation: Stirrups = shear reinforcement plus confinement; flexural strength comes from the longitudinal steel, not the stirrups.

questions.question: A steel rod with a diameter of 20 mm and a length of 2.0 m is subjected to an axial tensile force of 50 kN. If the modulus of elasticity of the steel is 200 GPa, what is the elongation of the rod?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Uniaxial Loading and Deformation section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\delta\), the axial elongation. We can determine \(\delta\) from the following equation:

$$\delta = \frac{PL}{AE}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\delta\):

$$\begin{aligned}
P &= 50\ \text{kN} = 50{,}000\ \text{N} \\
L &= 2.0\ \text{m} \\
d &= 20\ \text{mm} = 0.020\ \text{m} \\
A &= \frac{\pi d^2}{4} = \frac{\pi (0.020)^2}{4} = 3.1416 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2 \\
E &= 200\ \text{GPa} = 200 \times 10^9\ \text{Pa} \\
\delta &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\delta) = \frac{(P)(L)}{(A)(E)} \rightarrow (\delta) = \frac{(50{,}000)(2.0)}{(3.1416 \times 10^{-4})(200 \times 10^9)}$$

$$(\delta) = \frac{100{,}000}{6.2832 \times 10^7} = 1.59 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m} = 1.59\ \text{mm}$$
questions.explanation: Axial deformation scales with PL/AE. The classic traps: using the diameter in place of the radius when computing area (0.40 mm), or the radius as if it were the diameter (6.37 mm). Convert mm to m before computing the area.

questions.question: A cylindrical steel specimen with an original diameter of 12.0 mm is loaded in axial tension, producing an axial strain of 0.0020 mm/mm. If Poisson's ratio for the steel is 0.30, what is the change in the specimen's diameter?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Shear Stress-Strain section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\Delta d\), the change in diameter. Lateral strain is related to axial strain by Poisson's ratio:

$$\nu = -\frac{\epsilon_{\text{lateral}}}{\epsilon_{\text{axial}}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\Delta d\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\epsilon_{\text{axial}} &= 0.0020\ \text{mm/mm} \\
\nu &= 0.30 \\
d &= 12.0\ \text{mm} \\
\epsilon_{\text{lateral}} &= -\nu\,\epsilon_{\text{axial}} = -(0.30)(0.0020) = -0.0006\ \text{mm/mm} \\
\Delta d &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\Delta d) = (\epsilon_{\text{lateral}})(d) \rightarrow (\Delta d) = (-0.0006)(12.0)$$

$$(\Delta d) = -0.0072\ \text{mm}$$

The negative sign means the diameter decreases by 0.0072 mm.
questions.explanation: Tension stretches a bar axially but squeezes it laterally — the minus sign in Poisson's ratio is the whole point. Forgetting ν gives 0.0240 mm; dropping the sign claims the diameter grows.

questions.question: A steel bar 3.0 m long is fixed between two rigid supports at 20 C so that it cannot expand or contract. If the temperature of the bar rises to 50 C, what is the magnitude of the thermal stress developed in the bar? (\(\alpha = 12 \times 10^{-6}/^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), \(E = 200\ \text{GPa}\))
questions.solution:
Refer to the Thermal Deformations section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\sigma\), the restrained thermal stress. Because the supports prevent the free thermal expansion \(\alpha(\Delta T)L\), an equal and opposite mechanical strain develops, giving:

$$\sigma = E\,\alpha\,(\Delta T)$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\sigma\):

$$\begin{aligned}
E &= 200\ \text{GPa} = 200 \times 10^9\ \text{Pa} \\
\alpha &= 12 \times 10^{-6}\ /\!^\circ\text{C} \\
\Delta T &= 50 - 20 = 30^\circ\text{C} \\
\sigma &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\sigma) = (E)(\alpha)(\Delta T) \rightarrow (\sigma) = (200 \times 10^9)(12 \times 10^{-6})(30)$$

$$(\sigma) = 72 \times 10^6\ \text{Pa} = 72.0\ \text{MPa}\ (\text{compressive})$$
questions.explanation: Restrained thermal stress is just E times α times ΔT — length cancels out, so the 3.0 m is a distractor. A temperature rise in a restrained bar produces compressive stress.

questions.question: A steel has an ultimate tensile strength of \(S_{ut} = 900\ \text{MPa}\). Using the handbook approximation for the rotating-beam endurance limit of steels, estimate the endurance limit \(S_e'\).
questions.solution:
Refer to the Endurance Limit for Steels section in the Mechanical Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(S_e'\), the rotating-beam endurance limit. For steels with \(S_{ut} \le 1400\ \text{MPa}\), the handbook approximation is:

$$S_e' \approx 0.5\,S_{ut}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(S_e'\):

$$\begin{aligned}
S_{ut} &= 900\ \text{MPa} \le 1400\ \text{MPa} \\
S_e' &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(S_e') = (0.5)(S_{ut}) \rightarrow (S_e') = (0.5)(900)$$

$$(S_e') = 450\ \text{MPa}$$
questions.explanation: For most steels the endurance limit is roughly half the ultimate strength — the basis of infinite-life design under fully reversed loading. 900 MPa ignores the 0.5 factor entirely.

questions.question: In the structural steel designation “ASTM A36,” what does the number 36 signify?
choices: The ultimate tensile strength is 36 ksi
The minimum yield strength is 36 ksi
The maximum plate thickness is 36 mm
questions.solution:
Refer to the Materials Science/Structure of Matter chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Structural steel grades are designated by their minimum specified yield strength. In “ASTM A36,” the 36 denotes a minimum yield strength of 36 ksi (approximately 250 MPa) — the stress at which the steel begins to deform permanently.

The ultimate tensile strength of A36 is higher (58–80 ksi), the carbon content is far below 0.36%, and plate thickness has nothing to do with the grade number.

The minimum yield strength of 36 ksi is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: Steel grade numbers name the yield strength, not the ultimate strength. A36 = 36 ksi yield, the workhorse grade for ordinary structural steel.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of moist-curing freshly placed concrete?
choices: To speed up the initial set of the concrete
To lower the water–cement ratio after placement
To prevent segregation of the aggregates
To maintain moisture so hydration continues and strength develops
questions.solution:
Refer to the Materials Science/Structure of Matter chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Concrete gains strength through hydration — the chemical reaction between cement and water — which continues for days after placement only while moisture remains available. Moist curing (ponding, wet burlap, curing compounds) keeps the concrete damp so hydration continues and the design strength develops; concrete allowed to dry out stops gaining strength and becomes more permeable.

Accelerating the set, changing the water–cement ratio after placement, or preventing segregation are not purposes of curing.

Maintaining moisture so hydration continues and strength develops is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: Curing is about feeding the hydration reaction, not about setting time. Dry concrete stops gaining strength — that is why curing matters most in the first week.

questions.question: A concrete mix design by the absolute volume method calls for 175 kg of water per cubic meter of concrete with a water–cement ratio of 0.50. The mix also contains 1100 kg of coarse aggregate (specific gravity 2.65) and 2% entrapped air. What is the required mass of fine aggregate (specific gravity 2.62) per cubic meter of concrete? (Specific gravity of cement = 3.15; unit weight of water = 1000 kg/m^3)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Materials Science/Structure of Matter chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the mass of fine aggregate. By the absolute volume method, the volumes of all ingredients plus air sum to 1 m³, so the fine aggregate occupies whatever volume remains:

$$V_{\text{FA}} = 1 - (V_w + V_c + V_{CA} + V_{\text{air}})$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(m_{FA}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
m_w &= 175\ \text{kg/m}^3 \\
\text{w/c} &= 0.50 \rightarrow m_c = \frac{175}{0.50} = 350\ \text{kg/m}^3 \\
V_w &= \frac{175}{1000} = 0.175\ \text{m}^3 \\
V_c &= \frac{350}{(3.15)(1000)} = 0.111\ \text{m}^3 \\
V_{CA} &= \frac{1100}{(2.65)(1000)} = 0.415\ \text{m}^3 \\
V_{\text{air}} &= 0.020\ \text{m}^3 \\
V_{FA} &= 1 - (0.175 + 0.111 + 0.415 + 0.020) = 0.279\ \text{m}^3 \\
m_{FA} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(m_{FA}) = (V_{FA})(SG_{FA})(\gamma_w) \rightarrow (m_{FA}) = (0.279)(2.62)(1000)$$

$$(m_{FA}) = 730\ \text{kg/m}^3$$
questions.explanation: Absolute volume: everything must total exactly 1 m^3. The two classic slips are forgetting the entrapped air (783 kg) and inverting the w/c ratio when finding cement content (949 kg).
questions.videoTitle: Concrete Mix Design M40 Grade

questions.question: What is the gage pressure at a depth of 5.0 m below the surface of an oil with a specific gravity of 0.85? (Unit weight of water = 9.81 kN/m^3)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Pressure Field in a Static Liquid section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(p\), the gage pressure at depth. From hydrostatics:

$$p = \gamma h$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(p\):

$$\begin{aligned}
SG &= 0.85 \\
\gamma_{\text{oil}} &= (SG)(\gamma_{\text{water}}) = (0.85)(9.81) = 8.34\ \text{kN/m}^3 \\
h &= 5.0\ \text{m} \\
p &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(p) = (\gamma)(h) \rightarrow (p) = (8.34)(5.0)$$

$$(p) = 41.7\ \text{kPa}\ (\text{gage})$$
questions.explanation: Pressure is γh with the fluid's own unit weight — multiply water's 9.81 by the specific gravity first. 49.1 kPa uses water's unit weight; 35.4 kPa applies the 0.85 factor twice.
questions.videoTitle: Estimate the pressure needed to raise a column of water to the same height as a 35-m-tall oak tree.

questions.question: A vertical cylindrical tank with an inside diameter of 2.0 m is filled with water to a depth of 4.0 m above a sharp-edged circular orifice 50 mm in diameter at the bottom of the tank. If the orifice discharge coefficient is C_d = 0.61, approximately how long will it take to drain the tank completely? (g = 9.81 m/s^2)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Bernoulli Equation section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(t\), the drain time. Torricelli's law gives the instantaneous discharge \(Q = C_d A_o\sqrt{2gh}\); integrating as the head falls from \(H\) to zero gives:

$$t = \frac{2 A_T \sqrt{H}}{C_d A_o \sqrt{2g}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(t\):

$$\begin{aligned}
D_T &= 2.0\ \text{m} \rightarrow A_T = \frac{\pi(2.0)^2}{4} = 3.1416\ \text{m}^2 \\
d_o &= 50\ \text{mm} = 0.050\ \text{m} \rightarrow A_o = \frac{\pi(0.050)^2}{4} = 1.9635 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2 \\
H &= 4.0\ \text{m} \\
C_d &= 0.61 \\
g &= 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2 \\
t &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(t) = \frac{2(3.1416)\sqrt{4.0}}{(0.61)(1.9635 \times 10^{-3})\sqrt{2(9.81)}} \rightarrow (t) = \frac{12.566}{5.306 \times 10^{-3}}$$

$$(t) = 2368\ \text{s} = 39.5\ \text{min}$$
questions.explanation: Drain time comes from integrating Torricelli's law — the factor of 2 is essential (19.7 min drops it). Using C_d = 1.0 gives 24.1 min; real orifices discharge less.
questions.videoTitle: FE Exam Practice - Fluid Mechanics and Water Resources - Culvert Flow

questions.question: Cavitation damage in a centrifugal pump is most likely to occur when:
choices: the discharge valve is throttled nearly closed
the pump runs below its rated speed
the suction line is shorter than recommended
the pressure at the impeller inlet falls below the liquid's vapor pressure
questions.solution:
Refer to the Centrifugal Pump Characteristics section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Cavitation is the formation and violent collapse of vapor bubbles in a liquid. It occurs wherever the local absolute pressure drops to the liquid's vapor pressure — in a pump, that happens at the impeller eye when the suction head is insufficient (low NPSH available). The collapsing bubbles pit and erode the impeller.

Throttling the discharge, running below rated speed, or shortening the suction line do not by themselves create vapor cavities; the trigger is specifically pressure falling below vapor pressure.

The pressure at the impeller inlet falling below the liquid's vapor pressure is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: Cavitation = local pressure below vapor pressure, usually from starved suction. It sounds like gravel in the pump and eats impellers — raise the suction head or lower the pump to fix it.

questions.question: A flat billboard 10 m wide by 4 m high faces directly into a 30 m/s wind. If the drag coefficient is C_D = 1.20 and the mass density of air is 1.20 kg/m^3, what is the total drag force on the billboard?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Drag section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(F_D\), the drag force:

$$F_D = C_D \frac{\rho V^2}{2} A$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(F_D\):

$$\begin{aligned}
C_D &= 1.20 \\
\rho &= 1.20\ \text{kg/m}^3 \\
V &= 30\ \text{m/s} \\
A &= (10)(4) = 40\ \text{m}^2 \\
F_D &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(F_D) = (C_D)\frac{(\rho)(V)^2}{2}(A) \rightarrow (F_D) = (1.20)\frac{(1.20)(30)^2}{2}(40)$$

$$(F_D) = (1.20)(540)(40) = 25{,}920\ \text{N} = 25.9\ \text{kN}$$
questions.explanation: Drag is C_D times the dynamic pressure times the frontal area. 51.8 kN drops the 1/2; 21.6 kN assumes C_D = 1.0.
questions.videoTitle: Drag & Viscous Flow — Reynolds, Boundary Layers, Bluff Bodies

questions.question: An oil has a dynamic viscosity of 0.85 Pa-s and a mass density of 850 kg/m^3. What is its kinematic viscosity?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Stress, Pressure, and Viscosity section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\nu\), the kinematic viscosity:

$$\nu = \frac{\mu}{\rho}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\nu\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\mu &= 0.85\ \text{Pa}\cdot\text{s} \\
\rho &= 850\ \text{kg/m}^3 \\
\nu &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\nu) = \frac{(\mu)}{(\rho)} \rightarrow (\nu) = \frac{0.85}{850}$$

$$(\nu) = 1.00 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2\text{/s}$$
questions.explanation: Kinematic viscosity is dynamic viscosity divided by density — ‘kinematic’ means the mass has been divided out. Inverting the ratio gives 1000 m^2/s.
questions.videoTitle: Fluid Mechanics Tutorial 3

questions.question: Two reservoirs are connected by two pipes in parallel. Pipe 1 is 1000 m long with a 300-mm inside diameter; Pipe 2 is 1000 m long with a 200-mm inside diameter. The Darcy friction factor is f = 0.020 in both pipes and minor losses are neglected. If the total discharge through the system is 0.30 m^3/s, what is the head loss between the reservoirs?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Multipath Pipeline Problems section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(h_f\). In parallel, both pipes share the same head loss while their discharges sum to the total:

$$h_{f1} = h_{f2}, \quad Q_1 + Q_2 = 0.30\ \text{m}^3\text{/s}, \quad h_f = f\frac{L}{D}\frac{V^2}{2g}$$

With equal \(f\) and \(L\), equal head loss gives \(\dfrac{Q_1}{Q_2} = \left(\dfrac{D_1}{D_2}\right)^{2.5} = (1.5)^{2.5} = 2.756\). List the parameters in order to solve for \(h_f\):

$$\begin{aligned}
Q_1 &= \frac{2.756}{3.756}(0.30) = 0.220\ \text{m}^3\text{/s} \\
A_1 &= \frac{\pi(0.30)^2}{4} = 0.07069\ \text{m}^2 \\
V_1 &= \frac{0.220}{0.07069} = 3.11\ \text{m/s} \\
h_f &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(h_f) = (f)\frac{L}{D_1}\frac{V_1^2}{2g} \rightarrow (h_f) = (0.020)\frac{1000}{0.30}\frac{(3.11)^2}{2(9.81)}$$

$$(h_f) = (0.020)(3333.3)(0.494) = 33.0\ \text{m}$$

(Checking Pipe 2: \(V_2 = 2.54\ \text{m/s}\) gives the same \(h_f = 33.0\ \text{m}\).)
questions.explanation: Parallel pipes share head loss, not discharge — flow splits as D^2.5. 61.2 m forces all flow through the big pipe; 65.9 m uses V^2/g instead of V^2/2g.
questions.videoTitle: PIPES IN SERIES AND IN PARALLEL WITH SAMPLE PROBLEMS

questions.question: What is the approximate capillary rise of water at 20 C in a clean glass tube with an inside diameter of 1.0 mm? (Surface tension σ = 0.073 N/m, contact angle ≈ 0°, γ = 9.79 kN/m^3)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Surface Tension and Capillarity section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(h\), the capillary rise:

$$h = \frac{4\sigma\cos\beta}{\gamma d}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(h\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\sigma &= 0.073\ \text{N/m} \\
\beta &= 0^\circ \rightarrow \cos\beta = 1 \\
\gamma &= 9.79\ \text{kN/m}^3 = 9790\ \text{N/m}^3 \\
d &= 1.0\ \text{mm} = 0.001\ \text{m} \\
h &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(h) = \frac{4(0.073)(1)}{(9790)(0.001)}$$

$$(h) = 0.0298\ \text{m} = 29.8\ \text{mm}$$
questions.explanation: Capillary rise scales as 1/d — halve the tube diameter and the rise doubles (59.7 mm uses the radius as the diameter). Keep γ in N/m^3 so the units work.
questions.videoTitle: JASPE and JARLOC

questions.question: A vertical sight distance of 1.2 km is used in a leveling run. What is the magnitude of the combined correction for Earth's curvature and atmospheric refraction?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(C\), the combined correction:

$$C = 0.0675\,D^2$$

where \(D\) is in kilometers and \(C\) is in meters. List the parameters in order to solve for \(C\):

$$\begin{aligned}
D &= 1.2\ \text{km} \\
C &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(C) = (0.0675)(D)^2 \rightarrow (C) = (0.0675)(1.2)^2$$

$$(C) = (0.0675)(1.44) = 0.097\ \text{m}$$
questions.explanation: The 0.0675D^2 formula needs D in km — entering meters gives the absurd 97.2 m. Curvature dominates; refraction only shaves off about one-seventh.
questions.videoTitle: Reciprocal Levelling : Curvature and Refraction Correction

questions.question: A simple horizontal curve has a radius of 300 m and an intersection angle of 24°. What is the middle ordinate of the curve?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Horizontal Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(M\), the middle ordinate — the distance from the midpoint of the long chord to the midpoint of the curve:

$$M = R\left(1 - \cos\frac{I}{2}\right)$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(M\):

$$\begin{aligned}
R &= 300\ \text{m} \\
I &= 24^\circ \rightarrow \frac{I}{2} = 12^\circ \\
M &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(M) = (R)\left(1 - \cos\frac{I}{2}\right) \rightarrow (M) = (300)(1 - \cos 12^\circ)$$

$$(M) = (300)(1 - 0.97815) = 6.56\ \text{m}$$
questions.explanation: The middle ordinate uses the half-angle I/2 — the full angle gives 25.9 m. Don't confuse it with the external distance (6.70 m), which is measured to the PI instead.
questions.videoTitle: Horizontal Curves Elements Part 1 of 2

questions.question: Two consecutive cross sections on a roadway project are 25 m apart. The cut areas at the end sections are 42.5 m^2 and 30.0 m^2, and the cut area at the midpoint section is 38.0 m^2. Using the prismoidal formula, what is the volume of cut between the two end sections?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earthwork formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(V\), the volume by the prismoidal formula:

$$V = \frac{L}{6}\left(A_1 + 4A_m + A_2\right)$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(V\):

$$\begin{aligned}
L &= 25\ \text{m} \\
A_1 &= 42.5\ \text{m}^2 \\
A_m &= 38.0\ \text{m}^2 \\
A_2 &= 30.0\ \text{m}^2 \\
V &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(V) = \frac{(L)}{6}\left(A_1 + 4A_m + A_2\right) \rightarrow (V) = \frac{25}{6}\left(42.5 + 4(38.0) + 30.0\right)$$

$$(V) = \frac{25}{6}(224.5) = 935\ \text{m}^3$$
questions.explanation: The prismoidal formula weights the middle section by 4 — it is exact for prismoids. The average-end-area shortcut gives 906 m^3, slightly low here.

questions.question: A distance measured along a 4.0° slope is 250.00 m. What is the equivalent horizontal distance?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(H\), the horizontal distance. The measured slope distance is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with the horizontal leg:

$$H = S\cos\theta$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(H\):

$$\begin{aligned}
S &= 250.00\ \text{m} \\
\theta &= 4.0^\circ \\
H &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(H) = (S)\cos\theta \rightarrow (H) = (250.00)\cos 4.0^\circ$$

$$(H) = (250.00)(0.99756) = 249.39\ \text{m}$$
questions.explanation: Horizontal = slope distance × cosθ — the horizontal leg is always shorter. Dividing by cosθ (250.61 m) goes the wrong way.
questions.videoTitle: Reciprocal Levelling : Curvature and Refraction Correction

questions.question: In surveying, a benchmark is best defined as:
choices: any turning point used in a differential level run
the setup location of the leveling instrument
a permanent monument of known elevation used as a vertical reference
a foresight reading taken on an unknown point
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

A benchmark is a permanent, stable monument — a brass disk, chiseled mark, or similar — whose elevation above the datum is known and published. Level runs start from benchmarks and close on them so every elevation in the survey traces back to the datum.

A turning point is temporary, the instrument setup is just a vantage point, and a foresight reading is an observation — none of them is a benchmark.

A permanent monument of known elevation used as a vertical reference is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: Benchmarks anchor every elevation to the datum. If it isn't permanent and published, it isn't a benchmark — it's just a turning point.

questions.question: A closed traverse has a total perimeter of 800 m. The algebraic sum of the latitudes is −0.30 m. Using the compass (Bowditch) rule, what correction should be applied to the latitude of a course that is 120 m long?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Latitudes and Departures section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the latitude correction. The compass rule distributes the closure error in proportion to course length, with the opposite sign:

$$\text{correction} = -(\text{closure error})\frac{\text{course length}}{\text{perimeter}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for the correction:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{closure error} &= -0.30\ \text{m} \\
\text{course length} &= 120\ \text{m} \\
\text{perimeter} &= 800\ \text{m} \\
\text{correction} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\text{correction}) = -(-0.30)\frac{120}{800}$$

$$(\text{correction}) = +0.045\ \text{m}$$
questions.explanation: Bowditch prorates the error by length and flips the sign — the correction opposes the error. −0.045 m forgets the sign flip; +0.30 m dumps the whole error on one course.
questions.videoTitle: Balance the traverse by using Bowditch rule

questions.question: A sag vertical curve connects a −2.0% grade to a +3.0% grade. The curve is 200 m long, and the PVC is at station 10+00 with elevation 120.00 m. What is the elevation of the low point of the curve?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vertical Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the low-point elevation. The low point occurs where the grade is zero, at distance \(x\) from the PVC:

$$x = \frac{g_1 L}{g_1 - g_2}, \quad y = y_{PVC} + g_1 x + \frac{(g_2 - g_1)x^2}{2L}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(y\):

$$\begin{aligned}
g_1 &= -0.020 \\
g_2 &= +0.030 \\
L &= 200\ \text{m} \\
y_{PVC} &= 120.00\ \text{m} \\
x &= \frac{(-0.020)(200)}{-0.020 - 0.030} = \frac{-4.0}{-0.050} = 80\ \text{m} \\
y &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(y) = (120.00) + (-0.020)(80) + \frac{(0.050)(80)^2}{2(200)}$$

$$(y) = 120.00 - 1.60 + 0.80 = 119.20\ \text{m}\ (\text{at station } 10{+}80)$$
questions.explanation: On a sag curve the low point sits closer to the PVC — here at 80 m, not the midpoint. 118.40 m drops the parabolic offset; 120.80 m flips a sign.
questions.videoTitle: VERTICAL CURVES - Solving for SUMMIT, and ELEVATION and GRADE of CURVE! (SURVEYING)

questions.question: A suppressed sharp-crested rectangular weir is 2.0 m long. If the head above the weir crest is 0.30 m, what is the discharge? (Use Q = 1.84 L H^1.5 in SI units.)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Weir Formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(Q\), the weir discharge:

$$Q = 1.84\,L\,H^{1.5}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(Q\):

$$\begin{aligned}
L &= 2.0\ \text{m} \\
H &= 0.30\ \text{m} \\
Q &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(Q) = (1.84)(L)(H)^{1.5} \rightarrow (Q) = (1.84)(2.0)(0.30)^{1.5}$$

$$(Q) = (3.68)(0.1643) = 0.605\ \text{m}^3\text{/s}$$
questions.explanation: Rectangular weir discharge grows with H^1.5 — not linearly. 1.104 m^3/s uses H^1 and 0.331 m^3/s uses H^2.

questions.question: A confined aquifer 20 m thick has a hydraulic conductivity of 25 m/day. Steady radial flow to a fully penetrating well shows a 3.0-m head difference between two observation wells located 100 m and 0.20 m from the pumped well. What is the well discharge?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Thiem Equation section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(Q\), the steady well discharge. The Thiem equation for a confined aquifer is:

$$Q = \frac{2\pi K b\,(h_2 - h_1)}{\ln(r_2/r_1)}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(Q\):

$$\begin{aligned}
K &= 25\ \text{m/day} \\
b &= 20\ \text{m} \\
h_2 - h_1 &= 3.0\ \text{m} \\
r_2 &= 100\ \text{m},\ r_1 = 0.20\ \text{m} \\
Q &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(Q) = \frac{2\pi(25)(20)(3.0)}{\ln(100/0.20)} \rightarrow (Q) = \frac{9424.8}{\ln(500)}$$

$$(Q) = \frac{9424.8}{6.2146} = 1517\ \text{m}^3\text{/day}$$
questions.explanation: Thiem's equation uses the natural log of the radius ratio — base-10 log gives 3492 m^3/day. The 2π is part of the formula; dropping it halves the answer to 758.
questions.videoTitle: How to calculate Transmissivity and Storativity of a confined aquifer

questions.question: A rectangular channel 4.0 m wide carries 12 m^3/s. What is the critical depth of flow?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Specific Energy section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(y_c\), the critical depth. For a rectangular channel:

$$y_c = \left(\frac{q^2}{g}\right)^{1/3}, \quad q = \frac{Q}{b}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(y_c\):

$$\begin{aligned}
Q &= 12\ \text{m}^3\text{/s} \\
b &= 4.0\ \text{m} \rightarrow q = \frac{12}{4.0} = 3.0\ \text{m}^2\text{/s} \\
g &= 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2 \\
y_c &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(y_c) = \left(\frac{(q)^2}{g}\right)^{1/3} \rightarrow (y_c) = \left(\frac{(3.0)^2}{9.81}\right)^{1/3}$$

$$(y_c) = (0.9174)^{1/3} = 0.972\ \text{m}$$
questions.explanation: Critical depth needs the discharge per unit width q, then the cube root — skipping the root gives 0.917 m. It depends only on q, not on slope or roughness.

questions.question: A trapezoidal channel has a bottom width of 2.0 m, a flow depth of 1.5 m, and side slopes of 2H:1V. What is the hydraulic radius of the flow section?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Manning's Equation section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(R\), the hydraulic radius, \(R = A/P\):

$$A = (b + my)y, \quad P = b + 2y\sqrt{1 + m^2}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(R\):

$$\begin{aligned}
b &= 2.0\ \text{m} \\
y &= 1.5\ \text{m} \\
m &= 2 \\
A &= (2.0 + 2(1.5))(1.5) = 7.50\ \text{m}^2 \\
P &= 2.0 + 2(1.5)\sqrt{1 + 2^2} = 2.0 + 3.0\sqrt{5} = 8.708\ \text{m} \\
R &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(R) = \frac{(A)}{(P)} \rightarrow (R) = \frac{7.50}{8.708}$$

$$(R) = 0.861\ \text{m}$$
questions.explanation: The wetted perimeter follows the sloped sides — using b + 2y (1.500 m) or the top width (0.938 m) mismeasures it. R = A/P, always.

questions.question: A stormwater detention basin reduces the peak discharge at its outlet primarily by:
choices: conveying inflow downstream as quickly as possible
storing inflow temporarily and releasing it slowly
increasing infiltration into the underlying soil
reducing the total volume of runoff
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

A detention basin is a storage facility: it captures the inflow hydrograph, holds the water temporarily, and releases it through a controlled outlet over a longer time. The total runoff volume barely changes, but spreading it out flattens — attenuates — the peak discharge downstream.

Conveying flow faster would increase the peak, infiltration is the job of retention/infiltration basins, and detention does not meaningfully reduce total volume.

Storing inflow temporarily and releasing it slowly is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: Detention = peak shaving through temporary storage. It doesn't reduce how much water runs off, only how fast it arrives downstream.

questions.question: A rectangular concrete channel (n = 0.014) is 4.0 m wide and laid on a slope of 0.002. For a discharge of 8.0 m^3/s, what is the normal depth? (Solve by trial.)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Manning's Equation section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(y_n\), the normal depth. Manning's equation in SI units:

$$Q = \frac{1}{n} A R^{2/3} S^{1/2}, \quad A = by,\ R = \frac{by}{b + 2y}$$

List the known parameters and trial values in order to solve for \(y_n\):

$$\begin{aligned}
Q &= 8.0\ \text{m}^3\text{/s} \\
b &= 4.0\ \text{m},\ n = 0.014,\ S = 0.002 \\
\text{Trial } y = 0.80\ \text{m} &: A = 3.20,\ R = 0.571 \rightarrow Q = 7.04\ \text{m}^3\text{/s}\ (\text{low}) \\
\text{Trial } y = 0.90\ \text{m} &: A = 3.60,\ R = 0.621 \rightarrow Q = 8.37\ \text{m}^3\text{/s}\ (\text{high}) \\
y_n &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Interpolating between the trials for \(Q = 8.0\):

$$(y_n) = 0.80 + \frac{8.0 - 7.04}{8.37 - 7.04}(0.10)$$

$$(y_n) = 0.80 + 0.072 = 0.873\ \text{m}$$
questions.explanation: Normal depth needs iteration since y sits inside both A and R. 0.742 m is the critical depth — uniform flow on a mild slope runs deeper than critical, a good sanity check.
questions.videoTitle: How to Calculate Discharge (Q) in a Trapezoidal Channel

questions.question: A centrifugal pump running at 1200 rpm delivers 0.10 m^3/s against a 20-m head with a brake power of 15 kW. If the speed is increased to 1800 rpm, what is the new brake power? (Assume the affinity laws apply.)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Scaling Laws; Affinity Laws section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(P_2\), the brake power at the new speed. The pump affinity laws state:

$$\frac{Q_2}{Q_1} = \frac{N_2}{N_1}, \quad \frac{H_2}{H_1} = \left(\frac{N_2}{N_1}\right)^2, \quad \frac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\frac{N_2}{N_1}\right)^3$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(P_2\):

$$\begin{aligned}
N_1 &= 1200\ \text{rpm},\ N_2 = 1800\ \text{rpm} \rightarrow \frac{N_2}{N_1} = 1.5 \\
P_1 &= 15\ \text{kW} \\
P_2 &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(P_2) = (P_1)\left(\frac{N_2}{N_1}\right)^3 \rightarrow (P_2) = (15)(1.5)^3$$

$$(P_2) = (15)(3.375) = 50.6\ \text{kW}$$
questions.explanation: Power follows the cube of the speed ratio — a 50% speedup needs 3.375× the power. Linear scaling (22.5 kW) badly underestimates the motor required.

questions.question: A fine-grained soil has a liquid limit of 42 and a plastic limit of 19. What is the plasticity index of the soil?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Soil Classification section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(PI\), the plasticity index — the range of water contents over which the soil behaves plastically:

$$PI = LL - PL$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(PI\):

$$\begin{aligned}
LL &= 42 \\
PL &= 19 \\
PI &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(PI) = (LL) - (PL) \rightarrow (PI) = 42 - 19$$

$$(PI) = 23$$
questions.explanation: PI = LL − PL, a difference — not a sum (61) or a ratio (2.2). Higher PI means a more plastic, more clay-like soil.

questions.question: A sand has a specific gravity of solids G_s = 2.65 and a void ratio e = 0.60. What is the dry unit weight of the sand? (γ_w = 9.81 kN/m^3)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Phase Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\gamma_d\), the dry unit weight:

$$\gamma_d = \frac{G_s \gamma_w}{1 + e}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(\gamma_d\):

$$\begin{aligned}
G_s &= 2.65 \\
e &= 0.60 \\
\gamma_w &= 9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3 \\
\gamma_d &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(\gamma_d) = \frac{(G_s)(\gamma_w)}{1 + e} \rightarrow (\gamma_d) = \frac{(2.65)(9.81)}{1 + 0.60}$$

$$(\gamma_d) = \frac{26.00}{1.60} = 16.2\ \text{kN/m}^3$$
questions.explanation: Dry unit weight packs the solids' weight into the total volume — hence the (1 + e) divisor. 26.0 kN/m^3 skips it; 10.1 kN/m^3 is the submerged unit weight.
questions.videoTitle: Module-1 Part-3

questions.question: A 5-m-tall vertical retaining wall retains a level cohesionless backfill with φ = 30° and γ = 18 kN/m^3. A uniform surcharge of 10 kPa acts on the ground surface behind the wall. What is the total Rankine active thrust per meter of wall?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Horizontal Stress Profiles and Forces section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(P_a\), the total active thrust. A uniform surcharge adds a rectangular pressure diagram \(K_a q\) over the full wall height:

$$P_a = \frac{1}{2}K_a\gamma H^2 + K_a q H, \quad K_a = \frac{1 - \sin\phi}{1 + \sin\phi}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(P_a\):

$$\begin{aligned}
\phi &= 30^\circ \rightarrow K_a = \frac{1 - 0.5}{1 + 0.5} = 0.333 \\
\gamma &= 18\ \text{kN/m}^3 \\
H &= 5\ \text{m} \\
q &= 10\ \text{kPa} \\
P_a &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(P_a) = \frac{1}{2}(0.333)(18)(5)^2 + (0.333)(10)(5)$$

$$(P_a) = 75.0 + 16.7 = 91.7\ \text{kN/m}$$
questions.explanation: A uniform surcharge contributes a rectangular — not triangular — pressure block over the whole height. 75.0 kN/m ignores the surcharge; 83.3 kN/m wrongly treats it as triangular.
questions.videoTitle: Rankine Theory of Earth Pressure

questions.question: A flow net for seepage under a sheet-pile wall has 5 flow channels and 10 equipotential drops. If the hydraulic conductivity is \(2.0 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m/s}\) and the total head loss across the system is 4.0 m, what is the seepage rate per meter of wall?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Darcy's Law section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook for the hydraulic conductivity \(k\). Note: the flow-net relation below is a standard geotechnical result — it is not printed in the FE Reference Handbook 10.6, whose Darcy's Law section (printed p. 298) contains only \(Q = -KA(dh/dx)\), \(v = Ki\), and the average seepage velocity \(v/n\).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(q\), the seepage rate per unit length of wall:

$$q = kH\frac{N_f}{N_d}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(q\):

$$\begin{aligned}
k &= 2.0 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m/s} \\
H &= 4.0\ \text{m} \\
N_f &= 5 \\
N_d &= 10 \\
q &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(q) = (k)(H)\frac{N_f}{N_d} = (2.0 \times 10^{-5})(4.0)\frac{5}{10}$$

$$(q) = 4.0 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m}^3\text{/s per m}$$
questions.explanation: Seepage scales with flow channels over equipotential drops — N_f/N_d, not the inverse (8.0 × 10^-5). The head H belongs in the formula; 2.0 × 10^-5 drops it.
questions.videoTitle: Soil Permeability - Darcy's Law

questions.question: A 4.0-m-thick clay layer with drainage at both its top and bottom has a coefficient of consolidation c_v = 5.0 m^2/yr. Approximately how long will it take to reach 50% average consolidation?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Ultimate consolidation settlement in soil layer section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(t\), the time to 50% consolidation:

$$t = \frac{T_v H_{dr}^2}{c_v}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(t\):

$$\begin{aligned}
c_v &= 5.0\ \text{m}^2\text{/yr} \\
\text{double drainage} &\rightarrow H_{dr} = \frac{4.0}{2} = 2.0\ \text{m} \\
T_{50} &= 0.197 \\
t &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(t) = \frac{(T_{50})(H_{dr})^2}{c_v} \rightarrow (t) = \frac{(0.197)(2.0)^2}{5.0}$$

$$(t) = 0.1576\ \text{yr} = 58\ \text{days}$$
questions.explanation: Double drainage halves the drainage path — and time scales with H_dr^2, so that halves the time twice over. 230 days uses the full 4 m as if drainage were one-way.
questions.videoTitle: Terzaghi's Theory of Consolidation

questions.question: A 2.0-m-wide strip footing bears 1.0 m below the ground surface on a soil with c = 20 kPa, φ = 25°, and γ = 18 kN/m^3. Using Terzaghi's bearing capacity equation for general shear failure, what is the ultimate bearing capacity? (Terzaghi factors for φ = 25°: N_c = 25.1, N_q = 12.7, N_γ = 9.7)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Ultimate Bearing Capacity section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(q_{ult}\). Terzaghi's equation for a strip footing is:

$$q_{ult} = cN_c + \gamma D_f N_q + \frac{1}{2}\gamma B N_{\gamma}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(q_{ult}\):

$$\begin{aligned}
c &= 20\ \text{kPa},\ N_c = 25.1 \\
\gamma &= 18\ \text{kN/m}^3 \\
D_f &= 1.0\ \text{m},\ N_q = 12.7 \\
B &= 2.0\ \text{m},\ N_{\gamma} = 9.7 \\
q_{ult} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(q_{ult}) = (c)(N_c) + (\gamma)(D_f)(N_q) + \frac{1}{2}(\gamma)(B)(N_{\gamma})$$

$$(q_{ult}) = (20)(25.1) + (18)(1.0)(12.7) + \frac{1}{2}(18)(2.0)(9.7)$$

$$(q_{ult}) = 502 + 228.6 + 174.6 = 905\ \text{kPa}$$
questions.explanation: All three Terzaghi terms count: cohesion, surcharge, and self-weight. 731 kPa drops the ½γBN_γ term; 1080 kPa forgets the ½ in front of it.
questions.videoTitle: Bearing Capacity of Soil EXPLAINED: Terzaghi, Meyerhof, Hansen, Vesic, Skempton & IS Code

questions.question: In a Proctor compaction test, the dry unit weight decreases when water is added beyond the optimum water content. Why?
choices: the compactive effort becomes less effective in wet soil
excess water occupies voids and displaces soil solids, lowering the dry unit weight
the soil grains dissolve in the extra water
water lubricates the grains so they pack more tightly
questions.solution:
Refer to the Compaction section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Up to the optimum water content, water lubricates the grains and helps them pack tighter, so dry unit weight rises. Beyond the optimum, the voids are already as full of water as compaction can achieve — additional water cannot be squeezed out by the compactive effort, so it simply occupies space that soil solids would otherwise fill. Since dry unit weight counts only the solids, displacing solids with water lowers it.

The compactive effort doesn't change, grains don't dissolve, and extra lubrication can't pack grains tighter than the voids allow.

Excess water occupies voids and displaces soil solids, lowering the dry unit weight, is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: Past optimum, water is incompressible filler stealing space from solids. That is why the Proctor curve peaks — dry unit weight must fall on the wet side.

questions.question: A horizontal curve with a radius of 2,000 ft is designed for a speed of 60 mph. Using the AASHTO point-mass equation with a side friction factor of 0.11, what superelevation rate is required?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Horizontal Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the required superelevation rate \(e\). We can determine \(e\) from the AASHTO point-mass equation:

$$e + f_s = \frac{V^2}{15R}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(e\):

$$\begin{aligned} V &= 60\ \text{mph} \\ R &= 2000\ \text{ft} \\ f_s &= 0.11 \\ e &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting and solving for \(e\):

$$e = \frac{60^2}{15(2000)} - 0.11 = 0.12 - 0.11$$

$$e = 0.01 = 1.0\%$$
questions.explanation: Solve the point-mass equation for e: e = V²/(15R) − f_s. Forgetting to subtract the side friction factor is the classic error — it leads to the 12.0% trap.
questions.videoTitle: Critical SUPERELEVATION Calculations

questions.question: A crest vertical curve 400 ft long connects grades of +2% and −3%. If the elevation of the PVC is 98.00 ft, what is the elevation of a point on the curve 100 ft from the PVC?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vertical Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the elevation \(y\) of the point 100 ft from the PVC. We can determine \(y\) from the parabolic vertical curve equation:

$$y = y_{PVC} + g_1 x + \frac{(g_2 - g_1)x^2}{2L}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(y\):

$$\begin{aligned} y_{PVC} &= 98.00\ \text{ft} \\ g_1 &= +2\% = 0.02 \\ g_2 &= -3\% = -0.03 \\ L &= 400\ \text{ft} \\ x &= 100\ \text{ft} \\ y &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$y = 98.00 + (0.02)(100) + \frac{(-0.03 - 0.02)(100)^2}{2(400)} = 100.00 - 0.625$$

$$y = 99.375\ \text{ft} \approx 99.38\ \text{ft}$$
questions.explanation: On a vertical curve, elevation = tangent elevation plus the parabolic offset (g₂−g₁)x²/(2L); on a crest the offset is negative, so watch its sign.
questions.videoTitle: Vertical Curves: The Secret to Smooth Road Design

questions.question: A crest vertical curve connects grades of +4% and −4% on a highway with a required stopping sight distance of 196 ft. Assuming S > L, what is the minimum curve length?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Vertical Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the minimum crest curve length \(L\). Because \(S > L\), the governing equation is:

$$L = 2S - \frac{2158}{A}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(L\):

$$\begin{aligned} g_1 &= +4\% \\ g_2 &= -4\% \\ A &= |4 - (-4)| = 8\% \\ S &= 196\ \text{ft} \\ L &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$L = 2(196) - \frac{2158}{8} = 392 - 269.75$$

$$L = 122.25\ \text{ft} \approx 122\ \text{ft}$$

Since \(196 > 122\), the assumption \(S > L\) holds and the result is valid.
questions.explanation: Use L = 2S − 2158/A only when S > L, and always verify the assumption afterward — here 196 > 122 confirms it.
questions.videoTitle: Vertical Curves: The Secret to Smooth Road Design

questions.question: A directional freeway segment has 2 lanes, a peak-hour volume of 3,800 veh/hr, and a peak hour factor of 0.90. Using an ideal per-lane capacity of 2,400 pc/h/ln, what is the volume-to-capacity (v/c) ratio?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Traffic Flow Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the volume-to-capacity ratio \(v/c\). First convert the hourly volume to the peak 15-minute flow rate, then compare the per-lane flow to per-lane capacity:

$$v_p = \frac{V}{PHF}, \qquad v/c = \frac{v_p / N}{c}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(v/c\):

$$\begin{aligned} V &= 3800\ \text{veh/hr} \\ PHF &= 0.90 \\ N &= 2\ \text{lanes} \\ c &= 2400\ \text{pc/h/ln} \\ v/c &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$v_p = \frac{3800}{0.90} = 4222.2\ \text{veh/hr}, \qquad v/c = \frac{4222.2/2}{2400} = \frac{2111.1}{2400}$$

$$v/c = 0.88$$
questions.explanation: Divide by the PHF (not multiply) to get the peak 15-minute rate, and compare per-lane flow against per-lane capacity — skipping the lane split gives the 1.76 trap.

questions.question: A signalized intersection has three phases whose critical lane groups have flow ratios (v/s) of 0.30, 0.25, and 0.20. What is the intersection's critical v/c ratio, Xc?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Traffic Signal Timing section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the critical v/c ratio \(X_c\), the sum of the flow ratios of the critical lane groups:

$$X_c = \sum \left(\frac{v}{s}\right)_{\text{critical}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(X_c\):

$$\begin{aligned} (v/s)_1 &= 0.30 \\ (v/s)_2 &= 0.25 \\ (v/s)_3 &= 0.20 \\ X_c &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$X_c = 0.30 + 0.25 + 0.20$$

$$X_c = 0.75$$
questions.explanation: The critical v/c ratio is the sum of the critical lane groups' flow ratios — the bottleneck is the total demand, not the single worst phase.

questions.question: According to the Highway Capacity Manual, the level of service of a two-lane highway is defined by which measure(s) of effectiveness?
choices: Density in passenger cars per mile per lane
Percent time-spent-following and average travel speed
questions.solution:
The Highway Capacity Manual assigns each facility type its own measure of effectiveness for level of service. For a basic freeway segment that measure is density — but a two-lane highway is different: its LOS is defined by percent time-spent-following together with average travel speed, because passing opportunities and platooning govern the driver's experience.

Control delay is the measure for signalized intersections, and v/c is a capacity check rather than a LOS measure.

Percent time-spent-following and average travel speed is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: Two-lane highways are the odd ones out: LOS comes from percent time-spent-following and average travel speed, not density.

questions.question: A horizontal curve with a radius of 1,432.4 ft uses the arc definition of degree of curve. What is the degree of curve?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Horizontal Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the degree of curve \(D\). Under the arc definition:

$$D = \frac{5729.58}{R}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(D\):

$$\begin{aligned} R &= 1432.4\ \text{ft} \\ D &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$D = \frac{5729.58}{1432.4} = 4.000$$

$$D = 4.00^{\circ}$$
questions.explanation: Arc definition: D = 5729.58/R. The 0.25° trap comes from inverting the relationship instead of dividing.

questions.question: In CPM scheduling, the free float of an activity is defined as:
choices: The amount an activity can be delayed without delaying project completion
The amount an activity can be delayed without delaying the early start of any successor activity
The difference between the late start and the early finish of the activity
The scheduling slack that is always equal to the total float
questions.solution:
Free float is the scheduling slack available to an activity without affecting any other activity: it is the amount an activity can be delayed without delaying the early start of any successor activity.

Total float, by contrast, is the amount an activity can be delayed without delaying project completion.

Free float can never exceed total float, and an activity with zero total float (on the critical path) has zero free float.

The correct definition is delaying without pushing back the early start of any successor.
questions.explanation: Free float protects successors; total float protects the project finish. Free float can never exceed total float.

questions.question: An activity has a normal duration of 10 days at a direct cost of $20,000. It can be crashed to a duration of 6 days at a direct cost of $28,000. What is the activity's cost slope?
questions.solution:
Refer to the CPM Precedence Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the cost slope, the extra direct cost per day of shortening the activity:

$$\text{Cost slope} = \frac{\text{crash cost} - \text{normal cost}}{\text{normal time} - \text{crash time}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for the cost slope:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Normal time} &= 10\ \text{days} \\ \text{Normal cost} &= \$20{,}000 \\ \text{Crash time} &= 6\ \text{days} \\ \text{Crash cost} &= \$28{,}000 \\ \text{Cost slope} &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$\text{Cost slope} = \frac{28000 - 20000}{10 - 6} = \frac{8000}{4}$$

$$\text{Cost slope} = \$2{,}000/\text{day}$$
questions.explanation: Cost slope = Δcost/Δtime using normal-minus-crash in both — dividing the cost difference by the crash duration alone is the $1,333/day trap.

questions.question: A project has a budget at completion (BAC) of $200,000. At the status date, BCWS = $100,000, BCWP = $90,000, and ACWP = $95,000. If cost performance continues at its current rate, what is the estimate at completion (EAC)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earned-Value Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the estimate at completion \(EAC\). Assuming the current cost efficiency continues, \(EAC = BAC/CPI\) where \(CPI = BCWP/ACWP\):

$$CPI = \frac{BCWP}{ACWP}, \qquad EAC = \frac{BAC}{CPI}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(EAC\):

$$\begin{aligned} BAC &= \$200{,}000 \\ BCWS &= \$100{,}000 \\ BCWP &= \$90{,}000 \\ ACWP &= \$95{,}000 \\ EAC &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$CPI = \frac{90000}{95000} = 0.9474, \qquad EAC = \frac{200000}{0.9474}$$

$$EAC = \$211{,}111$$
questions.explanation: EAC = BAC/CPI projects current cost efficiency forward; using the schedule index (SPI) instead gives the $222,222 trap.
questions.videoTitle: Your Project Is Already Over Budget (You Just Don't Know)

questions.question: A contractor submits a monthly progress payment request for $100,000 of completed work. The contract specifies 10% retainage. What is the amount of the payment due to the contractor?
questions.solution:
Retainage is the percentage of each progress payment that the owner withholds until the project reaches substantial completion. The payment due is the requested amount minus the retainage:

$$\text{Payment} = 100000 \times (1 - 0.10) = 90000$$

$$\text{Payment} = \$90{,}000$$

The correct payment is $90,000.
questions.explanation: Retainage is withheld from each payment — the contractor receives request × (1 − retainage), not the full request.
questions.videoTitle: Retainage for Contractors Explained

questions.question: A scraper with a 20-CY heaped bucket operates on a 6-minute cycle and works a 50-minute hour. The soil swells 25%. What is the hourly production rate in bank cubic yards?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the hourly production in bank cubic yards. Chain the adjustments — cycles per hour, the 50-minute-hour efficiency, and the swell correction from loose yards to bank yards:

$$\text{Production} = \frac{60}{\text{cycle time}} \times \text{bucket} \times \frac{50}{60} \times \frac{1}{1 + \text{swell}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for the production:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Cycle time} &= 6\ \text{min} \\ \text{Bucket} &= 20\ \text{CY (loose)} \\ \text{Efficiency} &= 50/60 \\ \text{Swell} &= 25\% = 0.25 \\ \text{Production} &= ?\ \text{BCY/hr} \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$\text{Production} = \frac{60}{6}(20)\left(\frac{50}{60}\right)\left(\frac{1}{1.25}\right) = \frac{166.67}{1.25}$$

$$\text{Production} = 133\ \text{BCY/hr}$$
questions.explanation: Bank yards come last: divide loose-yard production by (1 + swell). Skipping the swell correction leaves the 167 BCY/hr trap.
questions.videoTitle: FECivil 98 Production analysis of the Best Excavator

questions.question: Under OSHA excavation standards, a trench 4 ft or deeper must have a stairway, ladder, ramp, or other safe means of egress located so that no worker must travel more than what lateral distance to reach it?
questions.solution:
The governing rule is OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P (Excavations), covered in the Safety section of the Construction Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook: trench excavations 4 ft or deeper require a stairway, ladder, ramp, or other safe means of egress, located so that no worker must travel more than 25 ft laterally to reach it.

The 25-ft limit is the correct choice — 50 ft and 100 ft are too lax, and 10 ft is stricter than the standard.
questions.explanation: Trench egress: 4 ft deep triggers the requirement, and no worker may be more than 25 ft of lateral travel from a ladder, stairway, or ramp.

questions.question: A contractor purchases a loader for $200,000 with an estimated salvage value of $20,000 after 5 years. The loader will operate 2,000 hours per year and the interest rate is 8%. What is the hourly ownership (fixed) cost of the loader?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the hourly ownership cost: the annual capital recovery on the depreciable amount, plus interest on the salvage value, divided by the annual operating hours:

$$\text{Hourly cost} = \frac{(P - S)(A/P, i, n) + S \cdot i}{\text{hours/year}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for the hourly cost:

$$\begin{aligned} P &= \$200{,}000 \\ S &= \$20{,}000 \\ i &= 8\% = 0.08 \\ n &= 5\ \text{years} \\ \text{Hours} &= 2000\ \text{hr/yr} \\ (A/P, 8\%, 5) &= 0.2505 \\ \text{Hourly cost} &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$\text{Hourly cost} = \frac{(200000 - 20000)(0.25046) + (20000)(0.08)}{2000} = \frac{45082 + 1600}{2000}$$

$$\text{Hourly cost} = \$23.34/\text{hr}$$
questions.explanation: Ownership cost = capital recovery on (P − S) plus interest on S, all divided by annual hours. Forgetting the salvage value in the capital recovery is the $25.05/hr trap.

questions.question: What uniform end-of-year deposit is required for 5 years at 8% annual interest to accumulate $50,000?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the uniform annual deposit \(A\). We can determine \(A\) from the sinking fund factor:

$$A = F(A/F, i, n) = F\frac{i}{(1+i)^n - 1}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(A\):

$$\begin{aligned} F &= \$50{,}000 \\ i &= 8\% = 0.08 \\ n &= 5\ \text{years} \\ A &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$A = 50000\frac{0.08}{(1.08)^5 - 1} = 50000(0.17046)$$

$$A = \$8{,}523$$
questions.explanation: Sinking fund: A = F(A/F, i, n). The $10,000 trap ignores interest entirely; the $34,029 trap discounts instead of accumulating.

questions.question: Annual maintenance costs are $1,000 in year 1 and grow at 5% per year through year 5. At 10% annual interest, what is the present worth of these costs?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the present worth \(P\) of a geometric gradient series, where each year's cost grows by the rate \(g\):

$$P = A_1\frac{1 - (1+g)^n(1+i)^{-n}}{i - g}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(P\):

$$\begin{aligned} A_1 &= \$1{,}000 \\ g &= 5\% = 0.05 \\ i &= 10\% = 0.10 \\ n &= 5\ \text{years} \\ P &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$P = 1000\frac{1 - (1.05)^5(1.10)^{-5}}{0.10 - 0.05} = 1000\frac{1 - 0.79247}{0.05}$$

$$P = \$4{,}151$$
questions.explanation: Geometric gradient: P = A₁[1 − (1+g)ⁿ(1+i)⁻ⁿ]/(i − g). Treating it as a level annuity gives the $3,791 trap.
questions.videoTitle: Engineering Economic Analysis - Gradient Series

questions.subtopic: Present worth of uneven cash flows
questions.question: A project requires an investment of $8,000 today and returns $3,000, $4,000, and $5,000 at the ends of years 1, 2, and 3. At 10% annual interest, what is the present worth of the project?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the present worth \(P\) by discounting each cash flow at its own year:

$$P = \sum_{t=0}^{n}\frac{CF_t}{(1+i)^t}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(P\):

$$\begin{aligned} CF_0 &= -\$8{,}000 \\ CF_1 &= \$3{,}000 \\ CF_2 &= \$4{,}000 \\ CF_3 &= \$5{,}000 \\ i &= 10\% = 0.10 \\ P &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$P = -8000 + \frac{3000}{1.10} + \frac{4000}{1.10^2} + \frac{5000}{1.10^3} = -8000 + 2727.27 + 3305.79 + 3756.57$$

$$P = \$1{,}790$$
questions.explanation: Discount each cash flow at its own year — averaging the inflows into an annuity gives the $1,947 trap.
questions.videoTitle: Simple and Compound Interest Explained

questions.question: A project requires an initial investment of $12,000 and generates $4,000 per year. At 10% annual interest, what is the discounted payback period?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the discounted payback period: the time until the cumulative discounted cash inflows recover the initial investment:

$$\sum_{t=1}^{n}\frac{A}{(1+i)^t} \geq P$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(n\):

$$\begin{aligned} P &= \$12{,}000 \\ A &= \$4{,}000/\text{yr} \\ i &= 10\% = 0.10 \\ n &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Accumulate the discounted inflows:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Year 1:} &\quad 4000/1.10 = 3636.36 \quad (\text{cum } 3636.36) \\ \text{Year 2:} &\quad 4000/1.10^2 = 3305.79 \quad (\text{cum } 6942.15) \\ \text{Year 3:} &\quad 4000/1.10^3 = 3005.26 \quad (\text{cum } 9947.41) \\ \text{Year 4:} &\quad 4000/1.10^4 = 2732.05 \quad (\text{cum } 12679.46) \end{aligned}$$

The investment is recovered during year 4:

$$n = 3 + \frac{12000 - 9947.41}{2732.05} = 3 + 0.75$$

$$n = 3.75\ \text{years}$$
questions.explanation: Discounted payback discounts first, then accumulates; the 3.00-year trap is the simple (undiscounted) payback.

questions.question: A $100,000 piece of equipment is classified as 5-year property under MACRS. What is the depreciation deduction in year 2?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Depreciation section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the year-2 MACRS depreciation. For 5-year property, the MACRS recovery percentages are 20.00%, 32.00%, 19.20%, 11.52%, 11.52%, and 5.76%:

$$D_2 = (\text{cost}) \times (\text{year-2 rate})$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(D_2\):

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Cost} &= \$100{,}000 \\ \text{Year-2 rate} &= 32.00\% = 0.32 \\ D_2 &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$D_2 = 100000(0.32)$$

$$D_2 = \$32{,}000$$
questions.explanation: MACRS 5-year property: year-2 rate is 32.00% of the full cost. The 40% trap applies double-declining without the half-year convention.
questions.videoTitle: Depreciation

questions.question: A proposed project has benefits of $800,000, disbenefits of $100,000, and costs of $500,000 (all present worths). What is the conventional benefit-cost ratio?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Benefit-Cost Analysis section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the conventional benefit-cost ratio, in which disbenefits are subtracted from benefits:

$$B/C = \frac{\text{benefits} - \text{disbenefits}}{\text{costs}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(B/C\):

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Benefits} &= \$800{,}000 \\ \text{Disbenefits} &= \$100{,}000 \\ \text{Costs} &= \$500{,}000 \\ B/C &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$B/C = \frac{800000 - 100000}{500000} = \frac{700000}{500000}$$

$$B/C = 1.40$$
questions.explanation: Conventional B/C subtracts disbenefits from benefits: (800 − 100)/500 = 1.40. Adding them instead gives the 1.80 trap.
questions.videoTitle: Engineering Economics VI: Benefit–Cost Analysis

questions.question: An investment of $5,000 grows to $8,000 in 4 years with annual compounding. What is the annual effective interest rate?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the annual effective interest rate \(i\). We can determine \(i\) from the single-payment compound amount relationship:

$$F = P(1+i)^n \quad\Rightarrow\quad i = \left(\frac{F}{P}\right)^{1/n} - 1$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(i\):

$$\begin{aligned} P &= \$5{,}000 \\ F &= \$8{,}000 \\ n &= 4\ \text{years} \\ i &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$i = \left(\frac{8000}{5000}\right)^{1/4} - 1 = (1.6)^{0.25} - 1 = 0.1247$$

$$i = 12.5\%$$
questions.explanation: Solve F = P(1+i)ⁿ for i: (F/P)^(1/n) − 1. Dividing the total 60% gain by 4 years gives the 15.0% trap.

questions.question: Concrete compressive strengths are normally distributed with a mean of 500 psi and a standard deviation of 100 psi. Approximately what percentile is a strength of 600 psi?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Normal Distribution (Gaussian Distribution) section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the percentile of \(x = 600\). Standardize with the z-score, then read the cumulative area from the standard normal table:

$$z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(z\):

$$\begin{aligned} \mu &= 500\ \text{psi} \\ \sigma &= 100\ \text{psi} \\ x &= 600\ \text{psi} \\ z &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$z = \frac{600 - 500}{100} = 1.00$$

From the standard normal table, \(\Phi(1.00) = 0.8413\), so a strength of 600 psi is at the 84.1st percentile.
questions.explanation: z = 1.00 → Φ(1) = 0.8413, the 84.1st percentile. The 68.3% trap confuses this with the within-one-sigma empirical-rule band.
questions.videoTitle: Statistics 6.3 – Finding Probability Using a Normal Distribution

questions.question: A manufactured part has a 5% defect rate, independently from part to part. If 4 parts are sampled, what is the probability that at least one is defective?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Laws of Probability section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(P(\text{at least one defective})\). Use the complement rule:

$$P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\text{none defective}) = 1 - (1 - p)^n$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(P\):

$$\begin{aligned} p &= 5\% = 0.05 \\ n &= 4 \\ P &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$P = 1 - (0.95)^4 = 1 - 0.81451$$

$$P = 0.185$$
questions.explanation: “At least one” means use the complement: 1 − (1−p)ⁿ. The 0.815 trap is P(none defective).
questions.videoTitle: Introduction to Probability, Basic Overview - Sample Space, & Tree Diagrams

questions.question: Steel yield strengths have a mean of 60 ksi and a standard deviation of 3 ksi. What is the coefficient of variation?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Dispersion, Mean, Median, and Mode Values section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the coefficient of variation \(CV\), the relative (dimensionless) measure of spread:

$$CV = \frac{\sigma}{\mu}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(CV\):

$$\begin{aligned} \mu &= 60\ \text{ksi} \\ \sigma &= 3\ \text{ksi} \\ CV &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$CV = \frac{3}{60} = 0.05$$

$$CV = 5\%$$
questions.explanation: CV = σ/μ is unitless relative spread — the 20 trap inverts the ratio.
questions.videoTitle: Statistics Basics: Mean, Median, Mode, Range & Standard Deviation Explained!

questions.question: In hypothesis testing, a Type I error is:
choices: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis
Accepting the alternative hypothesis when it is false
Using a significance level that is too large
questions.solution:
A Type I error is the error of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true — a false positive.

A Type II error is the opposite mistake: failing to reject a false null hypothesis (a false negative).

The significance level \(\alpha\) of a test is exactly the probability of committing a Type I error.

Rejecting a true null hypothesis is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: Type I = false positive (reject a true null); the significance level α is exactly P(Type I error).

questions.question: In a survey of 400 residents, 60% support a proposed transit project. What is the margin of error for a 95% confidence interval for the true proportion? (Use z = 1.96.)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Confidence Intervals section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the margin of error \(E\) of a 95% confidence interval for a proportion:

$$E = z\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(E\):

$$\begin{aligned} \hat{p} &= 60\% = 0.60 \\ n &= 400 \\ z &= 1.96 \\ E &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$E = 1.96\sqrt{\frac{0.60(0.40)}{400}} = 1.96(0.024495)$$

$$E = 0.048$$
questions.explanation: Margin of error = z√(p̂(1−p̂)/n). Forgetting the square root of n gives the 0.960 trap.
questions.videoTitle: Statistics 101: Confidence Interval Estimation, Sigma Known

questions.question: X and Y are independent random variables with Var(X) = 4 and Var(Y) = 9. What is Var(3X − 2Y)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Laws of Probability section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(Var(3X - 2Y)\). For independent random variables, variances add with squared coefficients — the minus sign does not survive squaring:

$$Var(aX + bY) = a^2Var(X) + b^2Var(Y)$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(Var(3X - 2Y)\):

$$\begin{aligned} Var(X) &= 4 \\ Var(Y) &= 9 \\ a &= 3,\ b = -2 \\ Var(3X - 2Y) &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$Var(3X - 2Y) = (3)^2(4) + (-2)^2(9) = 36 + 36$$

$$Var(3X - 2Y) = 72$$
questions.explanation: Variance squares the coefficients and the minus sign vanishes: 9(4) + 4(9) = 72. The −18 trap keeps the sign.
questions.videoTitle: Expected Value & Variance (Discrete Random Variables)

questions.question: Vehicles arrive at a toll booth at an average rate of 3 per minute. What is the probability that at most 1 vehicle arrives in a given minute?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Probability and Density Functions: Means and Variances section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \(P(X \le 1)\). Sum the probabilities for \(k = 0\) and \(k = 1\):

$$P(X = k) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{k}}{k!}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to solve for \(P(X \le 1)\):

$$\begin{aligned} \lambda &= 3 \\ k &= 0, 1 \\ P(X \le 1) &= ? \end{aligned}$$

Substituting:

$$P(X \le 1) = \frac{e^{-3}3^0}{0!} + \frac{e^{-3}3^1}{1!} = e^{-3}(1 + 3) = 4(0.049787)$$

$$P(X \le 1) = 0.199$$
questions.explanation: P(X ≤ 1) = e^( −λ)(1 + λ). The 0.801 trap answers the complement instead.

questions.question: Under the NCEES Model Rules, an engineer who has knowledge of another engineer's violation of the licensure laws should:
choices: Ignore it unless it directly affects her own work
Confront the engineer privately and take no further action
Report it to the appropriate licensing board
Report it to the news media first
questions.solution:
The NCEES Model Rules provide that engineers having knowledge of any alleged violation of the licensure act or rules shall cooperate with the licensing board and furnish information or assistance as required.

An engineer who observes a violation therefore has an affirmative duty to report it to the appropriate licensing board — ignoring it, handling it only privately, or going to the media first does not satisfy that duty.

Reporting to the licensing board is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: Knowledge of a licensure violation creates an affirmative duty to report it to the licensing board — private confrontation alone is not enough.

questions.question: An engineer uses her employer's licensed software and office equipment after hours to perform design work for a private client who competes with her employer. This conduct is:
choices: Ethical, since the work was performed on her own time
Ethical, as long as she charges the client a fair fee
Unethical — misuse of employer resources and an undisclosed conflict of interest
Ethical, provided the design work meets professional standards
questions.solution:
Under the NSPE Code of Ethics, engineers shall not use their employer's equipment, supplies, or staff for outside work without consent, and must disclose any conflict of interest to the affected parties.

Here the engineer commits both wrongs at once: using the employer's licensed software and equipment for private gain, and serving a competing client without disclosure.

Doing the work “on her own time” does not cure either violation.

The unethical — misuse of resources and undisclosed conflict — choice is correct.
questions.explanation: Employer resources are not for moonlighting, and competing side work without disclosure is a conflict of interest.

questions.question: An engineer retained as an expert witness in litigation must ensure that her testimony is:
choices: As favorable as possible to the side that retained her
Objective and based on technical facts, regardless of which side retained her
Withheld from the court until the retaining attorney approves it
