Limited to opinions that support the retaining client's position
questions.solution:
The NSPE Code of Ethics requires that engineers testifying as experts be objective and truthful: testimony must be founded on adequate knowledge of the facts and honest conviction, and must not be slanted to favor the party paying the bill.

An expert who tailors opinions to the retaining client's position violates the duty of honesty to the tribunal and the public.

Objective and based on technical facts, regardless of which side retained her, is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: An expert witness serves the truth, not the retaining client — testimony must stay objective regardless of who pays.

questions.question: In most states, a licensed professional engineer must do which of the following to renew her license?
choices: Retake the FE exam every renewal cycle
Complete a required number of professional development (continuing education) hours
Publish one technical paper per renewal cycle
Maintain membership in a national engineering society
questions.solution:
Most state licensing boards require licensed professional engineers to complete a set number of professional development hours (continuing education) in each renewal cycle as a condition of license renewal.

Retaking the FE exam, publishing papers, and society membership are not renewal requirements.

Completing the required professional development hours is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: License renewal in most states hinges on completing the required professional development hours.

questions.question: A supervisor asks a junior engineer to backdate an inspection certification to a date before the inspection actually occurred. Under the NCEES Code of Ethics, the engineer should:
choices: Comply, since the supervisor assumes responsibility for the decision
Refuse — falsifying the date misrepresents facts and is dishonest
Comply, but keep a private memo documenting the request
Backdate it only if the inspection results were satisfactory
questions.solution:
The NCEES Code of Ethics requires engineers to be honest and to avoid deceptive acts: engineers shall not falsify or misrepresent facts.

Backdating an inspection certification misrepresents when the inspection occurred, regardless of whether the results were satisfactory — and a supervisor's order does not transfer the ethical responsibility.

Refusing because falsifying the date is dishonest is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: Backdating any certification is falsification; a supervisor's instruction does not make it ethical.

questions.question: When an engineer issues a public statement on a technical matter (for example, testimony before a planning board), the NCEES Code of Ethics requires the statement to be:
choices: Supportive of the engineer's client position regardless of the facts
Objective and truthful, disclosing any interest the engineer has in the matter
Limited to information the client has approved for release
Delivered only through the client's public relations office
questions.solution:
Under the NSPE Code of Ethics, engineers shall be objective and truthful in professional reports, statements, and testimony, and shall include all relevant and pertinent information — and when issuing statements on behalf of an interested party, shall disclose that interest.

Slanting a public statement toward a client's position, or suppressing facts the client disfavors, violates that duty.

Objective and truthful, disclosing any interest, is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: Public statements must be objective and truthful, with any interest disclosed — the facts come before the client's position.

questions.question: A materials supplier offers an engineer a 5% commission for specifying the supplier's products on a client's project, in addition to the engineer's normal design fee. Under the NSPE Code of Ethics, the engineer may accept the commission only if:
choices: The commission is less than 10% of the design fee
The supplier's products are technically equal to competitors
The client is fully informed of the arrangement and consents to it
The engineer discloses the commission to the other engineers on the project
questions.solution:
The NSPE Code of Ethics provides that engineers shall not accept compensation, financial or otherwise, from more than one party for services on the same project unless the circumstances are fully disclosed to and agreed to by all interested parties.

A secret supplier commission for specifying its products is a textbook violation; technical equivalence of the products and the size of the commission do not cure it.

Full disclosure to and consent of the client is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: Compensation from two parties on one project is allowed only with full disclosure to and consent of all interested parties.

questions.question: Use one iteration of Newton's method for root extraction to estimate the root of \(f(x) = x^3 - 2x - 5\), starting from the initial estimate \(x_0 = 2\). What is \(x_1\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Newton's Method for Root Extraction section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(x_1\). The handbook gives the iteration formula:

$$x_{j+1} = x_j - \frac{f(x_j)}{f'(x_j)}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to compute \(x_1\):

$$\begin{aligned}
f(x) &= x^3 - 2x - 5 \\
f'(x) &= 3x^2 - 2 \\
x_0 &= 2 \\
x_1 &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Evaluate \(f\) and \(f'\) at the initial estimate:

$$(f(2)) = (2)^3 - 2(2) - 5 \rightarrow 8 - 4 - 5 = -1$$

$$(f'(2)) = 3(2)^2 - 2 \rightarrow 12 - 2 = 10$$

Substitute into the iteration formula:

$$(x_1) = (2) - \frac{(-1)}{(10)} \rightarrow 2 + 0.10 = 2.10$$

$$x_1 = 2.10$$
questions.explanation: Newton's method improves each guess by subtracting f/f'. Watch the sign: a negative f value moves the guess upward.

questions.question: Evaluate the definite integral \(\displaystyle\int_0^1 x e^x\,dx\).
questions.solution:
Refer to the Indefinite Integrals section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(\int_0^1 x e^x\,dx\). The handbook's integral equation #6 (integration by parts) gives:

$$\int u(x)\,dv(x) = u(x)v(x) - \int v(x)\,du(x)$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to apply the formula:

$$\begin{aligned}
u &= x \\
dv &= e^x\,dx \\
du &= dx \\
v &= e^x
\end{aligned}$$

Substitute into the integration-by-parts formula and evaluate from 0 to 1:

$$\left(\int_0^1 x e^x\,dx\right) = \left[x e^x\right]_0^1 - \int_0^1 e^x\,dx$$

Evaluate the boundary term on its own line:

$$\left[x e^x\right]_0^1 = (1)(e) - (0)(1) = e$$

Evaluate the remaining integral on its own line:

$$\left(\int_0^1 e^x\,dx\right) = \left[e^x\right]_0^1 = e - 1$$

Combine the two results:

$$\left(\int_0^1 x e^x\,dx\right) = (e) - (e - 1) = 1$$

$$\int_0^1 x e^x\,dx = 1$$
questions.explanation: Integration by parts splits the integrand into u (the part that simplifies when differentiated) and dv (the part that is easy to integrate).

questions.question: Consider the region bounded by the curve \(y = x^2\), the x-axis, and the vertical lines \(x = 0\) and \(x = 2\). What is the x-coordinate of the centroid of this region?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Centroids of Masses, Areas, Lengths, and Volumes section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(x_c\). The handbook gives, for an area bounded by the axes and the function \(y = f(x)\):

$$x_c = \frac{\int x\,dA}{A}, \qquad A = \int f(x)\,dx, \qquad dA = f(x)\,dx$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to compute \(x_c\):

$$\begin{aligned}
f(x) &= x^2 \\
dA &= x^2\,dx \\
A &= \int_0^2 x^2\,dx \\
\int x\,dA &= \int_0^2 x \cdot x^2\,dx = \int_0^2 x^3\,dx \\
x_c &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Compute the area on its own line:

$$(A) = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 = \frac{8}{3} - 0 = \frac{8}{3}$$

Compute the first moment with respect to the y-axis on its own line:

$$\left(\int x\,dA\right) = \left[\frac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^2 = \frac{16}{4} - 0 = 4$$

Divide the moment by the area:

$$(x_c) = \frac{(4)}{(8/3)} \rightarrow (4)\left(\frac{3}{8}\right) = \frac{12}{8} = 1.5$$

$$x_c = 1.5$$
questions.explanation: The x-centroid weights each vertical strip by its distance x from the y-axis; the taller strips on the right pull the centroid right of the midpoint.

questions.question: An engineering firm must select 3 engineers from a team of 8 to form a design review panel. How many distinct panels are possible?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Permutations and Combinations section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(C(8, 3)\). Because the order of the 3 engineers on the panel does not matter, the handbook's combination formula applies:

$$C(n, r) = \frac{n!}{r!(n - r)!}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to compute \(C(8, 3)\):

$$\begin{aligned}
n &= 8 \\
r &= 3 \\
C(8, 3) &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Substitute into the combination formula:

$$(C(8, 3)) = \frac{8!}{3!(8 - 3)!} = \frac{8!}{3!\,5!}$$

Cancel the common factors on their own line:

$$\left(\frac{8!}{3!\,5!}\right) = \frac{8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6}{3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1} = \frac{336}{6}$$

Evaluate the result:

$$C(8, 3) = 56$$
questions.explanation: Order doesn't matter for a panel, so use combinations. If the 3 seats were distinct roles, you would use permutations instead.

questions.question: In a batch of castings, 30% have a surface flaw (event \(F\)) and 12% have both a surface flaw and a dimensional deviation (event \(D\)). Given that a randomly selected casting has a surface flaw, what is the probability it also has a dimensional deviation?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Laws of Probability section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(P(D \mid F)\). Property 3 (Law of Compound or Joint Probability) gives:

$$P(A, B) = P(A) \cdot P(B \mid A)$$

Rearranging for the conditional probability:

$$P(D \mid F) = \frac{P(D, F)}{P(F)}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to compute \(P(D \mid F)\):

$$\begin{aligned}
P(F) &= 0.30 \\
P(D, F) &= 0.12 \\
P(D \mid F) &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Substitute into the rearranged formula:

$$(P(D \mid F)) = \frac{(0.12)}{(0.30)}$$

Evaluate the result:

$$P(D \mid F) = 0.40$$
questions.explanation: Given the condition, divide the 'both' probability by the probability of the condition. The answer must be at least as large as the joint probability.

questions.question: A continuous random variable \(X\) has probability density function \(f(x) = 1/10\) for \(0 \le x \le 10\) (and zero otherwise). What is the expected value of \(X^2\)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Expected Values section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(E[X^2]\). The handbook gives the expected value of a function \(Y = g(X)\) of a continuous random variable:

$$E[Y] = E[g(X)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x)\,f(x)\,dx$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to compute \(E[X^2]\):

$$\begin{aligned}
g(x) &= x^2 \\
f(x) &= \frac{1}{10}, \quad 0 \le x \le 10 \\
E[X^2] &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Substitute into the expected-value formula, noting the density is zero outside \([0, 10]\):

$$(E[X^2]) = \int_0^{10} x^2 \left(\frac{1}{10}\right)\,dx = \frac{1}{10}\int_0^{10} x^2\,dx$$

Evaluate the integral on its own line:

$$\left(\int_0^{10} x^2\,dx\right) = \left[\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^{10} = \frac{1000}{3} - 0 = \frac{1000}{3}$$

Multiply by the constant factor:

$$(E[X^2]) = \left(\frac{1}{10}\right)\left(\frac{1000}{3}\right) = \frac{100}{3} \approx 33.33$$

$$E[X^2] = 33.33$$
questions.explanation: E[X²] is not the square of E[X]. Integrate x² against the density directly — the variance is the difference between the two.

questions.question: A proposal an engineer submits to a client states that she 'led the structural design of three high-rise projects,' when in fact she only assisted on one mid-rise project and played no role in the other two. Under the NCEES Model Rules, this conduct:
choices: Violates the rule against misrepresenting academic or professional qualifications and degree of responsibility in prior assignments
Is acceptable because proposal language is marketing, not engineering practice
Is acceptable if no contract has been signed yet
Violates only the rule against political contributions
questions.solution:
Refer to the Obligations of Licensees to Other Licensees section in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

The Model Rules provide that licensees shall not falsify or permit misrepresentation of their, or their associates', academic or professional qualifications. They shall not misrepresent or exaggerate their degree of responsibility in prior assignments nor the complexity of said assignments.

Claiming to have led three high-rise designs when she only assisted on one mid-rise project exaggerates both her degree of responsibility and the complexity of her prior assignments, so it violates this rule. Proposal language is still a professional representation, and no signed contract is needed for the violation to occur.

Misrepresenting qualifications and degree of responsibility in prior assignments is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: Marketing language doesn't excuse misrepresentation. The rule covers proposals and employment solicitations, not just sealed documents.

questions.question: An engineer is invited to form a joint venture with a firm she knows has been falsifying concrete test results on public projects. Under the NCEES Model Rules, she should:
choices: Accept the invitation, because the other firm's past conduct is not her responsibility
Accept the invitation, but report the firm only if a client asks about it
Decline, because licensees must not partner or practice with any person or firm known to engage in fraudulent or dishonest business or professional practices
Decline only if her own current clients would find out about the partnership
questions.solution:
Refer to the Obligations of Licensees to the Public section in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

The Model Rules provide that licensees shall not partner, practice, or offer to practice with any person or firm that they know is engaged in fraudulent or dishonest business or professional practices.

Falsifying concrete test results on public projects is fraudulent and dishonest professional practice, and the engineer has knowledge of it. Accepting the joint venture would mean partnering with a known bad actor, which the rule prohibits regardless of whether her own clients ever learn of it. She also has a separate duty to report the violation to the board.

Declining the joint venture is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: You don't need to have participated in the fraud — knowingly associating your practice with it is itself the violation.

questions.question: To improve his firm's chances of winning a municipal design contract, an engineer makes a $5,000 personal contribution to the mayor's reelection campaign with the intent of influencing the contract award. Under the NCEES Model Rules, this is:
choices: Permitted, because personal political contributions are a private matter
A violation, because licensees must not make a political contribution with the intent to influence the award of a contract by public authority
Permitted, because the contribution went to a campaign rather than to an official directly
A violation only if the firm actually wins the contract
questions.solution:
Refer to the Obligations of Licensees to Other Licensees section in the Ethics and Professional Practice chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

The Model Rules provide that licensees shall not offer, give, solicit, or receive, either directly or indirectly, any commission, or gift, or other valuable consideration in order to secure work, and shall not make any political contribution with the intent to influence the award of a contract by public authority.

The engineer's contribution was made with the stated intent of influencing the award of a public contract, which is exactly what this rule prohibits. That the money went to a campaign rather than directly to an official does not change the intent, and the violation is complete when the contribution is made — whether or not the firm wins the contract is irrelevant.

A violation of the political-contribution rule is the correct choice.
questions.explanation: The intent to influence the award is what triggers the rule, whether or not the contract is actually won.

questions.question: A project cost is estimated in constant (year-0) dollars. If the market interest rate is 8% per year and general inflation is 3% per year, what inflation-adjusted interest rate should be used to compute the present worth of future costs stated in constant dollars?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Inflation section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for \(d\), the inflation-adjusted interest rate per interest period. The handbook gives:

$$d = i + f + (i \times f)$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to compute \(d\):

$$\begin{aligned}
i &= 8\% = 0.08 \\
f &= 3\% = 0.03 \\
d &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Substitute into the inflation formula:

$$(d) = (0.08) + (0.03) + (0.08)(0.03)$$

Evaluate the cross term on its own line:

$$((0.08)(0.03)) = 0.0024$$

Add the terms:

$$(d) = 0.08 + 0.03 + 0.0024 = 0.1124 = 11.24\%$$

$$d = 11.24\%$$
questions.explanation: The cross term i×f is small but not zero — dropping it is the classic 11.00% trap.

questions.question: A 10-year bond with a $1,000 face value pays 6% annual coupons at each year end. If the market interest rate is 8% per year, what is the bond's value?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Uniform Series and Single Payment sections in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

The Bonds section defines the bond value as the present worth of the payments the holder receives at interest rate \(i\). Ultimately, we must solve for the bond value \(V\):

$$V = C(P/A, i\%, n) + F(P/F, i\%, n)$$

The printed factor formulas are:

$$(P/A, i\%, n) = \frac{(1+i)^n - 1}{i(1+i)^n}, \qquad (P/F, i\%, n) = (1+i)^{-n}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to compute \(V\):

$$\begin{aligned}
C &= (0.06)(1000) = \$60 \\
F &= \$1{,}000 \\
i &= 8\% = 0.08 \\
n &= 10 \\
V &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Compute the uniform-series present worth factor on its own line:

$$((P/A, 8\%, 10)) = \frac{(1.08)^{10} - 1}{(0.08)(1.08)^{10}} = \frac{1.158925}{0.172714} = 6.7101$$

Compute the single-payment present worth factor on its own line:

$$((P/F, 8\%, 10)) = (1.08)^{-10} = 0.4632$$

Substitute both factors into the bond-value equation:

$$(V) = (60)(6.7101) + (1000)(0.4632) \rightarrow 402.61 + 463.19 = 865.80$$

$$V = \$865.80$$
questions.explanation: A bond is worth the present worth of its coupon stream plus the discounted face value. When the market rate exceeds the coupon rate, the bond sells at a discount (below face value).

questions.question: A machine upgrade will save $4,000 per year for 6 years, with the first savings occurring at the end of year 3 (the series is deferred 2 years). At 10% annual interest, what is the present worth of the savings?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Uniform Series and Single Payment sections in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.

Ultimately, we must solve for the present worth \(P\). A deferred annuity is priced as an ordinary annuity at the start of its first payment year, then discounted back through the deferral period:

$$P = A(P/A, i\%, n)(P/F, i\%, k)$$

The printed factor formulas are:

$$(P/A, i\%, n) = \frac{(1+i)^n - 1}{i(1+i)^n}, \qquad (P/F, i\%, k) = (1+i)^{-k}$$

List the known and unknown parameters in order to compute \(P\):

$$\begin{aligned}
A &= \$4{,}000 \\
i &= 10\% = 0.10 \\
n &= 6 \\
k &= 2 \\
P &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

Compute the uniform-series present worth factor on its own line:

$$((P/A, 10\%, 6)) = \frac{(1.10)^6 - 1}{(0.10)(1.10)^6} = \frac{0.771561}{0.177156} = 4.3553$$

Compute the deferral (single-payment) factor on its own line:

$$((P/F, 10\%, 2)) = (1.10)^{-2} = 0.8264$$

Substitute both factors:

$$(P) = (4000)(4.3553)(0.8264) \rightarrow (4000)(3.5994) = 14{,}397.56$$

$$P = \$14{,}398$$
questions.explanation: Deferral is handled by discounting the whole annuity back through the gap years with a P/F factor — forgetting that step prices the annuity as if it started today.

On a frictionless incline the only thing pulling the crate downhill is the downhill component of its own weight, W·sinθ. The holding force must exactly balance that component: 400·sin25° ≈ 169 N up the plane.
questions.question: A 400 N crate rests on a frictionless plane inclined at 25° to the horizontal. What force P, applied parallel to the plane, is required to hold the crate in equilibrium?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Equilibrium Requirements section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.
For equilibrium, the sum of force components along the plane must vanish: \(\sum F_{\parallel} = 0\).
The component of the crate's weight acting down the plane is \(W_{\parallel} = W \sin\theta\).
\(W_{\parallel} = (400\ \mathrm{N})(\sin 25^\circ)\).
\(W_{\parallel} = (400\ \mathrm{N})(0.4226) = 169\ \mathrm{N}\).
Therefore \(P = 169\ \mathrm{N}\) directed up the plane.
questions.subtopic: Particle equilibrium on an inclined plane

questions.explanation: Only the moment component along the hinge axis tends to rotate the bracket about its hinge. Using My = z·Fx − x·Fz gives (−15 + 24) = 9.0 N·m; the positive sign means it acts in the +y direction by the right-hand rule.
questions.question: A bracket is hinged along the y-axis (the hinge axis passes through the origin). A force \(\mathbf{F} = (-60\mathbf{i} + 25\mathbf{j} - 40\mathbf{k})\) N is applied at the point \((0.60, 0.10, 0.25)\) m measured from the origin. What is the scalar moment of the force about the y-axis?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Moments (Couples) section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.
The moment about an axis is the corresponding component of \(\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}\).
About the y-axis: \(M_y = zF_x - xF_z\).
\(M_y = (0.25\ \mathrm{m})(-60\ \mathrm{N}) - (0.60\ \mathrm{m})(-40\ \mathrm{N})\).
\(M_y = -15.0\ \mathrm{N{\cdot}m} + 24.0\ \mathrm{N{\cdot}m}\).
\(M_y = 9.0\ \mathrm{N{\cdot}m}\).
questions.subtopic: Moment of a force about an axis

questions.explanation: Two things can happen: the crate can slide (when P beats maximum static friction, 200 N) or tip over its bottom corner (when P's overturning moment beats the weight's restoring moment, 161 N). The smaller one wins — the crate tips first at about 161 N.
questions.question: A 500 N rectangular crate is 0.9 m wide and 1.4 m tall. It rests on a horizontal surface with coefficient of static friction \(\mu_s = 0.40\). A horizontal force P is applied at the top edge of the crate and slowly increased. Does the crate tip or slip first, and at what value of P does motion impend?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Friction section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.
Vertical equilibrium gives the normal force: \(N = 500\ \mathrm{N}\).
The limiting friction is \(F \le \mu_s N\).
\(F_{\max} = (0.40)(500\ \mathrm{N}) = 200\ \mathrm{N}\).
So slipping would impend at \(P = 200\ \mathrm{N}\).
Refer to the Equilibrium Requirements section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.
For tipping, take moments about the bottom corner on the side toward which P pushes, at the instant the normal force acts at that corner:
\(\sum M = 0 \Rightarrow P(1.4\ \mathrm{m}) - (500\ \mathrm{N})(0.45\ \mathrm{m}) = 0\).
\(P = \dfrac{(500)(0.45)}{1.4} = 160.7\ \mathrm{N}\).
Since \(160.7\ \mathrm{N} < 200\ \mathrm{N}\), tipping impends first at \(P \approx 161\ \mathrm{N}\).

questions.explanation: Pulling mass closer to the spin axis reduces the moment of inertia, so the spin rate must increase to keep angular momentum (I·ω) constant: 1.5 × (4.5/2.8) ≈ 2.41 rev/s.
questions.question: A figure skater spins with arms outstretched at 1.5 rev/s. Her mass moment of inertia about the spin axis is 4.5 kg·m² with arms out and 2.8 kg·m² with arms pulled in. Neglecting external moments about the spin axis, what is her spin rate after she pulls her arms in?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Conservation of Angular Momentum section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.
With no external moment, angular momentum is conserved: \(\sum (\text{syst. } H)_1 = \sum (\text{syst. } H)_2\).
Refer to the Angular Momentum or Moment of Momentum section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.
For rotation about a fixed axis, \(H = I\omega\), so \(I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2\).
\(\omega_2 = \omega_1 \dfrac{I_1}{I_2} = (1.5\ \mathrm{rev/s})\dfrac{4.5}{2.8}\).
\(\omega_2 = 2.41\ \mathrm{rev/s}\).

questions.explanation: When velocity is given as a function of position (not time), use the chain rule a = v·(dv/ds). Differentiating v = 0.25s² gives dv/ds = 0.50s, so a = 0.125s³ = 27.0 m/s² at s = 6 m.
questions.question: A particle moves along a straight line with velocity \(v = 0.25 s^2\) m/s, where s is the distance in meters from a fixed origin. Determine the acceleration of the particle when \(s = 6.0\) m.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Particle Rectilinear Motion section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.
The printed relation \(a\,ds = v\,dv\) gives \(a = v\dfrac{dv}{ds}\).
\(\dfrac{dv}{ds} = \dfrac{d}{ds}(0.25 s^2) = 0.50 s\).
\(a = (0.25 s^2)(0.50 s) = 0.125 s^3\).
At \(s = 6.0\ \mathrm{m}\): \(a = 0.125(6.0)^3\).
\(a = 0.125(216) = 27.0\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\).

questions.explanation: Momentum conservation gives one equation, the restitution definition gives a second. Solving the pair, ball A rebounds at 3.69 m/s opposite its original direction (the negative sign), while the heavier ball B carries on forward.
questions.question: A 3.0 kg ball A moving at 8.0 m/s strikes head-on a 5.0 kg ball B moving at 3.0 m/s in the opposite direction. The coefficient of restitution is e = 0.70. Determine the velocity of ball A just after impact (positive in A's original direction).
questions.solution:
Refer to the Impact section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.
Momentum is conserved: \(m_A v_A + m_B v_B = m_A v_A' + m_B v_B'\).
Take A's original direction as positive, so \(v_B = -3.0\ \mathrm{m/s}\).
\((3.0)(8.0) + (5.0)(-3.0) = 3.0\,v_A' + 5.0\,v_B'\).
\(9.0 = 3.0\,v_A' + 5.0\,v_B'\).
The coefficient of restitution: \(e = \dfrac{v_B' - v_A'}{v_A - v_B} = 0.70\).
\(v_B' - v_A' = 0.70[8.0 - (-3.0)] = 7.70\ \mathrm{m/s}\).
Substitute \(v_B' = v_A' + 7.70\) into the momentum equation:
\(3.0\,v_A' + 5.0(v_A' + 7.70) = 9.0\).
\(8.0\,v_A' = 9.0 - 38.5 = -29.5\).
\(v_A' = -3.69\ \mathrm{m/s}\).

questions.explanation: Percent elongation measures ductility — how much the material permanently stretched before breaking, relative to its original gage length: (61.5 − 50)/50 × 100 = 23.0%.
questions.question: A tensile test specimen has an original gage length of 50.0 mm. After fracture, the two pieces are fitted together and the final gage length is measured as 61.5 mm. What is the percent elongation of the material?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Percent Elongation section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. (Note: although percent elongation is a materials property, the handbook prints this section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter, not in Materials Science/Structure of Matter.)
The printed relation is \(\%\text{ Elongation} = \dfrac{\Delta L}{L_0} \times 100\).
\(\Delta L = 61.5\ \mathrm{mm} - 50.0\ \mathrm{mm} = 11.5\ \mathrm{mm}\).
\(\%\text{ Elongation} = \dfrac{11.5}{50.0} \times 100\).
\(\%\text{ Elongation} = 23.0\%\).

questions.explanation: The lever rule splits the alloy between the two phases in proportion to the opposite segment lengths on the composition axis: (55−18)/(82−18) = 37/64 ≈ 57.8% β phase (the rest is α).
questions.question: At a certain temperature, a binary alloy of overall composition 55 wt% B lies in a two-phase (α + β) region of its phase diagram. At this temperature the α phase contains 18 wt% B and the β phase contains 82 wt% B. Using the lever rule, determine the weight percent of the β phase present.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Lever Rule section in the Materials Science/Structure of Matter chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.
For average composition \(x\) between phase compositions \(x_\alpha\) and \(x_\beta\):
$$\text{wt}\%\ \beta = \frac{x - x_\alpha}{x_\beta - x_\alpha} \times 100$$
\(\text{wt}\%\ \beta = \dfrac{55 - 18}{82 - 18} \times 100\).
\(\text{wt}\%\ \beta = \dfrac{37}{64} \times 100\).
\(\text{wt}\%\ \beta = 57.8\%\).

questions.explanation: True stress uses the actual shrunken cross-section at that instant, not the original one — that's why it's larger than the engineering stress (398 MPa, computed with the original 12.0 mm diameter).
questions.question: A round tensile specimen has an original diameter of 12.0 mm. At a certain point during the test, the applied load is 45.0 kN and the instantaneous (actual) diameter of the specimen is 11.1 mm. What is the true stress in the specimen at that instant?
questions.solution:
Refer to the True stress section in the Materials Science/Structure of Matter chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.
The printed relation is \(\sigma_T = \dfrac{F}{A}\), where \(A\) is the actual (instantaneous) cross-sectional area.
\(A = \dfrac{\pi d^2}{4} = \dfrac{\pi (11.1\ \mathrm{mm})^2}{4}\).
\(A = 96.8\ \mathrm{mm^2}\).
\(\sigma_T = \dfrac{45.0 \times 10^3\ \mathrm{N}}{96.8\ \mathrm{mm^2}}\).
\(\sigma_T = 465\ \mathrm{N/mm^2} = 465\ \mathrm{MPa}\).

questions.explanation: A flagpole-like column (fixed at the base, free at the top) buckles as if it were twice as long as it really is: K = 2.0, so the effective length is 2.0 × 4.0 = 8.0 m. That's why flagpoles buckle so easily.
questions.question: A 4.0 m steel column is fixed at its base and free at its top (flagpole condition). What is the effective length \(KL\) used in Euler's buckling formula?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Columns section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.
Euler's formula uses the effective length \(KL\), where \(K\) is the effective-length factor for the end supports.
For fixed-free ends, the printed factor is \(K = 2.0\).
\(KL = (2.0)(4.0\ \mathrm{m})\).
\(KL = 8.0\ \mathrm{m}\).

questions.explanation: Power and speed fix the torque (T = P/ω ≈ 796 N·m); the torsion formula then gives the peak shear stress at the shaft surface, about 18.8 MPa — well below steel's strength, as you'd expect for a transmission shaft.
questions.question: A solid steel shaft with diameter 60 mm transmits 75 kW of power while rotating at 900 rpm. What is the maximum torsional shear stress in the shaft?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Torsion section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook. (Note: the relation \(P = T\omega\) used below to get torque from power is not printed in the Mechanics of Materials chapter; the shear-stress relation \(\tau = T\rho/J\) is.)
Convert speed to angular velocity: \(\omega = (900\ \mathrm{rev/min})\dfrac{2\pi\ \mathrm{rad/rev}}{60\ \mathrm{s/min}} = 94.2\ \mathrm{rad/s}\).
Torque from power: \(T = \dfrac{P}{\omega} = \dfrac{75{,}000\ \mathrm{W}}{94.2\ \mathrm{rad/s}} = 796\ \mathrm{N{\cdot}m}\).
Maximum shear stress at the outer fiber: \(\tau_{\max} = \dfrac{T\rho}{J}\) with \(J = \pi d^4/32\) and \(\rho = d/2\).
This reduces to \(\tau_{\max} = \dfrac{16T}{\pi d^3}\).
\(\tau_{\max} = \dfrac{16(796\ \mathrm{N{\cdot}m})}{\pi (0.060\ \mathrm{m})^3}\).
\(\tau_{\max} = \dfrac{12{,}736}{6.786 \times 10^{-4}} = 1.88 \times 10^7\ \mathrm{Pa}\).
\(\tau_{\max} = 18.8\ \mathrm{MPa}\).
questions.subtopic: Shaft power and torsional shear stress

questions.explanation: Bending gives a normal stress (65.2 MPa) and torsion gives a shear stress (48.9 MPa) on the shaft's outer fiber. Combining them via the principal-stress equations yields σ1 = 91.4 MPa and σ2 = −26.2 MPa, and the Tresca maximum shear stress is half their difference: 58.8 MPa.
questions.question: A solid circular shaft of diameter 50 mm is subjected to a bending moment of 800 N·m and a torque of 1200 N·m acting simultaneously. Determine the maximum shear stress in the shaft (Tresca/maximum-shear-stress basis).
questions.solution:
Refer to the Stresses in Beams section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.
Bending produces \(\sigma_x = \pm Mc/I\); for a solid circle this becomes \(\sigma_x = 32M/(\pi d^3)\).
\(\sigma_x = \dfrac{32(800\ \mathrm{N{\cdot}m})}{\pi (0.050\ \mathrm{m})^3}\).
\(\sigma_x = 6.52 \times 10^7\ \mathrm{Pa} = 65.2\ \mathrm{MPa}\).
Refer to the Torsion section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.
Torsion produces \(\tau_{xy} = T\rho/J\); for a solid circle \(\tau_{xy} = 16T/(\pi d^3)\).
\(\tau_{xy} = \dfrac{16(1200\ \mathrm{N{\cdot}m})}{\pi (0.050\ \mathrm{m})^3}\).
\(\tau_{xy} = 4.89 \times 10^7\ \mathrm{Pa} = 48.9\ \mathrm{MPa}\).
Refer to the Principal Stresses section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.
\(\sigma_{1,2} = \dfrac{\sigma_x}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\sigma_x}{2}\right)^2 + \tau_{xy}^2}\).
\(\sigma_{1,2} = 32.6 \pm \sqrt{(32.6)^2 + (48.9)^2} = 32.6 \pm 58.8\).
\(\sigma_1 = 91.4\ \mathrm{MPa},\quad \sigma_2 = -26.2\ \mathrm{MPa}\).
Refer to the Mohr's Circle—Stress, 2D section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.
The circle's radius is the maximum shear stress; with principal stresses of opposite sign this equals \(\tau_{\max} = \dfrac{\sigma_1 - \sigma_2}{2}\) (Tresca basis).
\(\tau_{\max} = \dfrac{91.4 - (-26.2)}{2}\).
\(\tau_{\max} = 58.8\ \mathrm{MPa}\).
questions.subtopic: Combined bending and torsion (maximum shear stress)

questions.explanation: The water itself only receives γQH ≈ 8.83 kW, but because the pump is 75% efficient you must supply more at the shaft: 8.83/0.75 ≈ 11.8 kW. The extra ~3 kW is lost to friction and turbulence inside the pump.
questions.question: A pump delivers 0.060 m³/s of water against a total head of 15 m. If the pump efficiency is 75%, what brake power must be supplied to the pump?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Pump Power Equation section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.
Fluid (water) power: \(W_{\text{fluid}} = \gamma Q H\).
\(W_{\text{fluid}} = (9.81\ \mathrm{kN/m^3})(0.060\ \mathrm{m^3/s})(15\ \mathrm{m})\).
\(W_{\text{fluid}} = 8.83\ \mathrm{kW}\).
Brake power accounts for pump efficiency: \(W_{\text{brake}} = W_{\text{fluid}}/\eta_{\text{pump}}\).
\(W_{\text{brake}} = \dfrac{8.83\ \mathrm{kW}}{0.75}\).
\(W_{\text{brake}} = 11.8\ \mathrm{kW}\).

questions.explanation: The total push on the gate equals the pressure at its centroid depth times its area: the centroid is 2.75 m down, so F = 9.81 × 2.75 × 3.0 ≈ 80.9 kN. (It acts below the centroid, at the center of pressure, because pressure grows with depth.)
questions.question: A vertical rectangular gate 2.0 m wide and 1.5 m tall has its top edge 2.0 m below the water surface. Determine the magnitude of the resultant hydrostatic force acting on the gate.
questions.solution:
Refer to the Forces on Submerged Surfaces and the Center of Pressure section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.
With atmospheric pressure acting on both sides, the net resultant is \(F_R = (\rho g h_C) A = \gamma h_C A\), where \(h_C\) is the vertical depth of the centroid.
\(h_C = 2.00\ \mathrm{m} + \dfrac{1.50\ \mathrm{m}}{2} = 2.75\ \mathrm{m}\).
\(A = (2.0\ \mathrm{m})(1.5\ \mathrm{m}) = 3.00\ \mathrm{m^2}\).
\(F_R = (9.81\ \mathrm{kN/m^3})(2.75\ \mathrm{m})(3.00\ \mathrm{m^2})\).
\(F_R = 80.9\ \mathrm{kN}\).
questions.subtopic: Hydrostatic force on a plane surface

questions.explanation: Manning's equation estimates open-channel flow from the channel's roughness, shape, and slope. With A = 3.6 m², wetted perimeter 5.4 m (both sides plus bottom), hydraulic radius 0.667 m, and slope 0.001, the discharge works out to about 6.68 m³/s.
questions.question: A rectangular concrete channel (Manning's n = 0.013) is 3.0 m wide and carries water 1.2 m deep on a longitudinal slope of 0.0010. Estimate the discharge in the channel using Manning's equation (SI units).
questions.solution:
Refer to the Manning's Equation section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook.
The printed SI form is \(Q = \dfrac{K}{n} A R_H^{2/3} S^{1/2}\) with \(K = 1.0\).
Flow area: \(A = (3.0\ \mathrm{m})(1.2\ \mathrm{m}) = 3.60\ \mathrm{m^2}\).
Wetted perimeter: \(P = 3.0 + 2(1.2) = 5.40\ \mathrm{m}\).
Hydraulic radius: \(R_H = A/P = 3.60/5.40 = 0.6667\ \mathrm{m}\).
\(Q = \dfrac{1.0}{0.013}(3.60)(0.6667)^{2/3}(0.0010)^{1/2}\).
\((0.6667)^{2/3} = 0.763\); \((0.0010)^{1/2} = 0.03162\).
\(Q = (76.92)(3.60)(0.763)(0.03162)\).
\(Q = 6.68\ \mathrm{m^3/s}\).

questions.question: An irregular shoreline is offset from a straight survey line at 10-m intervals. The seven perpendicular offsets, in meters, are 0, 3.2, 4.1, 3.8, 4.5, 2.9, and 0. Using Simpson's one-third rule, what is the approximate area between the survey line and the shoreline?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Latitudes and Departures section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the area \(A\) by Simpson's one-third rule:

$$A = \frac{w}{3}\left[h_1 + h_7 + 4(h_2 + h_4 + h_6) + 2(h_3 + h_5)\right]$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
w &= 10\ \text{m} \\
h_1 &= 0\ \text{m} \\
h_2 &= 3.2\ \text{m} \\
h_3 &= 4.1\ \text{m} \\
h_4 &= 3.8\ \text{m} \\
h_5 &= 4.5\ \text{m} \\
h_6 &= 2.9\ \text{m} \\
h_7 &= 0\ \text{m} \\
A &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(A) = \frac{10}{3}\left[0 + 0 + 4(3.2 + 3.8 + 2.9) + 2(4.1 + 4.5)\right]$$

$$(A) = \frac{10}{3}\left[4(9.9) + 2(8.6)\right]$$

$$(A) = \frac{10}{3}\left[39.6 + 17.2\right]$$

$$(A) = \frac{10}{3}(56.8) = 189.3\ \text{m}^2$$

The closest choice is \(189\ \text{m}^2\).
questions.explanation: Simpson's one-third rule weights alternating interior offsets by 4 and 2 (starting with 4 on the second offset) and requires an odd number of offsets. Using the trapezoidal rule instead gives 185 m^2, a common wrong pick.

questions.question: A simple horizontal curve with a radius of 250 m is to be staked from the PC using 20-m sub-chords. What deflection angle should be turned from the tangent at the PC to set the first 20-m stake on the curve?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Horizontal Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).
Ultimately, we must solve for the deflection angle turned from the tangent at the PC. The deflection angle from the tangent equals half the central angle subtended by the chord. The handbook prints the arc-length relation for the central angle:
$$l = R\,\Delta\,\frac{\pi}{180}$$
List the known and unknown parameters:
$$\begin{aligned}
R &= 250\ \text{m} \\
l &= 20\ \text{m} \\
\Delta &= ? \\
\delta &= ?
\end{aligned}$$
Solve the arc-length relation for the central angle \(\Delta\):
$$(\Delta) = \frac{l \cdot 180}{R\,\pi}$$
$$(\Delta) = \frac{20 \cdot 180}{250\,\pi}$$
$$(\Delta) = \frac{3600}{785.40} = 4.58^\circ$$
Halve the central angle to get the deflection angle \(\delta\):
$$(\delta) = \frac{4.58^\circ}{2}$$
$$(\delta) = 2.29^\circ$$
Turn \(2.29^\circ\) from the tangent at the PC.
questions.explanation: The deflection angle from the tangent is half the central angle subtended by the chord: 4.58 degrees is the central angle, not the deflection angle. Doubling to 9.17 degrees confuses the two.

questions.question: A differential leveling run starts at BM-A with an elevation of 50.00 m. At the first setup the backsight is 1.50 m and the foresight to TP-1 is 2.10 m. The instrument is then moved, and at the second setup the backsight on TP-1 is 2.40 m and the foresight to TP-2 is 0.90 m. What is the elevation of TP-2?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the elevation of TP-2 using the height-of-instrument method: each setup's height of instrument is \(HI = Elev + BS\), and each point's elevation is \(Elev = HI - FS\).

List the known parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
Elev_{BM\text{-}A} &= 50.00\ \text{m} \\
BS_1 &= 1.50\ \text{m},\quad FS_1 = 2.10\ \text{m} \\
BS_2 &= 2.40\ \text{m},\quad FS_2 = 0.90\ \text{m}
\end{aligned}$$

First setup:

$$(HI_1) = 50.00 + 1.50 = 51.50\ \text{m}$$

$$(Elev_{TP\text{-}1}) = 51.50 - 2.10 = 49.40\ \text{m}$$

Second setup:

$$(HI_2) = 49.40 + 2.40 = 51.80\ \text{m}$$

$$(Elev_{TP\text{-}2}) = 51.80 - 0.90 = 50.90\ \text{m}$$

Check: \(\sum BS - \sum FS = (1.50 + 2.40) - (2.10 + 0.90) = 0.90\) m, and \(50.00 + 0.90 = 50.90\) m. The elevation of TP-2 is \(50.90\) m.
questions.explanation: The arithmetic check (sum of backsights minus sum of foresights equals last elevation minus first) catches a sign slip at any turning point. Subtracting the backsight instead of adding it is the classic leveling error.

questions.question: A prismatic beam AB is pinned at A and fixed at B. A 60 kN-m moment is applied at end A. Using the moment-carryover concept, what moment is carried over to the fixed end B?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Structural Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the carryover moment \(M_B\). The handbook prints:

$$M_B = \frac{M_A}{2}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
M_A &= 60\ \text{kN-m} \\
M_B &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(M_B) = \frac{60}{2}$$

$$(M_B) = 30\ \text{kN-m}$$

The carryover factor from a pinned (or moment-applied) end to a fixed far end is one-half, so \(30\ \text{kN-m}\) is carried to B.
questions.explanation: Carryover is one-half of the applied end moment when the far end is fixed. Carrying over the full 60 kN-m forgets the 1/2 factor.

questions.question: A prismatic beam fixed at both ends spans 6 m. A concentrated load of 20 kN acts 2 m from the left support. What is the magnitude of the fixed-end moment at the left support?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Structural Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the fixed-end moment at the left support, \(FEM_{AB}\). The handbook prints, for a concentrated load \(P\) at distance \(a\) from A and \(b\) from B:

$$FEM_{AB} = \frac{P\,a\,b^2}{L^2}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
P &= 20\ \text{kN} \\
a &= 2\ \text{m} \\
b &= 6 - 2 = 4\ \text{m} \\
L &= 6\ \text{m} \\
FEM_{AB} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(FEM_{AB}) = \frac{20 \cdot 2 \cdot 4^2}{6^2}$$

$$(FEM_{AB}) = \frac{20 \cdot 2 \cdot 16}{36}$$

$$(FEM_{AB}) = \frac{640}{36} = 17.8\ \text{kN-m}$$

The fixed-end moment at the left support is \(17.8\ \text{kN-m}\).
questions.explanation: The squared term belongs to the distance from the far end (b^2 at support A). Using P a^2 b / L^2 gives 8.9 kN-m, which is the fixed-end moment at the right support instead.

questions.question: A prismatic beam AB has E = 200 GPa, I = 50 x 10^6 mm^4, and a span L = 4 m. What is the flexural stiffness factor k_AB used in slope-deflection analysis?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Structural Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the flexural stiffness \(k_{AB}\). The handbook prints:

$$k_{AB} = \frac{4EI}{L}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
E &= 200\ \text{GPa} = 200 \times 10^9\ \text{Pa} \\
I &= 50 \times 10^6\ \text{mm}^4 = 50 \times 10^6 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{m}^4 \\
L &= 4\ \text{m} \\
k_{AB} &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

First convert \(EI\) to consistent units:

$$(EI) = (200 \times 10^9)(50 \times 10^6 \times 10^{-12})$$

$$(EI) = (200 \times 10^9)(50 \times 10^{-6}) = 10 \times 10^6\ \text{N-m}^2$$

$$(EI) = 10{,}000\ \text{kN-m}^2$$

$$(k_{AB}) = \frac{4 \cdot 10{,}000}{4}$$

$$(k_{AB}) = 10{,}000\ \text{kN-m/rad}$$

The flexural stiffness factor is \(10{,}000\ \text{kN-m/rad}\).
questions.explanation: The mm^4 to m^4 conversion (x10^-12) is where this problem is usually lost. Skipping it inflates EI by a factor of 10^12.

questions.question: A sand has a maximum void ratio of 0.90, a minimum void ratio of 0.40, and an in-place void ratio of 0.65. What is the relative density of the sand?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Phase Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the relative density \(D_r\). The handbook prints:

$$D_r = \frac{e_{max} - e}{e_{max} - e_{min}} \times 100$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
e_{max} &= 0.90 \\
e_{min} &= 0.40 \\
e &= 0.65 \\
D_r &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(D_r) = \frac{0.90 - 0.65}{0.90 - 0.40} \times 100$$

$$(D_r) = \frac{0.25}{0.50} \times 100$$

$$(D_r) = 0.50 \times 100 = 50\%$$

The sand is at \(50\%\) relative density (medium dense).
questions.explanation: Relative density compares the in-place void ratio to the loosest state in the numerator (emax - e). A result of 0% means the loosest possible state and 100% the densest.

questions.question: A 4-m-tall smooth vertical wall retains level cohesionless backfill with a friction angle of 28 degrees and a unit weight of 19 kN/m^3. What is the total Rankine passive force per meter of wall?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Horizontal Stress Profiles and Forces section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the total passive force \(P_P\). The handbook prints the Rankine passive coefficient:

$$K_P = \tan^2\!\left(45^\circ + \frac{\phi}{2}\right)$$

and passive forces follow the same form as the printed active forces, so for one layer:

$$P_P = \frac{1}{2}\,\gamma\,H^2\,K_P$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
H &= 4\ \text{m} \\
\phi &= 28^\circ \\
\gamma &= 19\ \text{kN/m}^3 \\
K_P &= ? \\
P_P &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(K_P) = \tan^2\!\left(45^\circ + \frac{28^\circ}{2}\right) = \tan^2(59^\circ)$$

$$(K_P) = (1.6643)^2 = 2.770$$

$$(P_P) = \frac{1}{2}(19)(4^2)(2.770)$$

$$(P_P) = (152)(2.770) = 421\ \text{kN/m}$$

The total passive force is \(421\ \text{kN/m}\).
questions.explanation: Passive pressure uses 45 + phi/2 while active uses 45 - phi/2; 55 kN/m is the active force for the same wall, a classic mix-up. Passive resistance is much larger because the wall pushes into the soil.

questions.question: Upward seepage through a saturated sand layer produces an exit gradient of 0.35. The saturated unit weight of the sand is 20.0 kN/m^3. What is the factor of safety against seepage liquefaction (quicksand)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Phase Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the factor of safety against seepage liquefaction \(FS_s\). The handbook prints:

$$FS_s = \frac{i_c}{i_e}, \qquad i_c = \frac{\gamma_{sat} - \gamma_w}{\gamma_w}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
i_e &= 0.35 \\
\gamma_{sat} &= 20.0\ \text{kN/m}^3 \\
\gamma_w &= 9.81\ \text{kN/m}^3 \\
i_c &= ? \\
FS_s &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

First find the critical (quick) gradient:

$$(i_c) = \frac{20.0 - 9.81}{9.81}$$

$$(i_c) = \frac{10.19}{9.81} = 1.039$$

Then the factor of safety:

$$(FS_s) = \frac{1.039}{0.35}$$

$$(FS_s) = 2.97$$

The factor of safety against seepage liquefaction is \(2.97\).
questions.explanation: Quicksand initiates when the upward seepage gradient reaches the critical gradient ic (about 1.0 for most sands). Dividing ie by ic instead gives 0.34, the inverse of the factor of safety.

questions.question: A freeway lane has a free-flow speed of 60 mph and a jam density of 200 veh/mi/ln. Using the Greenshields linear speed-density model, what is the maximum flow (capacity) per lane?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Traffic Flow Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the maximum flow \(V_m\). The handbook prints for the Greenshields model:

$$V_m = \frac{S_f\,D_j}{4}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
S_f &= 60\ \text{mph} \\
D_j &= 200\ \text{veh/mi/ln} \\
V_m &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(V_m) = \frac{60 \cdot 200}{4}$$

$$(V_m) = \frac{12{,}000}{4} = 3{,}000\ \text{veh/hr/ln}$$

The maximum flow per lane is \(3{,}000\ \text{veh/hr/ln}\).
questions.explanation: The factor of 4 comes from the parabolic flow-density curve peaking at half the jam density and half the free-flow speed. Multiplying Sf by Dj directly gives 12,000, which ignores it.

questions.question: A signalized intersection approach has a vehicle approach speed of 50 ft/s, a driver reaction time of 1.0 s, and a comfortable deceleration of 10 ft/s^2 on level grade. What yellow interval, to the nearest 0.1 s, is required?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Traffic Signal Timing section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the yellow interval \(y\). The handbook prints:

$$y = t + \frac{v}{2a \pm 64.4\,G}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
t &= 1.0\ \text{s} \\
v &= 50\ \text{ft/s} \\
a &= 10\ \text{ft/s}^2 \\
G &= 0\ \text{(level grade)} \\
y &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(y) = 1.0 + \frac{50}{2(10) + 64.4(0)}$$

$$(y) = 1.0 + \frac{50}{20}$$

$$(y) = 1.0 + 2.5 = 3.5\ \text{s}$$

The required yellow interval is \(3.5\ \text{s}\).
questions.explanation: The yellow interval covers the driver's reaction distance (t term) plus the braking distance at a comfortable deceleration. Omitting the reaction time gives 2.5 s, which strands drivers in the dilemma zone.

questions.question: A flexible pavement has 3 in. of asphalt surface (a1 = 0.44), 8 in. of granular base (a2 = 0.14, m2 = 1.0), and 12 in. of granular subbase (a3 = 0.11, m3 = 0.9). What is the AASHTO structural number SN?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Highway Pavement Design section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the structural number \(SN\). The handbook prints the AASHTO Structural Number Equation:

$$SN = a_1D_1 + a_2D_2m_2 + a_3D_3m_3$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
a_1 &= 0.44,\quad D_1 = 3\ \text{in.} \\
a_2 &= 0.14,\quad D_2 = 8\ \text{in.},\quad m_2 = 1.0 \\
a_3 &= 0.11,\quad D_3 = 12\ \text{in.},\quad m_3 = 0.9 \\
SN &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(SN) = (0.44)(3) + (0.14)(8)(1.0) + (0.11)(12)(0.9)$$

$$(SN) = 1.32 + 1.12 + 1.188$$

$$(SN) = 3.628 \approx 3.63$$

The structural number is \(3.63\).
questions.explanation: Drainage coefficients (m) apply to the base and subbase but never to the surface layer. Forgetting the subbase drainage factor (using m3 = 1.0) gives 3.76.

questions.question: A 90-degree V-notch weir is used to measure flow in a small channel. If the head over the weir crest is 0.25 m, what is the discharge? (Use SI units.)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Weir Formulas section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the discharge \(Q\). The handbook prints for a V-notch weir:

$$Q = C\,H^{5/2}$$

with \(C = 1.40\) for a 90-degree V-notch weir in SI units.

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
C &= 1.40 \\
H &= 0.25\ \text{m} \\
Q &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(Q) = 1.40 \cdot (0.25)^{5/2}$$

$$(Q) = 1.40 \cdot (0.03125)$$

$$(Q) = 0.04375 \approx 0.0438\ \text{m}^3\text{/s}$$

The discharge is \(0.0438\ \text{m}^3\text{/s}\).
questions.explanation: A V-notch weir discharge varies with H^2.5, not H^1.5 like a rectangular weir. Using the rectangular exponent gives 0.0875, and the USCS coefficient 2.54 gives a much larger wrong answer.

questions.question: Steady flow to a fully penetrating well in an unconfined aquifer gives water-surface heights above the aquifer bottom of h1 = 8.0 m at the well (r1 = 0.15 m) and h2 = 12.0 m at r2 = 60 m. If the hydraulic conductivity is 25 m/day, what is the well discharge?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Well Drawdown section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the well discharge \(Q\). The handbook prints Dupuit's Formula:

$$Q = \frac{\pi\,K\,(h_2^2 - h_1^2)}{\ln(r_2/r_1)}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
K &= 25\ \text{m/day} \\
h_1 &= 8.0\ \text{m} \\
h_2 &= 12.0\ \text{m} \\
r_1 &= 0.15\ \text{m} \\
r_2 &= 60\ \text{m} \\
Q &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(Q) = \frac{\pi(25)\left(12.0^2 - 8.0^2\right)}{\ln(60/0.15)}$$

$$(Q) = \frac{\pi(25)(144 - 64)}{\ln(400)}$$

$$(Q) = \frac{6283.19}{5.9915} = 1048.7\ \text{m}^3\text{/day}$$

The well discharge is \(1{,}049\ \text{m}^3\text{/day}\).
questions.explanation: Dupuit's formula for unconfined flow uses the difference of squared heads; the confined (Thiem) form uses the plain head difference. Swapping in (h2 - h1) = 4 m gives a far smaller answer.

questions.question: A rectangular channel 3.0 m wide carries 9.0 m^3/s at a flow depth of 1.5 m. What is the specific energy of the flow? (Use alpha = 1.0.)
questions.solution:
Refer to the Specific Energy section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the specific energy \(E\). The handbook prints:

$$E = \frac{\alpha\,V^2}{2g} + y$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
Q &= 9.0\ \text{m}^3\text{/s} \\
B &= 3.0\ \text{m} \\
y &= 1.5\ \text{m} \\
\alpha &= 1.0 \\
g &= 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2 \\
V &= ? \\
E &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

First find the velocity:

$$(V) = \frac{Q}{A} = \frac{9.0}{(3.0)(1.5)}$$

$$(V) = \frac{9.0}{4.5} = 2.0\ \text{m/s}$$

Then the specific energy:

$$(E) = \frac{(1.0)(2.0)^2}{2(9.81)} + 1.5$$

$$(E) = \frac{4.0}{19.62} + 1.5$$

$$(E) = 0.2039 + 1.5 = 1.70\ \text{m}$$

The specific energy is \(1.70\ \text{m}\).
questions.explanation: Specific energy is the velocity head plus the flow depth, measured from the channel bottom. Using g instead of 2g in the velocity head gives 1.91 m.

questions.question: At the status date, a project has BCWP = $90,000 (earned value) and ACWP = $95,000 (actual cost). What is the cost performance index (CPI)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earned-Value Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the cost performance index \(CPI\). The handbook prints:

$$CPI = \frac{BCWP}{ACWP}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
BCWP &= \$90{,}000 \\
ACWP &= \$95{,}000 \\
CPI &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(CPI) = \frac{90{,}000}{95{,}000}$$

$$(CPI) = 0.9474 \approx 0.95$$

The cost performance index is \(0.95\).
questions.explanation: CPI = Earned / Actual, so below 1.0 means over budget (here about 5% over). The $5,000 cost variance (BCWP - ACWP) is a dollar amount, not an index.

questions.question: A project has a budget at completion BAC = $200,000, earned value BCWP = $90,000, and a cost performance index CPI = 0.90. Assuming cost performance continues at the same rate, what is the estimate to complete (ETC)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Earned-Value Analysis section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the estimate to complete \(ETC\). The handbook prints:

$$ETC = \frac{BAC - BCWP}{CPI}$$

List the known and unknown parameters:

$$\begin{aligned}
BAC &= \$200{,}000 \\
BCWP &= \$90{,}000 \\
CPI &= 0.90 \\
ETC &= ?
\end{aligned}$$

$$(ETC) = \frac{200{,}000 - 90{,}000}{0.90}$$

$$(ETC) = \frac{110{,}000}{0.90}$$

$$(ETC) = 122{,}222.22 \approx \$122{,}222$$

The estimate to complete is \(\$122{,}222\).
questions.explanation: ETC divides the remaining budgeted work by the CPI, because at 0.90 efficiency each future dollar of budgeted work costs about $1.11. Using the unadjusted $110,000 assumes efficiency returns to 1.0.

questions.question: A project uses finish-to-start relationships: activity A (4 days) precedes B (5 days) and C (6 days); both B and C precede D (3 days). What is the late start of activity B?
questions.solution:
Refer to the CPM Precedence Relationships section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the late start \(LS_B\). The handbook prints \(LF =\) earliest \(LS\) of successors and \(LS = LF - D\). First run the forward pass to find the project duration:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Path A-B-D} &= 4 + 5 + 3 = 12\ \text{days} \\
\text{Path A-C-D} &= 4 + 6 + 3 = 13\ \text{days}
\end{aligned}$$

The critical path is A-C-D, so the project duration is 13 days. Now run the backward pass from D:

$$(LF_D) = 13, \qquad (LS_D) = 13 - 3 = 10$$

Activity B's only successor is D, so:

$$(LF_B) = LS_D = 10$$

$$(LS_B) = LF_B - D_B$$

$$(LS_B) = 10 - 5 = 5$$

The late start of activity B is day \(5\).
questions.explanation: Backward pass: B inherits its late finish from D's late start (day 10), then subtracts its own 5-day duration. Day 10 is the late finish, not the late start, and day 4 is the late start of C.

Divergence measures the net outflow of a vector field at a point. It is the sum of three partial derivatives, each taken with respect to its own coordinate -- a common slip is differentiating a component with respect to the wrong variable.
questions.question: The vector field is given by F = (x^2 * y, y * z^2, x * z). What is the divergence of F at the point (1, 2, 3)?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Gradient, Divergence, and Curl section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(\\nabla \\cdot \\mathbf{F}\\). The handbook prints:

$$\\nabla \\cdot \\mathbf{F} = \\frac{\\partial P}{\\partial x} + \\frac{\\partial Q}{\\partial y} + \\frac{\\partial R}{\\partial z}$$

Identify the components:

$$\\begin{aligned}
P &= x^2 y \\\\
Q &= y z^2 \\\\
R &= x z
\\end{aligned}$$

Differentiate each component with respect to its own variable:

$$\\begin{aligned}
\\frac{\\partial P}{\\partial x} &= 2xy \\\\
\\frac{\\partial Q}{\\partial y} &= z^2 \\\\
\\frac{\\partial R}{\\partial z} &= x
\\end{aligned}$$

Evaluate at \\((1, 2, 3)\\):

$$\\begin{aligned}
2xy &= 2(1)(2) = 4 \\\\
z^2 &= (3)^2 = 9 \\\\
x &= 1
\\end{aligned}$$

$$(\\nabla \\cdot \\mathbf{F}) = 4 + 9 + 1 = 14$$

questions.explanation: Simpson's rule fits a parabola through each pair of subintervals, so it is exact for polynomials up to degree 3. With n = 2 there is a single parabola through the three points.
questions.question: Use Simpson's rule with n = 2 to approximate the integral of (1/x) dx from x = 1 to x = 3. What is the approximate value?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Simpson's Rule section in the Mathematics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(I\\). For \\(n = 2\\), the handbook prints:

$$\\int_{a}^{b} f(x) \\, dx \\approx \\frac{h}{3}\\,[f(x_0) + 4f(x_1) + f(x_2)]$$

Compute the step size:

$$h = \\frac{b - a}{n} = \\frac{3 - 1}{2} = 1$$

Evaluate the function at the three nodes:

$$\\begin{aligned}
f(x_0) &= f(1) = \\frac{1}{1} = 1 \\\\
f(x_1) &= f(2) = \\frac{1}{2} = 0.5 \\\\
f(x_2) &= f(3) = \\frac{1}{3} \\approx 0.3333
\\end{aligned}$$

Apply Simpson's rule:

$$(I) \\approx \\frac{1}{3}\\,[1 + 4(0.5) + 0.3333]$$

$$(I) \\approx \\frac{1}{3}(3.3333) \\approx 1.111$$

questions.explanation: The correlation coefficient standardizes the covariance by the two standard deviations, so it always lies between -1 and 1. A value near 1 means the points lie close to a rising line.
questions.question: Four paired observations are (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 5), and (4, 4). What is the sample correlation coefficient R?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Sample Correlation Coefficient section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(R\\). The handbook prints:

$$R = \\frac{S_{xy}}{\\sqrt{S_{xx} \\, S_{yy}}}$$

Compute the means:

$$\\begin{aligned}
\\bar{x} &= \\frac{1 + 2 + 3 + 4}{4} = 2.5 \\\\
\\bar{y} &= \\frac{2 + 3 + 5 + 4}{4} = 3.5
\\end{aligned}$$

Compute the sums of squares and cross-products:

$$\\begin{aligned}
S_{xy} &= (-1.5)(-1.5) + (-0.5)(-0.5) + (0.5)(1.5) + (1.5)(0.5) = 4.0 \\\\
S_{xx} &= (-1.5)^2 + (-0.5)^2 + (0.5)^2 + (1.5)^2 = 5.0 \\\\
S_{yy} &= (-1.5)^2 + (-0.5)^2 + (1.5)^2 + (0.5)^2 = 5.0
\\end{aligned}$$

$$(R) = \\frac{4.0}{\\sqrt{(5.0)(5.0)}} = \\frac{4.0}{5.0} = 0.80$$

questions.explanation: The least-squares line always passes through the point of the two means. Once the slope is known, the intercept is forced by that single fact.
questions.question: Three data points (1, 3), (2, 5), and (3, 7) are fit with the least-squares line y = a + bx. What is the intercept a?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Linear Regression and Goodness of Fit section in the Engineering Probability and Statistics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(a\\). The handbook prints the intercept as:

$$a = \\bar{y} - b\\bar{x}$$

Compute the means:

$$\\begin{aligned}
\\bar{x} &= \\frac{1 + 2 + 3}{3} = 2 \\\\
\\bar{y} &= \\frac{3 + 5 + 7}{3} = 5
\\end{aligned}$$

Compute the slope:

$$b = \\frac{\\sum (x_i - \\bar{x})(y_i - \\bar{y})}{\\sum (x_i - \\bar{x})^2} = \\frac{(-1)(-2) + (0)(0) + (1)(2)}{1 + 0 + 1} = \\frac{4}{2} = 2$$

$$(a) = 5 - (2)(2) = 1$$

questions.explanation: A Gerber beam is solved from the free end inward: analyze the secondary segment first to find the hinge force, then apply it reversed to the primary segment. The hinge transmits force but no moment.
questions.question: A compound beam has segment AB with a pin support at A (x = 0 m) and a roller at B (x = 6 m). Segment BD is connected by an internal hinge at B, rests on a roller at C (x = 10 m), and carries a 10 kN downward load at D (x = 12 m). Segment AB carries a uniform load of 2 kN/m over its full length. What is the vertical reaction at the pin support A?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Equilibrium Requirements section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(A_y\\). Start with the free-body diagram of the secondary segment BD (hinge at B, roller at C, 10 kN at D):

$$\\sum M_B = 0: \\quad C_y(4) - 10(6) = 0$$

$$(C_y) = \\frac{60}{4} = 15 \\text{ kN (upward)}$$

$$\\sum F_y = 0: \\quad B_y + 15 - 10 = 0$$

$$(B_y) = -5 \\text{ kN}$$

The hinge pulls downward on segment BD with 5 kN, so it pushes upward on segment AB with 5 kN.

Now draw segment AB: pin at A, roller at B, uniform load \\((2 \\text{ kN/m})(6 \\text{ m}) = 12 \\text{ kN}\\) at \\(x = 3 \\text{ m}\\), and the 5 kN hinge force upward at B.

$$\\sum M_A = 0: \\quad R_B(6) + 5(6) - 12(3) = 0$$

$$(R_B) = \\frac{36 - 30}{6} = 1 \\text{ kN (upward)}$$

$$\\sum F_y = 0: \\quad A_y + 1 + 5 - 12 = 0$$

$$(A_y) = 6 \\text{ kN (upward)}$$

questions.explanation: The resultant of parallel forces is their algebraic sum, and its position comes from Varignon's theorem: the moment of the resultant about any point equals the sum of the moments of the components.
questions.question: Three parallel downward forces of 10 kN, 20 kN, and 30 kN act at x = 1 m, x = 4 m, and x = 7 m along a horizontal bar. What is the resultant force, and how far is its line of action from the 10 kN force?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Resultant (Two Dimensions) section in the Statics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(R\\) and its location. The resultant magnitude is the sum of the parallel forces:

$$(R) = 10 + 20 + 30 = 60 \\text{ kN (downward)}$$

Take moments about the origin (\\(x = 0\\)) to locate the resultant at \\(\\bar{x}\\):

$$R\\,\\bar{x} = 10(1) + 20(4) + 30(7)$$

$$60\\,\\bar{x} = 10 + 80 + 210 = 300$$

$$(\\bar{x}) = \\frac{300}{60} = 5 \\text{ m from the origin}$$

The 10 kN force acts at \\(x = 1 \\text{ m}\\), so the distance from it is:

$$(d) = 5 - 1 = 4 \\text{ m}$$
questions.subtopic: Resultant of a parallel force system

questions.explanation: The instant center sits where the perpendiculars to the two known velocity directions meet. Every point's speed is the angular velocity times its distance from the instant center.
questions.question: A rigid bar AB, 2 m long, has end A constrained to horizontal motion and end B constrained to vertical motion. At the instant the bar makes 60 degrees with the horizontal, end A moves to the right at 6 m/s. Using the instantaneous center method, what is the velocity of end B?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Instantaneous Center of Rotation section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(v_B\\). Place A at the origin: \\(A = (0, 0)\\), so \\(B = (2\\cos 60^\\circ, 2\\sin 60^\\circ) = (1, 1.732) \\text{ m}\\).

The perpendicular to \\(v_A\\) (horizontal) through A is the vertical line \\(x = 0\\); the perpendicular to \\(v_B\\) (vertical) through B is the horizontal line \\(y = 1.732 \\text{ m}\\).

$$(IC) = (0, 1.732) \\text{ m}$$

The angular velocity about the instant center is:

$$\\omega = \\frac{v_A}{d_{IC \\to A}} = \\frac{6}{1.732} = 3.464 \\text{ rad/s}$$

The speed of B is:

$$(v_B) = \\omega \\, d_{IC \\to B} = (3.464)(1) = 3.46 \\text{ m/s}$$

Point A moves right while directly below the IC, so the rotation is clockwise; point B, to the right of the IC, therefore moves downward.

$$(v_B) = 3.46 \\text{ m/s downward}$$

questions.explanation: Angular impulse and momentum is the rotational twin of linear impulse and momentum: a moment acting over time changes the angular momentum. For a constant moment, the integral is just moment times time.
questions.question: A 10-kg solid disk of radius 0.30 m spins on a frictionless axle and is initially at rest. A constant couple moment of 5 N-m is applied for 4 s. What is the angular velocity of the disk at the end of the 4 s?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Principle of Angular Impulse and Momentum section in the Dynamics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(\\omega_2\\). The handbook prints:

$$\\int_{t_1}^{t_2} M \\, dt = I\\omega_2 - I\\omega_1$$

For a constant couple moment starting from rest:

$$M\\Delta t = I\\omega_2$$

The mass moment of inertia of a solid disk about its central axle is:

$$(I) = \\frac{1}{2}mr^2 = \\frac{1}{2}(10)(0.30)^2 = 0.45 \\text{ kg-m}^2$$

$$(\\omega_2) = \\frac{M\\Delta t}{I} = \\frac{(5)(4)}{0.45} = \\frac{20}{0.45} \\approx 44.4 \\text{ rad/s}$$

questions.explanation: The handbook prints separate formulas for hoop and axial stress in a cylindrical vessel. The axial stress is half the hoop stress because the end-cap force acts on twice the wall area of the hoop section.
questions.question: A thin-walled cylindrical pressure vessel with end caps has an inner radius of 0.40 m and a wall thickness of 12 mm. It holds gas at an internal pressure of 1.5 MPa. What is the axial stress in the wall?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Cylindrical Pressure Vessel section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(\\sigma_a\\). The handbook prints:

$$\\sigma_a = \\frac{Pr}{2t}$$

Convert the thickness to meters:

$$(t) = 12 \\text{ mm} = 0.012 \\text{ m}$$

$$(\\sigma_a) = \\frac{(1.5 \\times 10^6)(0.40)}{2(0.012)} = \\frac{600{,}000}{0.024} = 25{,}000{,}000 \\text{ Pa} = 25 \\text{ MPa}$$

questions.explanation: In a stepped shaft each segment twists by its own TL/(GJ) and the twists add, because the free end rotates by the accumulated twist of every segment. The smaller-diameter segment dominates since J scales with diameter to the fourth power.
questions.question: A steel shaft (G = 79 GPa) is fixed at one end and consists of two segments in series: segment 1 has diameter 50 mm and length 1.0 m, and segment 2 has diameter 40 mm and length 1.5 m. A torque of 2 kN-m is applied at the free end. What is the total angle of twist at the free end, in radians?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Torsion section in the Mechanics of Materials chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(\\phi\\). The handbook prints:

$$\\phi = \\frac{TL}{GJ}$$

The polar moment of inertia of a solid circular shaft is:

$$J = \\frac{\\pi d^4}{32}$$

Compute each segment's polar moment of inertia:

$$\\begin{aligned}
J_1 &= \\frac{\\pi (0.050)^4}{32} = 6.136 \\times 10^{-7} \\text{ m}^4 \\\\
J_2 &= \\frac{\\pi (0.040)^4}{32} = 2.513 \\times 10^{-7} \\text{ m}^4
\\end{aligned}$$

Twist of each segment (the full 2 kN-m acts in both segments):

$$\\begin{aligned}
\\phi_1 &= \\frac{(2000)(1.0)}{(79 \\times 10^9)(6.136 \\times 10^{-7})} = 0.0413 \\text{ rad} \\\\
\\phi_2 &= \\frac{(2000)(1.5)}{(79 \\times 10^9)(2.513 \\times 10^{-7})} = 0.1511 \\text{ rad}
\\end{aligned}$$

$$(\\phi) = \\phi_1 + \\phi_2 = 0.0413 + 0.1511 = 0.192 \\text{ rad}$$

questions.explanation: The Buckingham Pi theorem turns a dimensional guessing game into a counting exercise: list the variables, count the fundamental dimensions they span, and the difference is the number of pi groups.
questions.question: The drag force F on a sphere is assumed to depend on the fluid density rho, the approach velocity V, the sphere diameter D, and the fluid dynamic viscosity mu. Using the M-L-T system, how many independent dimensionless pi terms are needed to describe this relationship?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Dimensional Analysis section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the number of pi terms. The handbook prints the Buckingham Pi Theorem:

$$\\text{number of } \\pi \\text{ terms} = n - k$$

Count the variables: \\(F\\), \\(\\rho\\), \\(V\\), \\(D\\), \\(\\mu\\).

$$(n) = 5$$

Count the independent fundamental dimensions spanned (M, L, T):

$$(k) = 3$$

$$(\\text{pi terms}) = 5 - 3 = 2$$

questions.explanation: A siphon is just the energy equation between the reservoir surface and the outlet. The reservoir is large, so its surface velocity is negligible, and both points are at atmospheric pressure.
questions.question: A siphon discharges water from a large reservoir. The reservoir surface is 5.0 m above the siphon outlet, and the total head loss through the siphon is 1.5 m of water. What is the velocity at the outlet?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Bernoulli Equation section in the Fluid Mechanics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(V_2\\). Write the energy equation from the reservoir surface (1) to the outlet (2):

$$z_1 = \\frac{p_2}{\\gamma} + \\frac{V_2^2}{2g} + z_2 + h_L$$

Both points are at atmospheric pressure and the reservoir surface velocity is negligible, so with the outlet as the datum:

$$5.0 = \\frac{V_2^2}{2(9.81)} + 0 + 1.5$$

$$\\frac{V_2^2}{19.62} = 5.0 - 1.5 = 3.5$$

$$(V_2) = \\sqrt{19.62 \\times 3.5} = \\sqrt{68.67} = 8.29 \\text{ m/s}$$

questions.explanation: Normal depth is the depth where Manning's equation reproduces the given discharge. For a triangular section both area and wetted perimeter are simple powers of depth, so the equation can be solved directly for depth.
questions.question: A triangular channel with side slopes 2H:1V carries 3.0 m^3/s on a bed slope of 0.001. Manning's n is 0.013. What is the normal depth?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Manning's Equation section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(y_n\\). The handbook prints (SI units):

$$Q = \\frac{1}{n} A R^{2/3} S^{1/2}$$

For a triangular channel with side slope \\(m = 2\\):

$$\\begin{aligned}
A &= m y^2 = 2y^2 \\\\
P &= 2y\\sqrt{1 + m^2} = 2y\\sqrt{5} \\\\
R &= \\frac{A}{P} = \\frac{2y^2}{2y\\sqrt{5}} = \\frac{y}{\\sqrt{5}}
\\end{aligned}$$

Substitute into Manning's equation:

$$3.0 = \\frac{1}{0.013} (2y^2) \\left(\\frac{y}{\\sqrt{5}}\\right)^{2/3} (0.001)^{1/2}$$

$$3.0 = \\left(\\frac{2\\sqrt{0.001}}{0.013 \\times 5^{1/3}}\\right) y^{8/3} = 2.841 \\, y^{8/3}$$

$$(y^{8/3}) = \\frac{3.0}{2.841} = 1.056$$

$$(y_n) = 1.056^{3/8} = 1.02 \\text{ m}$$

questions.explanation: The critical slope is the bed slope that would make the given discharge flow at critical depth. Find the critical depth first, then ask Manning's equation which slope produces the same discharge at that depth.
questions.question: A rectangular channel 3.0 m wide carries 9.0 m^3/s with Manning's n = 0.015. What is the critical slope?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Manning's Equation and Specific Energy sections in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(S_c\\). First find the critical depth for a rectangular channel:

$$y_c = \\left(\\frac{q^2}{g}\\right)^{1/3}$$

$$q = \\frac{9.0}{3.0} = 3.0 \\text{ m}^2\\text{/s}$$

$$(y_c) = \\left(\\frac{3.0^2}{9.81}\\right)^{1/3} = (0.9174)^{1/3} = 0.9717 \\text{ m}$$

At critical depth:

$$\\begin{aligned}
A_c &= (3.0)(0.9717) = 2.915 \\text{ m}^2 \\\\
P_c &= 3.0 + 2(0.9717) = 4.943 \\text{ m} \\\\
R_c &= \\frac{2.915}{4.943} = 0.5897 \\text{ m}
\\end{aligned}$$

Now set Manning's equation equal to the discharge and solve for the slope:

$$9.0 = \\frac{1}{0.015} (2.915)(0.5897)^{2/3} S_c^{1/2}$$

$$(S_c^{1/2}) = \\frac{9.0 \\times 0.015}{2.915 \\times 0.7025} = 0.06593$$

$$(S_c) = (0.06593)^2 = 0.00434$$

questions.explanation: The gradation coefficients describe the shape of the grain-size curve: Cu measures its spread and Cc measures its curvature. Together they decide whether a coarse soil is well graded or poorly graded.
questions.question: A sieve analysis gives D10 = 0.10 mm, D30 = 0.40 mm, and D60 = 1.20 mm for a sand. What is the coefficient of curvature Cc?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Coefficient of concavity (or curvature) section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(C_c\\). The handbook prints:

$$C_c = \\frac{(D_{30})^2}{D_{10} \\times D_{60}}$$

$$(C_c) = \\frac{(0.40)^2}{(0.10)(1.20)} = \\frac{0.16}{0.12} = 1.33$$

questions.explanation: At-rest pressure applies when the soil cannot strain laterally -- the natural state of a flat ground surface. For normally consolidated soils the handbook gives K0 directly from the friction angle.
questions.question: A 5-m-thick deposit of normally consolidated clean sand has a total unit weight of 18 kN/m^3 and an effective friction angle of 30 degrees. The water table is below the deposit. What is the horizontal effective stress at 5 m depth?
questions.solution:
Refer to the At-Rest Earth Pressure section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(\\sigma'_h\\). The handbook prints, for normally consolidated soil:

$$K_0 \\approx 1 - \\sin\\phi'$$

$$(K_0) = 1 - \\sin 30^\\circ = 1 - 0.5 = 0.5$$

The vertical effective stress at 5 m (no pore pressure, water table below):

$$(\\sigma'_v) = (18)(5) = 90 \\text{ kPa}$$

$$(\\sigma'_h) = K_0 \\, \\sigma'_v = (0.5)(90) = 45 \\text{ kPa}$$

questions.explanation: The unit load method is virtual work for trusses: apply a dummy unit load at the point of interest, multiply real and virtual member forces member by member, and sum nNL/AE. Tension-positive signs take care of themselves.
questions.question: A truss has joints A(0,0) pinned, B(6,0) on a roller, and C(3,4) carrying a 200 kN downward load. Members AC and BC are each 5 m long, and member AB is 6 m long. All members have AE = 100 MN. Using the unit load method, what is the vertical deflection at C?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Truss Deflection by Unit Load Method section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(\\Delta_C\\). The handbook prints:

$$\\Delta = \\sum \\frac{nNL}{AE}$$

Reactions for the real 200 kN load: \\(A_y = B_y = 100 \\text{ kN}\\).

Member forces \\(N\\) (tension positive) by joint equilibrium:

$$\\begin{aligned}
N_{AC} &= -\\frac{100}{\\sin 53.13^\\circ} = -125 \\text{ kN} \\\\
N_{BC} &= -125 \\text{ kN (by symmetry)} \\\\
N_{AB} &= 125\\cos 53.13^\\circ = 75 \\text{ kN}
\\end{aligned}$$

Apply a dummy 1 kN downward load at C; the virtual forces \\(n\\) scale by \\(1/200\\):

$$\\begin{aligned}
n_{AC} &= n_{BC} = -\\frac{125}{200} = -0.625 \\\\
n_{AB} &= \\frac{75}{200} = 0.375
\\end{aligned}$$

$$(\\Delta_C) = \\frac{2(-0.625)(-125)(5) + (0.375)(75)(6)}{100{,}000} = \\frac{781.25 + 168.75}{100{,}000}$$

$$(\\Delta_C) = \\frac{950}{100{,}000} = 0.0095 \\text{ m} = 9.50 \\text{ mm (downward)}$$

questions.explanation: Fixed-end moments are the starting point of slope-deflection and moment distribution. For the common cases the handbook tabulates them, so no integration is needed.
questions.question: A prismatic beam fixed at both ends spans 6 m and carries a uniform load of 10 kN/m over its entire length. What is the fixed-end moment at each support?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Member Fixed-End Moments section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(FEM\\). The handbook prints, for a uniform load on a fixed-fixed beam:

$$FEM = \\frac{wL^2}{12}$$

$$(FEM) = \\frac{(10)(6)^2}{12} = \\frac{360}{12} = 30 \\text{ kN-m}$$

The moments are equal at both ends (hogging at the supports).

questions.explanation: The balance after any payment is the present worth of the payments still owed -- never the original principal minus payments made, because each payment is part interest. Work forward to the payment, then discount the remaining ones.
questions.question: A $50,000 loan at 6% annual interest is repaid with 10 equal end-of-year payments. What is the remaining balance immediately after the 4th payment?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for the balance \\(B_4\\). First find the annual payment with the capital recovery factor:

$$A = P(A/P, i, n) = 50{,}000 \\left[\\frac{0.06(1.06)^{10}}{(1.06)^{10} - 1}\\right]$$

$$(A) = 50{,}000(0.13587) = 6{,}793.36$$

The balance after 4 payments is the present worth of the 6 remaining payments:

$$B_4 = A(P/A, i, 6) = 6{,}793.36 \\left[\\frac{(1.06)^6 - 1}{0.06(1.06)^6}\\right]$$

$$(B_4) = 6{,}793.36(4.91732) = 33{,}405 \\approx \\$33{,}400$$

questions.explanation: MACRS depreciation uses statutory recovery percentages, not the straight-line formula. Book value is always cost minus accumulated depreciation, whatever method produced the depreciation.
questions.question: A $20,000 asset is classified as 5-year MACRS property. What is its book value at the end of year 2?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Depreciation section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(BV_2\\). The handbook's MACRS table gives, for 5-year property:

$$\\begin{aligned}
\\text{Year 1 rate} &= 20.00\\% \\\\
\\text{Year 2 rate} &= 32.00\\%
\\end{aligned}$$

Accumulated depreciation through year 2:

$$(D_{acc}) = 20{,}000(0.2000 + 0.3200) = 20{,}000(0.52) = 10{,}400$$

Book value is cost minus accumulated depreciation:

$$(BV_2) = 20{,}000 - 10{,}400 = 9{,}600$$
