questions.explanation: Engineering strain divides elongation by the original length, but true strain accumulates each incremental stretch against the current length. The two agree at small strains and diverge as deformation grows.
questions.question: A tensile specimen elongates 25% before necking begins. What is the true strain at the onset of necking?
questions.solution:
Refer to the True strain section in the Materials Science/Structure of Matter chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(\\varepsilon_T\\). The handbook prints:

$$\\varepsilon_T = \\ln(1 + \\varepsilon)$$

The engineering strain is:

$$(\\varepsilon) = 0.25$$

$$(\\varepsilon_T) = \\ln(1 + 0.25) = \\ln(1.25) = 0.223$$

questions.explanation: Degree of curve and radius are inversely related: a sharper curve has a larger degree. The constant 5729.58 ft comes from the arc length of one degree on a 100-ft arc.
questions.question: A horizontal curve has a radius of 500 ft. Using the arc definition, what is the degree of curve?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Horizontal Curves section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(D\\). The handbook prints, for the arc definition:

$$D = \\frac{5729.58}{R}$$

$$(D) = \\frac{5729.58}{500} = 11.46^\\circ$$

questions.explanation: Straight-line depreciation spreads the depreciable amount evenly over the life. Salvage value is never depreciated -- only cost minus salvage is.
questions.question: Equipment purchased for $12,000 has an estimated salvage value of $2,000 and a 4-year useful life. Using straight-line depreciation, what is the book value at the end of year 2?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Depreciation section in the Engineering Economics chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(BV_2\\). The handbook prints the straight-line annual depreciation:

$$D = \\frac{C - S}{N}$$

$$(D) = \\frac{12{,}000 - 2{,}000}{4} = \\frac{10{,}000}{4} = 2{,}500 \\text{ per year}$$

Book value is cost minus accumulated depreciation:

$$(BV_2) = 12{,}000 - 2(2{,}500) = 12{,}000 - 5{,}000 = 7{,}000$$

questions.explanation: The all-red interval lets a vehicle that legally entered at the end of yellow clear the intersection before cross traffic starts. Convert the approach speed to ft/s first -- mixing mph with feet is the classic error here.
questions.question: At a signalized intersection, the curb-to-curb width is 60 ft, the design vehicle is 20 ft long, and the approach speed is 45 mph. What is the all-red clearance interval?
questions.solution:
Refer to the Traffic Signal Timing section in the Civil Engineering chapter of the FE Reference Handbook (v10.6).

Ultimately, we must solve for \\(r\\). The handbook prints:

$$r = \\frac{W + l}{v}$$

Convert the approach speed to ft/s:

$$(v) = 45 \\text{ mph} \\times 1.46667 = 66 \\text{ ft/s}$$

$$(r) = \\frac{60 + 20}{66} = \\frac{80}{66} = 1.21 \\text{ s} \\approx 1.2 \\text{ s}$$

choices: Seal them after checking the title block
Refuse to seal work not prepared under his responsible charge
Seal them since the other firm employs licensed engineers
Seal them with a written disclaimer of authorship
questions.explanation: A seal is a certification of professional responsibility, not a rubber stamp. The NSPE Code ties sealing to responsible charge -- direct supervision or thorough review -- and no disclaimer cures its absence.
questions.question: A licensed engineer is asked by a client to sign and seal drawings prepared by another firm's engineers, whom the engineer has never supervised or reviewed. What is the ethical course of action?
questions.solution:
This question is governed by the NSPE Code of Ethics (adopted by NCEES model rules), not by a handbook equation.

Ultimately, we must decide whether sealing is permitted. The Code requires engineers to approve and seal only design documents prepared under their responsible charge.

The engineer neither supervised nor reviewed the other firm's work.

Therefore the engineer must refuse to seal the drawings.

Checking the title block, relying on the other firm's licenses, or adding a disclaimer does not create responsible charge.

The ethical course is to refuse to seal work not prepared under his responsible charge.
